title: Web UI Port issue 4040
description:
I'm having difficulty accessing Spark's web interface through `sparklyr`.

When I run the following code it opens a webpage (http://localhost:4040/jobs/) which has an error: **Firefox can’t establish a connection to the server at localhost:4040.** 

```
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.3") # create active Spark Connection
spark_web(sc) # access the web application interface
```

According to the ?`spark_connect()` man page you can specify `master = spark://HOST:PORT`. Our IT specialist confirmed that the HOST:PORT is 172.100.100.101:8081 (and that the port _is_ open with _netstat_).

However, when I run `sc <- spark_connect(master = "spark://172.100.100.101:8081")` I get the following error:
> Error in shell_connection(master = master, spark_home = spark_home, app_name = app_name, : Failed to connect to Spark (SPARK_HOME is not set).

Okay this shouldn't be a big problem as I can find the path with `spark_installed_versions()`:

Then set `SPARK_HOME` via: `Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = "/exports/meaney.lab/moldach/spark/spark-2.3.3-bin-hadoop2.7")`

description: There is a small typo on the documentation of the function `ml_generalized_linear_regression` on version `0.8.4`. When the family is chosen as `binomial` the link function available is not `loglog` (as written in the help), but the complementary loglog, `cloglog`.

title: `spark_apply(columns = )` rejects the named vector its documentation promises; only an undocumented DDL string works
description:
`?spark_apply` documents `columns` as "a vector of column names or a named vector of column types".
Under `spark_connect(method = "databricks_connect")` that named-vector form fails, and so does the
named-list equivalent. What works is a Spark DDL string, which the argument's documentation never
mentions.

The workaround is easy once you know it, so this is not a blocker. What costs time is the
diagnosis: neither error names the argument at fault, and one of them surfaces a PySpark internal
that appears nowhere in `spark_apply()`'s documentation. Both failures look like a problem with your
function or your data, and they are neither.

### Observed vs expected

| `columns = ` | Result |
|---|---|
| omitted entirely | works, schema inferred |
| `list(id = "character", m = "double")`, the named-list equivalent | `Error: non-character argument` |
| `c(id = "character", m = "double")`, **the documented form** | `PySparkTypeError: [NOT_DATATYPE_OR_STR] Argument `returnType` should be a DataType or str, got list.` |
| `"id string, m double"`, a DDL string | works |
| `"id STRING, m DOUBLE"` | works |

Expected: the second and third rows either work, or fail with an error that names `columns` and
says a DDL string is wanted.

Two controls, so this is not a general transport fault. With `columns` omitted the same function
returns correct results, and a worker-side probe reported R 4.3.2 across 4 distinct PIDs, so R is
running on the cluster as expected.

### Where it happens

`R/sparklyr-spark-apply.R:122`, in `sa_in_pandas()`:

```r
fields <- unlist(strsplit(.schema, ","))
col_names <- map_chr(fields, \(.x) unlist(strsplit(trimws(.x), " "))[[1]])
```

That line assumes `.schema` is a single DDL string, and nothing checks the assumption:

- a **named list** makes `strsplit()` signal `non-character argument` before Spark is contacted, which is why the message names neither the argument nor the expected type
- a **named character vector** splits on the values instead, so `col_names` becomes `"character", "double"`, the types rather than the names, and `.schema` reaches `mapInPandas(schema = )` as a vector, which PySpark rejects

The same function's inference branch builds a DDL string and then tells you to
`use the following schema: columns = "id string, m double"`. So the package's own advice is already
the DDL form; the documented named-vector form is the outlier.

### Reproducible example

Four rows of local data, no catalogue table and no warehouse. Needs only a cluster you can reach,
with `DATABRICKS_CLUSTER_ID` set.

```r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

sc <- spark_connect(
  method = "databricks_connect",
  cluster_id = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_CLUSTER_ID")
)

local_df <- data.frame(id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"), m = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5))
tbl <- copy_to(sc, local_df, name = "reprex_df", overwrite = TRUE)

f <- function(df) data.frame(id = df$id, m = df$m * 2)

spark_apply(tbl, f) |> collect()                                          # works
spark_apply(tbl, f, columns = list(id = "character", m = "double")) |> collect()  # non-character argument
spark_apply(tbl, f, columns = c(id = "character", m = "double")) |> collect()     # NOT_DATATYPE_OR_STR
spark_apply(tbl, f, columns = "id string, m double") |> collect()          # works
```

### Versions

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| R | 4.5.2 |
| `sparklyr` | 1.9.5 |
| `pysparklyr` | 0.2.2 |
| DBR | 15.4, Dedicated / `SINGLE_USER` |
| Worker R | 4.3.2 |

Both packages are at the current CRAN release, and `R/sparklyr-spark-apply.R:122` is unchanged on
`main`, so this is not fixed in the development version either.

### Suggested resolutions, in the maintainers' hands

Any one of these would have saved the diagnosis:

- accept the documented named vector and translate it to DDL inside `sa_in_pandas()`
- validate `.schema` and raise an error naming `columns` and the DDL form it wants
- document the DDL string as the accepted form, and note the restriction on this connection method

I have not tested whether `spark_connect(method = "databricks")` or a local Spark behave the same
way, so I cannot say how far this reaches beyond `databricks_connect`.

title: "Subscript out of bounds" when attempting to run collected data from `sdf_sql()` to Databricks
description:
Hello!

I'm having an issue where when I try to access data from our Databricks instance I receive an error instead of the data.

Here's an example of the kinds of code I'm using:

```
library(sparklyr)

sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(
  cluster_id = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_CLUSTER_ID"),
  method     = "databricks_connect"
)

df_string <- "<sql query here>"

df_data <- sdf_sql(sc, df_string)

df <- collect(df_data)
```

But when I get to the final `collect()` step, instead of the data being returned, I receive `Error in x[[1]] : subscript out of bounds`.

I haven't had to do this in a while, so I'm not sure how long this issue has been going on.

description:

I am trying to append to a table, but since the table do not exists in the first iteration of the process (say it is a daily process), it fails.

I running this code on the latest Databricks LTS runtime (17.3 with Scala 2.13)

```{r}

# Environment: Databricks + sparklyr

library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

# Connect to Spark
sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

catalog_name <- "my_catalog"

# Sample data
my_data <- copy_to(sc, data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  value = c(10, 20, 30)
))

spark_write_table(

  name = sprintf("`%s`.`curated`.`my_table`", catalog_name),

When `mode = "append"` is used with a non-existent table, it should create the table first, then append the data (similar to mode = "overwrite" behavior for new tables). At least, the documentation is a bit ambiguous and you could understand that this expected behavior is actually the case.

title: Unable to connect `sparklyr` to remote Kubernetes Spark cluster (EMR on EKS)
description:
Hi folks.

I'm trying to connect to a remote Kubernetes-based Spark cluster (AWS EMR on EKS) from R using `sparklyr`, but keep running into connection errors. The equivalent PySpark code works as expected. I'm not sure if this is a limitation of `sparklyr` with Kubernetes deployments or if I'm missing something in my configuration.

## What I'm trying to do

### Python Code (Works)
This PySpark code successfully connects to my remote Kubernetes cluster:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .master("k8s://https://<myurl>:443") \
    .appName("TestConnection") \
    .config("spark.kubernetes.container.image", "<my-spark-image>") \
    .config("spark.executor.instances", "2") \
    .config("spark.executor.memory", "4g") \
    .config("spark.executor.cores", "2") \
    .getOrCreate()

sc = spark.sparkContext
```

This works perfectly. It connects to the Kubernetes API server, spawns executor pods, and I can run queries.

### R Code (Fails)
Unfortunately, I come unstuck with the following R equivalent:

```r
library(sparklyr)

sc = spark_connect(
  master = "k8s://https://<myurl>:443",
  spark_home = "/usr/lib/spark",
  config = list(
    spark.kubernetes.container.image = "<my-spark-image>",
    spark.executor.instances = 2,
    spark.executor.memory = "4g",
    spark.executor.cores = 2
  )
)
```

**Error:**
```
Error in spark_connect_gateway(gatewayAddress, gatewayPort, sessionId, ...) : 
  Gateway in localhost:8880 did not respond.


Try running `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)` followed by `sc <- spark_connect(...)` for more debugging info.
```

Side note: Running `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)` didn't actually give me any more info.

## My understanding (with help from Claude)

I must admit that I'm a bit out of my comfort zone here, so I tried to troubleshoot further with Claude 4.5 Sonnet. See the summary below, although I can't speak to it's full accuracy.

**Claude's Technical Summary:**

The issue appears to be an architectural difference between `sparklyr` and PySpark:

1. **sparklyr's Gateway Architecture**: `sparklyr` tries to start a local gateway process on `localhost:8880` that acts as a bridge between R and Spark. This architecture works for local, YARN, and Mesos deployments.

2. **Kubernetes Client Mode**: When connecting to a Kubernetes cluster with a `k8s://` master URL, the driver needs to run locally and communicate directly with the Kubernetes API server to spawn executor pods. There's no intermediate gateway in this model.

3. **The Mismatch**: `sparklyr` attempts to start its gateway and wait for a response, but the gateway can't establish a connection to a remote Kubernetes cluster. The connection fails before any Spark application is created.

PySpark works because the Python process becomes the Spark driver directly and communicates with Kubernetes natively, without needing a gateway.

## Questions

1. **Is this a known limitation?** Does `sparklyr` currently support connecting to remote Kubernetes Spark clusters?
2. **Am I doing something wrong?** Is there a different way I should be configuring the connection?
3. **Are there workarounds?**
   - Should I rather be using `pysparklyr` / `reticulate`?

Any guidance would be much appreciated. Happy to provide more info RE my setup as needed. Thanks in advance!

title: ml_load() throws java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Cannot access the UC Volume path
description:
Problem:
- ml_load() fails on Unity Catalog Volume paths (/Volumes/...) with IllegalArgumentException.

Root cause:
- Legacy SparkContext.textFile(...) path handling can treat /Volumes as local/driver FS and fail access checks.
- Spark SQL DataFrameReader is UC-aware and resolves /Volumes correctly.

Fix:
- Prefer Spark JSON glob: file.path(path, 'metadata', 'part-*'), parse class, then class.load(path).
- Keep original textFile('part-00*') as fallback for backward-compat.

Tests:
- tests/testthat/test-ml-load.R covers happy path (glob) and forced-failure fallback.

No API/behavior change for non-UC paths.

title: `Error in get(x) : object 'unknown' not found`
description:
Issue occurs when `dials` is loaded into the R session:

```r
library(parsnip)
library(modeldata)
library(dials)
library(sparklyr)

data("hpc_data")
ctrl          <- control_parsnip(verbosity = 1, catch = FALSE)
hpc <- hpc_data[1:150, c(2:5, 8)]


sc <- try(spark_connect(master = "local"), silent = TRUE)

hpc_bt_tr <- copy_to(sc, hpc[-(1:4),   ], "hpc_bt_tr", overwrite = TRUE)
hpc_bt_te <- copy_to(sc, hpc[  1:4 , -1], "hpc_bt_te", overwrite = TRUE)

spark_reg_fit <-
  fit(
    boost_tree(trees = 5, mode = "regression") %>%
      set_engine("spark", seed = 12),
    control = ctrl,
    compounds ~ .,
    data = hpc_bt_tr
  )

spark_reg_pred <- predict(spark_reg_fit, hpc_bt_te)
#> Error in fn(0): unused argument (0)
```

The root cause is that `dials` has an exported function named `unknown()` which makes is accidentally called by https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/main/R/utils.R#L493, and trying to call `unknown(0)`, which is what in effect the error returned. Patch forthcoming

title: Package doesn't seem to pick up auth settings in `.databrickscfg`
description:
I've previously been using pyspark and authenticating using the Databricks CLI with my auth settings defined in `~/.databrickscfg`. I'm now experimenting with sparklyr and noticed that these settings don't seem to be picked up when I run `spark_connect(method = "databricks_connect")`. Perhaps this is an issue on my end, as the [documentation](https://spark.posit.co/deployment/databricks-connect.html#setup-credentials) does note Databricks configuration profiles as being supported:

> How do I actually “set” my credentials? There are two options to provide your credential information (PAT, Host, user name, Resource ID, etc.):
>
> Set environment variables in your R session. There are some best practices to set those variables found in the [Environment Variables](https://spark.posit.co/deployment/databricks-connect.html?q=authentication#environment-variables) section
> 
> Create and use a [Databricks Configuration Profile](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/auth/config-profiles) file (.databrickscfg).

An easy workaround is for me to simply create some environmental variables with my credentials, but it would be nice to be able to manage them using profiles if possible.

Thank you!

title: Issue with SQL translation for ARRAY type spark SQL function args
description:
My use case here is that I want to compute several percentile values using the [Spark SQL `approx_percentile()` function](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/sql/#approx_percentile). So I want to use the `approx_percentile(COLUMN, ARRAY<DOUBLE>)` signature.

### Setup

First, some reprex setup:
``` r
# sc <- spark_connect(...)
iris_spk <- copy_to(sc, iris)

quantiles <- c(0.5, 0.9)
quantiles_array_string <- paste0("array(", paste0(quantiles, collapse = ", "), ")")
quantiles_array_string
#> [1] "array(0.5, 0.9)"
```

### Ways this can be done

I found 2 methods that work, but neither is ideal. 

First, I got it to work when using `array(literal, numbers, here)` like in the following.
This gets annoying and very verbose when you want many (e.g., 1 percentage increments) percentiles of several different variables though.

```r
# works, but need to write out quantile values
success_mode1 <- iris_spk |> 
  summarize(q = approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, array(0.5, 0.9)))

success_mode1 |> sdf_unnest_longer(q)
#> Warning in arrow_collect(object, ...): NAs introduced by coercion to integer
#> range
#> # Source:   table<`sparklyr_tmp_8938abc9_eda7_4a32_bba7_f13720900219`> [2 x 1]
#> # Database: spark_connection
#>       q
#>   <dbl>
#> 1   5.8
#> 2   6.9

success_mode1 |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT approx_percentile(`Sepal_Length`, array(0.5, 0.9)) AS `q`
#> FROM `iris`
```

The only other successful approach I could find was by using the `sql()` function.
This is better from a maintainability of code perspective, but previously I've only needed to resort to `sql()` when doing nested things or HOF work-arounds.
```r
# success
success_mode2 <- iris_spk |> 
  summarize(q = sql(paste0("approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, ", quantiles_array_string, ")")))

success_mode2 |> sdf_unnest_longer(q)
#> Warning in arrow_collect(object, ...): NAs introduced by coercion to integer
#> range
#> # Source:   table<`sparklyr_tmp_2a76a73f_9e7e_4fbe_ab0f_02e05a5d289f`> [2 x 1]
#> # Database: spark_connection
#>       q
#>   <dbl>
#> 1   5.8
#> 2   6.9

success_mode2 |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, array(0.5, 0.9)) AS `q`
#> FROM `iris`
```

### Failure modes

I tried three different approaches for making things work in the more usual `dbplyr` way of doing things.

The closest I got was using `array(quantiles)`. This appears to fail because the SQL resolves to `array((0.5, 0.9))` with a double set of parenthesis.
```r
# fails, puts too many parens in `array` call
failure_mode1 <- iris_spk |> 
  summarize(q = approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, array(quantiles)))

failure_mode1 |> sdf_unnest_longer(q)
#> Error:
#> ! org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException:
#>   [DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE] Cannot resolve
#>   "approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, array(named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2, 0.9)),
#>   10000)" due to data type mismatch: Parameter 2 requires the ("DOUBLE" or
#>   "ARRAY<DOUBLE>") type, however "array(named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2, 0.9))"
#>   has the type "ARRAY<STRUCT<col1: DECIMAL(1,1), col2: DECIMAL(1,1)>>".; line 1
#>   pos 7; 'Aggregate [approx_percentile(Sepal_Length#17,
#>   array(named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2, 0.9)), 10000, 0, 0) AS q#146] +-
#>   SubqueryAlias iris +- View (`iris`,
#>   [Sepal_Length#17,Sepal_Width#18,Petal_Length#19,Petal_Width#20,Species#21])
#>   +- LogicalRDD [Sepal_Length#17, Sepal_Width#18, Petal_Length#19,
#>   Petal_Width#20, Species#21], false
#> 
#> Run ]8;;x-r-run:sparklyr::spark_last_error()`sparklyr::spark_last_error()`]8;; to see the full Spark error (multiple lines)
#> To use the previous style of error message set
#> `options("sparklyr.simple.errors" = TRUE)`

failure_mode1 |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT approx_percentile(`Sepal_Length`, array((0.5, 0.9))) AS `q`
#> FROM `iris`
```

I also tried just passing `quantiles` in as the second argument, but it is of the wrong type. It isn't obvious to me that there is a very easy fix here though, since the SQL conversion does not know the expected argument type of the spark SQL function. I'm not clear on why it was coerced to a "named_struct` type, but that probably doesn't matter for this discussion.
```r
# fails, quantiles is not an `ARRAY<DOUBLE>` type
failure_mode2 <- iris_spk |> 
  summarize(q = approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, quantiles))

failure_mode2 |> sdf_unnest_longer(q)
#> Error:
#> ! org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException:
#>   [DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE] Cannot resolve
#>   "approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2, 0.9), 10000)"
#>   due to data type mismatch: Parameter 2 requires the ("DOUBLE" or
#>   "ARRAY<DOUBLE>") type, however "named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2, 0.9)" has the
#>   type "STRUCT<col1: DECIMAL(1,1), col2: DECIMAL(1,1)>".; line 1 pos 7;
#>   'Aggregate [approx_percentile(Sepal_Length#17, named_struct(col1, 0.5, col2,
#>   0.9), 10000, 0, 0) AS q#148] +- SubqueryAlias iris +- View (`iris`,
#>   [Sepal_Length#17,Sepal_Width#18,Petal_Length#19,Petal_Width#20,Species#21])
#>   +- LogicalRDD [Sepal_Length#17, Sepal_Width#18, Petal_Length#19,
#>   Petal_Width#20, Species#21], false
#> 
#> Run ]8;;x-r-run:sparklyr::spark_last_error()`sparklyr::spark_last_error()`]8;; to see the full Spark error (multiple lines)
#> To use the previous style of error message set
#> `options("sparklyr.simple.errors" = TRUE)`

failure_mode2 |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT approx_percentile(`Sepal_Length`, (0.5, 0.9)) AS `q`
#> FROM `iris`
```

Finally, trying to make just the second argument a string with `paste0` to inject the numeric values fail because it (correctly) interprets the second argument as as string, which is not `ARRAY<DOUBLE>`. This was a long-shot and it's probably a good thing that it doesn't work.
```r
# fails, quantiles_array_string is a string
failure_mode3 <- iris_spk |> 
  summarize(q = approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, quantiles_array_string))

failure_mode3 |> sdf_unnest_longer(q)
#> Error:
#> ! org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException:
#>   [DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_NULL] Cannot resolve
#>   "approx_percentile(Sepal_Length, array(0.5, 0.9), 10000)" due to data type
#>   mismatch: The percentage must not be null.; line 1 pos 7; 'Aggregate
#>   [approx_percentile(Sepal_Length#17, cast(array(0.5, 0.9) as double), 10000,
#>   0, 0) AS q#150] +- SubqueryAlias iris +- View (`iris`,
#>   [Sepal_Length#17,Sepal_Width#18,Petal_Length#19,Petal_Width#20,Species#21])
#>   +- LogicalRDD [Sepal_Length#17, Sepal_Width#18, Petal_Length#19,
#>   Petal_Width#20, Species#21], false
#> 
#> Run ]8;;x-r-run:sparklyr::spark_last_error()`sparklyr::spark_last_error()`]8;; to see the full Spark error (multiple lines)
#> To use the previous style of error message set
#> `options("sparklyr.simple.errors" = TRUE)`

failure_mode3 |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT approx_percentile(`Sepal_Length`, "array(0.5, 0.9)") AS `q`
#> FROM `iris`
```

### Conclusion/Ask

Perhaps this is enough of an edge case that you don't want to worry about it, but:

1. I think it would be nice to handle `array()` in the SQL conversion such that my `failure_mode1` (above) worked without needing to resort to writing out all the numbers inside `array()` or using `sql()` (success modes 1 and 2). 
2. If `failure_mode2` could be made to work I think that would be the most natural experience for end-users, but I appreciate that it may be difficult to support that without messing up SQL conversion for other queries.

title: Returning port number and handling interrupts in the backend
description:
Hello!  This is potentially more of a feature request, but I was wondering whether the following two ideas are possible today and, if not, whether you would be open to the changes.  For context, they would help improve the Databricks integration by allowing multiple sparklyr backends without leaking them 🙂.

1. **The sparklyr backend returns the port it is listening on.**
The entry point for sparklyr requires passing in a `port` parameter, but since ports cannot be "reserved", it is theoretically possible for another process to identify the target port to be free and bind to it before sparklyr can.  sparklyr will automatically find the next available port, but the caller would be unaware of the new choice.  Optionally, with the above change, it could be an option for users to not specify a port and have sparklyr choose a free one for them.  Both would be similar in behavior to SparkR's [backend](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/bbb33af2e4c90d679542298f56073a71de001fb7/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/api/r/RBackend.scala#L49).
2. **Gracefully exit the sparklyr backend when the thread is interrupted in `service` mode.**
When the sparklyr shell is initialized with the `--service` flag, it never exits (by design).  However, when the thread is interrupted by the caller (i.e. `Thread.interrupt()`), it does not appear that sparklyr handles it.  Attempting to interrupt the backend thread would then cause it to leak.

Do you have any insight into potential options and/or solutions to the above?  Thanks in advance!

title: spark_read_source does not support non-file paths
description:
Spark's [`DataFrameReader` API ](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/DataFrameReader.html) does not make any assumptions on what `path` (or `paths`) might be. It's a generic `String` and leaves interpretation up to the datasource. 

An example use of this is Google's [Apache Spark SQL connector for Google BigQuery](https://github.com/GoogleCloudDataproc/spark-bigquery-connector) where path can be:

- [a (fully-qualified) table identifier](https://github.com/GoogleCloudDataproc/spark-bigquery-connector?tab=readme-ov-file#reading-data-from-a-bigquery-table) of the form `[project].[dataset].[table]`
- [a SQL query](https://github.com/GoogleCloudDataproc/spark-bigquery-connector?tab=readme-ov-file#reading-data-from-a-bigquery-query)

`spark_read_source()`, however, assumes `path` to be a file path and performs path normalization:
```r
...
if (sc$method != "databricks-connect") {
  path <- spark_normalize_path(path)
}
invoke(df_reader, "load", path)
...
```

This can lead to issues with non-file path use cases as specified above, specifically on Windows, due to the use of `normalizePath` which converts relative paths to absolute paths on Windows, and as such anything which is not an actual path in the first place becomes nonsensical (such as e.g. the SQL query in the BigQuery use case stated above).

title: Cannot call spark_read_source with a NULL path
description:
I would like to call `spark_read_source` with a `NULL` path, i.e. `spark_read_source(sc, name, path = NULL, ...)`. Looking at the implementation of `spark_read_source`, this seems to be an intended use case:

```r
...
df <- if (is.null(path)) {
  invoke(df_reader, "load")
}
...
```

The intention behind using a `NULL` path is basically to invoke `load()` on the underlying data frame reader instead of `load(...)` with the path.

The problem, however, is that a `NULL` path does not seem to work with `spark_read_compat_param` as this will lead to the following error: ```Error in `c(name, path) %<-% spark_read_compat_param(sc, name, path)`: Assignment must contain same number of elements```

**Example**

Instead of 
```r
spark_read_source(sc, name="test", path = "test.csv", source="csv")
```
I would like to write
```r
spark_read_source(sc, name="test", path = NULL, source="csv", options=list(path = "test.csv"))
```

The latter can directly be used as a reproducible example since even though the files may not exist, this will immediately fail with
```
Error in c(name, path) %<-% spark_read_compat_param(sc, name, path) : 
  Assignment must contain same number of elements
```

title: `T` is mistakenly translated to a SQL identifier for a `case_when` inside a callback.
description:
`T` is translated to a SQL identifier for a `case_when` inside a callback.

This example:
```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
df <- sdf_len(sc, 5) %>%
  mutate(value = floor(100))
vars <- c('value')
result <- df %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars), function(x) { case_when(x == "" ~ 0, T ~ as.numeric(x)) }))
```

Produces:
```
Error:
! org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: [UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column or function parameter with name `T` cannot be resolved. Did you mean
  one of the following? [`id`, `value`].; line 3 pos 41; 'Project [id#5, CASE WHEN (cast(value#17 as double) = cast( as double)) THEN 0.0 WHEN 'T THEN
  cast(value#17 as double) END AS value#18] +- SubqueryAlias q01 +- Project [id#5, FLOOR(100.0) AS value#17] +- SubqueryAlias
  sparklyr_tmp_53dbd6ce_737d_4168_a8bc_0b5fb0e82d0b +- View (`sparklyr_tmp_53dbd6ce_737d_4168_a8bc_0b5fb0e82d0b`, [id#5]) +- LogicalRDD [id#5], false

Run `sparklyr::spark_last_error()` to see the full Spark error (multiple lines)
To use the previous style of error message set `options("sparklyr.simple.errors" = TRUE)`
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

But this works fine:
```r
result <- df %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars), function(x) { case_when(x == "" ~ 0, TRUE ~ as.numeric(x)) }))
```

And this works fine:
```r
result <- df %>%
  mutate(case_when(value == "" ~ 0, T ~ as.numeric(value)))
```

title: Unable to list the databases using `src_databases`
description:
The error message:
```R
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version='3.5.2')
> src_databases(sc)
Error:
! org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: [UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column or function
  parameter with name `databaseName` cannot be resolved. Did you mean one of the following?
  [`namespace`].; 'Project ['databaseName] +- CommandResult [namespace#17], ShowNamespaces [namespace#17],
  V2SessionCatalog(spark_catalog), [[0,1000000007,746c7561666564]] +- ShowNamespaces [namespace#17] +-
  ResolvedNamespace V2SessionCatalog(spark_catalog)

```
It seems this is because the column name of the table is hardcoded as 'databaseName.' However, in some versions of the system, it may be 'namespace' instead.
https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/374c376f1a7f1bec7163531209e0bdf581c6a7e5/R/tables_spark.R#L109
```R
> sql <- hive_context(sc)
> invoke(sql, "sql", "SHOW DATABASES")
<jobj[16]>
  org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
  [namespace: string]
```



I propose adding a `col` argument to allow users to customize the column name.
```R
src_databases <- function(sc, col = "databaseName", ...) {
  sql <- hive_context(sc)
  dbs <- invoke(sql, "sql", "SHOW DATABASES")
  databaseNames <- sdf_read_column(dbs, col)
  sort(databaseNames)
}
```

title: Error in `src_databases()` when connected to Spark through the `Spark Connect` method
description:
Cannot list the database using `src_databases()` when connected to Spark through the `Spark Connect` method.
```R
> pysparklyr::spark_connect_service_start("3.5")
> sc <- spark_connect(
  master = "sc://localhost", 
  method = "spark_connect", 
  version = "3.5"
)
> src_databases(sc)

Error in py_call_impl(x, dots$unnamed, dots$named) : 
  pyspark.errors.exceptions.base.PySparkTypeError: [NOT_LIST_OF_COLUMN_OR_STR] Argument `columns` should be a list[Column].
── R Traceback ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    ▆
 1. └─sparklyr::src_databases(sc)
 2.   ├─sparklyr::sdf_read_column(dbs, "databaseName")
 3.   └─sparklyr:::sdf_read_column.spark_jobj(dbs, "databaseName")
 4.     ├─sparklyr::invoke(sdf, "select", column, list())
 5.     └─pysparklyr:::invoke.spark_pyobj(sdf, "select", column, list())
 6.       └─pysparklyr:::invoke_conn(...)
 7.         └─reticulate::py_call(x, ...)
 8.           └─reticulate:::py_call_impl(x, dots$unnamed, dots$named)
```
I tried to narrow it down and found that the issue might be a bug in `sdf_read_column.spark_jobj()`. 
https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/34daa972f1f9839a430fdf02af8defb8a85ab0ae/R/sdf_wrapper.R#L147

Original code:
```R
> sdf <- spark_dataframe(invoke(hive_context(sc), "sql", "SHOW DATABASES"))
> invoke(sdf, "select","namespace" ,list())

Error in py_call_impl(x, dots$unnamed, dots$named) : 
  pyspark.errors.exceptions.base.PySparkTypeError: [NOT_LIST_OF_COLUMN_OR_STR] Argument `columns` should be a list[Column].
```
Revised code:
```R
> sdf <- spark_dataframe(invoke(hive_context(sc), "sql", "SHOW DATABASES"))
> invoke(sdf, "select", list("namespace"))

- PySpark object
  pyspark.sql.connect.dataframe.DataFrame
  DataFrame[namespace: string]
```
I propose revising the code to:
```R
col_df <- invoke(sdf, "select", list(column))
```

title: Tidymodels on Azure Databricks
spark_read_parquet deletes Unity Catalogue table in Databricks
description:
Hi

This issue is experienced using sparklyr on Databricks platform.

For a few weeks, I had one of our tables in Unity Catalogue being deleted every week around the same time. After investigating logs and trying different methods to prevent the deletion, I changed ownership of the table to another user. When that happened, I found out the source of the error.

```r
df_UCTable <- spark_read_parquet(sc,name = 'UCTable', path=paste0(endpoint,"/UCTable"),memory=F)
```

The error:
Error : com.databricks.sql.managedcatalog.acl.UnauthorizedAccessException: PERMISSION_DENIED: User is not an owner of Table main.default.UCTable
at com.databricks.managedcatalog.UCReliableHttpClient.reliablyAndTranslateExceptions(UCReliableHttpClient.scala:87)
	at com.databricks.managedcatalog.UCReliableHttpClient.delete(UCReliableHttpClient.scala:118)
	at com.databricks.managedcatalog.ManagedCatalogClientImpl.$anonfun$deleteTable$1(ManagedCatalogClientImpl.scala:1272)
	at com.databricks.managedcatalog.ManagedCatalogClientImpl.$anonfun$recordAndWrapException$2(ManagedCatalogClientImpl.scala:4555)

To reproduce this issue, I have to change the default value for Default catalog for the workspace into the catalog that holds UCTable

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/89fcaa62-5344-41e1-b581-e330aa253a1a)

After that I have to use in  spark_read_parquet the name of a table that already exists in the new default catalog.

The version of sparklyr is 1.8.1

I believe the source of the issue is the way it was setup and the following line https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/22aa571c1cb2820b916fff9e0860647c2ea024f5/R/data_interface.R#L275

This emits a delete table statement and it only deletes the metadata related to that table in Unity Catalogue. The table can be put back by using UNDROP TABLE, but this is not expected behaviour when using name='' in Databricks.

I will close the ticket if this is not the right place to report this, so please let me know.

title: Use multiple sdf as input parameter for spark_apply
description:
We have a function inside our customer library in native R, which basically check & combines & merge couple of native data.table together. We tried to execute this function in Spark cluster with `spark_apply()`, however seems spark_apply would only accept ONE `x` as input. How can we pass multiple sdf as function input varibles? 


function we need to invoke in `spark_apply` looks like:
```r
merge_func <- function(df1, df2, df3, df4){
   ...  ### some check logics here
   return c(out_1, out_2, out_3)
}
```

And in our code, df1-4 are output from previous calls, and we've successfully converted them from native R object to `tbl_spark` type, via "spark_apply" successfully. )

title: sparklyr errors when arrow is enabled in Databricks Runtime Environment 14.3 LTS
description:
I have encountered a problem with sparklyr interacting with arrow in Databricks Runtime 14.3 LTS. The below example code of creating/dropping a table and displaying a data frame fails in DBR 14.3 (which uses arrow version 12.0.1, sparklyr version 1.8.1). The error message is pasted at the bottom.  I note that this same example code runs successfully if either:

- the code is run in DBR 13.3 LTS (which uses arrow version 10.0.1 and sparklyr version 1.7.9)
- the "sparklyr.arrow" option is set to FALSE instead of TRUE in the example code below

I have also experimented with trying to install and load other specific versions of arrow & sparklyr within DBR 14.3, but this has not resulted in successfully running the example. Any help would be appreciated.

title: unnest() fails on Databricks
description:
I have an interesting issue running sparklyr::unnest() inside of Databricks.  The first time I use the function after a cluster restart, the function works perfectly.  However, if I either restart my R session when using RStudio, or if I detach/reattach a notebook, the function will fail claiming it cannot locate a tmp table.

This is reproducible using the default sparklyr 1.7.5 provided by Databricks and also if I upgrade to 1.7.7.  I am also using Databricks 10.4.

I assume the error is coming out of the creation of the temporary table near the bottom of this function, but it is not apparent to me what would cause this error, especially only upon a restart of the RSession.

Here is an easily reproducible example using a simple test case.

Let me know if I can provide any other info to help troubleshoot.
```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  a = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3),
  b = lapply(seq(7), function(x) rep(1, x)),
  c = seq(7),
  d = lapply(seq(7), function(x) list(a = x, b = 2 * x, c = -x)),
  e = seq(-7, -1)
)
sdf <- copy_to(sc, tbl, overwrite = TRUE)
sdf.nested <- sdf %>% tidyr::nest(n1 = c(b, c), n2 = c(d, e))

sdf.nested %>%
  tidyr::unnest(c(n1, n2)) %>%
  collect() %>%
  dplyr::arrange(c)

```

title: dplyr to Spark SQL Translation Error: Unresolved Column When Selecting All Columns
description:
Hello,

I am trying to filter table data from Databricks connection using dplyr. I am encountering an issue if I skip the 'select' statement - it seems that if you skip the selection of the columns, when translating the statement to SQL, instead of `SELECT *` it creates `SELECT <table_name>.*`, which leads to throwing Spark SQL error:

```
Error in py_call_impl(callable, call_args$unnamed, call_args$named) : 
  pyspark.errors.exceptions.connect.AnalysisException: [UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function parameter with name `table`.`*` cannot be resolved. Did you mean one of the following? [...]. SQLSTATE: 42703; line 1 pos 7;
'Project ['table.*]
```

### What works - when I specify column names to select
```r
con <- sparklyr::spark_connect(
  cluster_id = "...",
  method = "databricks_connect",
  version = "14.3"
)

table <- dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::in_catalog("catalog", "db", "table"))

filtered <- table %>%
  dplyr::select(col1, col2) %>%
  dplyr::filter(col1 == 'some_val') %>%
  dplyr::collect()

print(filtered)
```

### What doesn't work - when I want to select all and do not specify column names to select

filtered <- table %>%
  dplyr::filter(col1 == 'some_val') %>%
  dplyr::collect()

print(filtered)
```

Thanks in advance!
S.

description:

library(sparklyr)

reviews_tb <- sdf_copy_to(sc, reviews, "reviews")

I am loading about 5000 parquet files (2 billion rows) with sparklyr 0.7 and the following code

df_new <- spark_read_parquet(sc, "/mypath/parquet/pq*",
                             overwrite = TRUE,
                             name = "df_new",
                             memory = FALSE,
                             options = list(mergeSchema = "true"))

unfortunately I get the error

`error: org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure: Task 5 in stage 39734.0 failed 4 times, most recent failure: Lost task 5.3 in stage 39734.0 (TID 11111, 10.111.111.11, executor 1): org.apache.spark.SparkException: Failed merging schema of file file:/mypath/parquet/pq_20170205.csv/part-00000.snappy.parquet:`

My guess is that there is a variable that has two different schemas, otherwise I do not understand why merging the schemas would fail. here

I see that there is a `sdf_schema()` available in sparklyr that returns the schema. However the documentation does not explain how I can use it. 

For instance, can I use the output of `sdf_schema()` to feed the argument `schema=` in `spark_read_parquet()` ? That would allow me to choose a particular schema for my variables and avoid this error. Doing so manually its impossible - I have hundreds of variables.

What do you think?
Thanks!

title: partial list of columns in spark_read_x produces unexpected behaviors
description:
A partial named columns list in spark_read_x seems to rewrite the names of the first x columns up to the length of the partial list and thereby likely refer to the wrong columns. So it seems like a partial columns list would not be useful and could be misleading / produce unexpected results for most users. 

Suggestion: sparklyr should disable this partial list option (error out) or warn that not all columns are included or the columns you thought you were selecting and specifying type for are not the actual ones you are reading.

title: Correctly shutdown on YARN cluster for deploy mode "cluster"
description:
[This sparklyr line](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/661fc4cf8ef61c70d84968f106007e1df809985e/java/spark-1.5.2/backend.scala#L207C35-L207C35) calls `System.exit(0)` for non-service connections. However, according to [this comment in the YARN ApplicationMaster code](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/7db85642600b1e3b39ca11e41d4e3e0bf1c8962b/resource-managers/yarn/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/deploy/yarn/ApplicationMaster.scala#L234C8-L244C1), it is incorrect for `System.exit(0)`  (or status) to be called by the ending spark context.

Failure to exit correctly leads to a reported status of "FAILED" by the YARN ApplicationMaster, which can lead to spurious re-attempts of the submitted job.

To fix, I suggest updating the conditional logic so it is
``` 
if (!isService && !isBatch) System.exit(0)
```

title: possible bug in sparklyr logical planner (selections pushed down too far)
description:
# Reporting an Issue with sparklyr

Hi there, I'm seeing what looks like a bug in the sparklyr logical planner on `tbl_spark` objects. The tl;dr is that it looks like, in certain cases, selections can be pushed too far down in the logical plan (i.e., past `groupby` and `mutate` operations that can introduce new columns). The below example, which works fine for vanilla R dataframes, fails for `tbl_spark` dataframes:

```r
# Install and load the dplyr package if not already installed
# install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

# Create a data frame with some sample data
df <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"),
  Subject = c("Math", "Math", "English", "English", "Math"),
  Score = c(90, 85, 88, 92, 78)
)

sc <- spark_connect(master="local")

spark_df <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, df, "spark_df", overwrite=TRUE)

print(spark_df)

# Group the data frame by the "Name" column
# ------------------ NOTE: Switch between `df` and `spark_df` below to contrast execution behavior for native and spark dataframes
grouped_df <- spark_df %>%
  group_by(Name)

# Use mutate to add a new column "AvgScore" (won't actually contain the average score within each group; just a fake column for testing)
result_df <- grouped_df %>%
  mutate(AvgScore = 1)

# Print the original and result data frames
# print("Original Data Frame:")
# print(df)

# print("Grouped Data Frame:")
# print(grouped_df)

# print("Result Data Frame:")
# print(result_df)

# bug in sparklyr, but not vanilla R dataframes
arranged <- result_df %>% ungroup() %>% arrange(AvgScore, Name)
print(arranged)

print(arranged %>% select(Name))
```

title: Repeated calls to `mutate` and other functions take increasingly long to return
description:
I'm suffering from a degradation of performance of sparklyr.  I'm using sparklyr version 1.8.3 and Spark 3.4.0.

I'm building an ETL tool which ingests rows from a CSV file to determine what transformations are needed.  Each source table is a `tbl_spark` from sparklyr and the tool uses dplyr to apply mutations/joins to that table for each tranformation.  Essentially, for each source table, my ETL tool operates like this:

```R
t <- tbl(sc, "source_table")

for(i in 1:nrow(csv_rows)) {
	t <- t |> left_join(other_table, ...)
	t <- t |> mutate(...)
}

t |> compute()

```

I'm finding that each subsequent call to mutate takes longer and longer to complete.  In my ETL tool, it ends up taking 5-10 seconds for a call to mutate to complete.  My ETL specifications contain thousands of transformations.  Currently, my ETL tool takes ~8 hours to complete. Half of that time is Spark performing translations on the data.  But the other half of that time is waiting for calls mutate/join to finish.

In profiling my code, it appears that mutate is spending most of its time rendering out the SQL for the `tbl_spark` and all the mutations/joins applied to it so far.  I assume each subsequent call re-renders all of that SQL plus the additional SQL from the new call.

I have a simple script that illustrates the slow down.  On my system, initial calls to mutate return in 0.1 seconds.  By the end of 50 calls, mutate is taking 1.5 seconds to complete.

```R
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect("local")
d <- data.frame(
  d01 = c(1), d02 = c(2), d03 = c(3), d04 = c(4), d05 = c(5), d06 = c(6), d07 = c(7), d08 = c(8), d09 = c(9), d10 = c(10)
  , d11 = c(1), d12 = c(2), d13 = c(3), d14 = c(4), d15 = c(5), d16 = c(6), d17 = c(7), d18 = c(8), d19 = c(9), d20 = c(10)
  , d21 = c(1), d22 = c(2), d23 = c(3), d24 = c(4), d25 = c(5), d26 = c(6), d27 = c(7), d28 = c(8), d29 = c(9), d30 = c(10)
)
copy_to(sc, d, name = "some_data", overwrite = TRUE)

ds <- tbl(sc, "some_data") |> rename_all(tolower)

for(i in 1:50) {
  new_col <- paste0("col", i)
  print(system.time({ds <- ds |> mutate("{new_col}" := i)}))
}
spark_disconnect(sc)
```

Output:

```
   user  system elapsed 
  0.059   0.000   0.120

...

   user  system elapsed 
  1.407   0.000   1.543
```

I have another script that illustrates the behavior I'm expecting.  It uses RSQLite in place of sparklyr.  On my system, initial calls to mutate return in 0.02 seconds. title: Databricks 13 support
description:
Starting from Databricks DBR 13 and the associated python package databricks-connect 13.0.0, [the connection now use the new Spark Connect](https://www.databricks.com/blog/2023/04/18/use-databricks-anywhere-databricks-connect-v2.html).

It seems to change a few things in the connection, and Sparklyr doesn't seems to be compatible.

For example, if I use the traditionnal way to connect, which works with older version, I get this:

```r
> sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks", spark_home = system("databricks-connect get-spark-home", intern = TRUE))
Error in system2(file.path(spark_home, "bin", "spark-submit"), "--version",  : 
  error in running command
```

I tested this connection and it works in python, my guess is that it's a big change in the internal way to connect that is not compatible with Sparklyr (I have the version 1.8.1).

I expected that seeing it's brand new, but my question is: is there a support planned for this new databricks-connect for Sparklyr ? Or do I have to switch to ODBC (which lack features compared to Sparklyr) ?

title: Azure Databricks Connection Issue
description:
First, I appreciate Posit and Databricks work on databricks_connect. 

I followed the Databricks Connect [documentation](https://spark.rstudio.com/deployment/databricks-spark-connect.html) to connect to our Azure Databricks workspace. Well-written documentation! I also appreciated James and Rafi's [presentation](https://github.com/blairj09-talks/crossing-bridges) at Posit::conf 2023.

After installing the required packages and locating the needed IDs from Databricks, I attempted a connection and received the `Error: Unable to find conda binary. Is Anaconda installed?` error. Using the documentation (linked above) and noting this error was included in the common errors, I followed the recommended action and I installed the dev version of the pysparklyr package and attempted the connection again. Another error, this time different:

Connection Code Run:
```r
sc <- spark_connect(
  master = my_azure_databricks_workspace_url, 
  cluster_id = my_cluster_id, # cluster runtime is 14.0
  token = my_databricks_pat,
  method = "databricks_connect",
  dbr_version = "14.0"
)
```

title: Incompatible types error for joins not occurring.
description:

title: Copy files to Databricks Managed Volumes
description:
Hi,

I'm wondering if Sparklyr will make it available to copy local files to Databricks Managed Volumes like Databricks Connect allows for in Python: https://pypi.org/project/databricks-connect/

In Databricks Connect Python, when the spark session object is created, you can call a function called "copyFromLocalToFs", which will copy a local file to a folder location in Databricks, like in a managed volume.

Example of code doing so in Python:

```
from databricks.connect import DatabricksSession

workspace_url = "<workspace-url>"
cluster_id = "<cluster-id>"

session = DatabricksSession.builder\
    .remote(f"sc://{workspace_url};token={<oauth-token/pat>};x-databricks-cluster-id={cluster_id}")\
    .getOrCreate()

session.copyFromLocalToFs("./google.png", "/Volumes/main/my_schema/my-volume/google.png")
```

title: mutate_all/mutate_at: Considerable performance degradation after version 1.7.5
description:
---
I am seeing a considerable performance degradation in mutate_at and mutate_all transformation functions after sparklyr version 1.7.5.  The performance deterioration is proportional to the number of columns in the Spark dataframe. As the number of columns increase, the performance deteriorates further.

Below is a reproducible example to demonstrate it.
I have created a dataframe named d with columns d01-d30 having 1 row. I am trying to perform a pmin() operation to cap the values at a given number. 
Sparklyr version 1.7.5 effortlessly processes it and produces the result. mutate_all and mutate_at take 0.182 and 0.048 seconds respectively.
However, sparklyr 1.7.8 takes considerable time to process it. mutate_all and mutate_at take 86.031 and 78.637 seconds respectively.

title: Spark standalone write permissions failure.
description:
My issue is exactly the same as #3284.

To expand on the non-response of the previous issue, my workflow is as follows.

I have HostA with users and Rstudio, this host is used to connect to a cluster on HostB with a running spark standalone deployment. 

The standalone deployment is started by user `spark`. Hence the spark processes are running as `spark` on the master and worker nodes.

The user can connect to the host ok, starting the sparklyr application and data can be loaded from disk, as long as the spark user has read permissions to the data location. 

When using the `spark_write_csv` command, spark first creates a folder to hold the output files giving file permissions `rwxr-x---` and the file belongs to the user who initiated the app on HostA. The `spark_write_csv` process fails due to inadequate permissions.

From what I understand, you cannot use `proxy-user` with Spark submit on the Stand-alone deployment, so the solution seems to be to make the owner of the output directory the same as the user which initiates the spark cluster.

title: Sparklyr is incompatible with Spark3.5 due to a refactor of RowEncoder
description:
In Spark 3.5, API `RowEncoder` is refactored to `ExpressionEncoder`. Please see:  https://github.com/apache/spark/commit/071feabbd4325504332679dfa620bc5ee4359370. Sparklyr is incompatible with Spark 3.5 due to this change. `RowEncoder` is used in `workerhelper.scala`, and this is expected to be changed to `ExpressionEncoder`
https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/4d49e40c8cefd394358f64261fceeaeaef13f8cc/java/spark-2.0.0/workerhelper.scala#L100

Can this be fixed and published to CRAN?

title: Misinterpreted na.rm = TRUE argument when translated into SQL conditional function, if()
description:
Below is an example which demonstrates the use of na.rm = TRUE argument for pmax() function.
The arguments are translated incorrectly into SQL and the condition appear as "arg1 >= arg2 and ... and **argN-1 >= TRUE**".
Similar is the case with pmin() function.
The obvious workaround at this point is to substitute NA as something to get these functions work.

#> 
#> Attaching package: 'sparklyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#>

#> [1] 0

title: `spark_install()` installs unexpected version when patch version is not specified
description:
Following the instructions in [Mastering Spark with R - 2.2.2 Installing Spark](https://therinspark.com/starting.html#starting-prerequisites), I hit what might be a minor bug, or at least some unexpected behavior.

The book asks you to install version 2.3 to be aligned with its examples. It suggests doing this with `spark_install("2.3")`, presumably making the assumption that the most recent patch version number will be automatically determined however, because a 3.2.3 version exists `spark_install("2.3")` installs version 3.2.3.

``` r
library(sparklyr)
spark_install("2.3")
spark_installed_versions()
#>   spark hadoop                                          dir
#> 1 2.4.3    2.7 /Users/cjrmi/spark/spark-2.4.3-bin-hadoop2.7
#> 2 3.2.3    3.2 /Users/cjrmi/spark/spark-3.2.3-bin-hadoop3.2
```

Digging deeper, this happens because of how `spark_install_find()` and `sparklyr:::spark_install_version_expand()` currently work...

``` r
library(sparklyr)

desired_version <- "2.3"

spark_install_find(
  version = desired_version,
  hadoop_version = NULL,
  installed_only = FALSE,
  latest = TRUE
)$sparkVersion
#> [1] "3.2.3"

sparklyr:::spark_install_version_expand(version = desired_version, installed_only = FALSE)
#> [1] "3.2.3"
```

This somewhat unexpected behavior occurs here...

https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/a58fea9a3b6bb98e489291663496bde0813e8154/R/install_spark.R#L16-L19

a minor change to the regex could fix this (assuming the intent is to allow passing a `[major].[minor]` syntax)...

``` r
library(sparklyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'sparklyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter

version <- "2.3"

versions <- spark_available_versions(show_minor = TRUE)$spark
versions[grepl(version, versions)]
#> [1] "2.2.3" "2.3.0" "2.3.1" "2.3.2" "2.3.3" "2.3.4" "3.2.3"

versions <- spark_available_versions(show_minor = TRUE)$spark
versions[grepl(paste0("^", version), versions)]
#> [1] "2.3.0" "2.3.1" "2.3.2" "2.3.3" "2.3.4"
```

title: sparklyr arrange behavior is different than dplyr arrange - order null values after non-null values
description:
sparklyr arrange behavior is different than dplyr arrange. 

dplyr arrange places missing value or null after all non-null values (https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/arrange.html#missing-values)

Sparklyr arrange does not place null values in the end as shown in the generate query below

index_conditions_sparklyr <- index_conditions %>%
    arrange(PersonId, RecordedDateTime, EncounterId) %>% 
    group_by(PersonId) %>%
    mutate(row_number = row_number())  %>%
    filter(row_number == 1) %>%
    show_query()

SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT
    *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY `PersonId` ORDER BY `PersonId`, `RecordedDateTime`, `EncounterId`) AS `row_number`
  FROM `table_1692663744`
) `q01`
WHERE (`row_number` = 1.0)

SparkSQL supports ordering null values after non-null values 
https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-orderby.html

Example: 
SELECT * FROM (
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY PersonId **ORDER BY RecordedDateTime NULLS LAST, EncounterId NULLS LAST**) AS row_number FROM tbl_index_conditions) t 
WHERE row_number = 1

Pyspark supports this - https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.Column.asc_nulls_last.html

Requesting to support ordering null values after non-null values in arrange method

title: sparklyr::sdf_bind_cols not great for lots of columns that are generated from another table
description:
`sparklyr::sdf_bind_cols` seems to fail when combining a lot of columns that were generated from another table.

I needed to process some fixed width files in spark.  There isn't a fixed width reader in spark, so I wrote some code to do it manually.

The way I would handle this in local memory is use `purrr` to split things into a list with a single column each, then combine.

At least the way I generated those columns, `sparklyr::sdf_bind_cols` fails when you get too many columns.  I know I'm not running the latest copies of `sparklyr`.  I booted up posit.cloud and tried my reprex there with the latest copies of all the packages, and it didn't fail with the same error, but it went on for hours without completion, so I figured that this older reprex is sufficient.

I can certainly work around this.  I show another approach down below where I can stitch together my own SQL code and do the same task that way.  But it would certainly be nice if the straightforward approach would work.  Maybe I'm missing something that would avoid the recursion, but I tried a few things and couldn't get around the fact that the laziness of the tables seems to compound when you stitch them together and then it errors out.

# library(sparklyr)
# library(purrr)
# library(dplyr)

SparkR::sparkR.session()
#> Spark package found in SPARK_HOME: /databricks/spark
#> Java ref type org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession id 1
sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(method = "databricks")

## pushing to a temp table

tempname <- sparklyr::spark_table_name("")

# I get data that is all one big string each line that I will need to parse
# creating some placeholder text

line_text <- "1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i10jj11kk12ll13mm14nn15oo16pp17qq18rr19ss20tt21uu22vv23ww24xx25yy26zz27AA28BB29CC30DD31EE32FF33GG34HH35II36JJ37KK38LL39MM40NN41OO42PP43QQ44RR45SS46TT47UU48VV49WW50XX51YY52ZZ5000.01aaaaaaa50.0001bbbbbbb"

# repeating it a couple of times with a little variation
lines_text <- c(
  line_text,
  toupper(line_text),
  tolower(line_text)
)            

# changing to a table             
my_table <- tibble::tibble(
  line = lines_text
)

# uploading table to spark
initial_fwf <- dplyr::copy_to(
  sc,
  my_table,
  name = tempname,
  overwrite = TRUE)

# I get metadata with column name, width, scale (for numeric variables), and type
# creating some placeholder metadata here

this_metadata_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:108,

title: spark_write_csv fails when connecting to Spark as a user that does not start the cluster
description:
I am running a standalone spark cluster using Spark 3.3.0 consisting of 1 master and 4 worker nodes. I am starting the cluster from user `ubuntu` on all 5 involved nodes. All nodes have access to the same storage via NFS, provided by the master.

In my environment, I have multiple users that need to connect to the cluster and submit spark applications. None of those users is the `ubuntu` user that starts the cluster master and workers. Here, I use the `test` user to log into RStudio Server and run the Spark application via sparklyr.

```r
# Load libs
library(sparklyr)
library(tidyverse)


config <- spark_config()
config$spark.executor.memory = "5G"
config$spark.executor.cores = "2"
config$spark.shuffle.service.enabled = T
config$spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled = T

Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME="/opt/spark/",
                 JAVA_HOME="/usr/lib/jvm/java-8-openjdk-amd64/")

sc <- spark_connect(master = "spark://172.16.44.70:7077",
                    config = config,
                    app_name = "app-test")

sdf_data <- spark_read_parquet(sc, name = "sdf_data", path = "/mnt/storage/example_data", memory = F)

### Everything works until here
### The following fails

spark_write_csv(sdf_data %>% head(100), path = "/mnt/storage/test-data/")
```

The resulting error is as follows.

```
Error: org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted.
at org.apache.spark.sql.errors.QueryExecutionErrors$.jobAbortedError(QueryExecutionErrors.scala:638)
...
Caused by: org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure: Task 0 in stage 38.0 failed 4 times, most recent failure: Lost task 0.3 in stage 38.0 (TID 2255) (172.16.44.80 executor 309): java.io.IOException: Mkdirs failed to create file:/mnt/storage/test-data/_temporary/0/_temporary/attempt_202208121311203632496408213281273_0038_m_000000_2255 (exists=false, cwd=file:/home/ubuntu/spark-3.3.0-bin-hadoop3/work/app-20220812114226-0003/309)
...
```

The underlying issue is, that the destination folder `/mnt/storage/test-data` is created by the R user instead of the cluster user. Hence, the cluster is unable to actually write the data into the folder.

```
test@compute1:/mnt/storage$ ls -l
total 124
drwxrwxrwx   2 ubuntu   spark      73728 Aug 12 09:17 example_data
drwxr-xr-x   3 test     test       4096  Aug 12 13:10 test-data
```

I already tried to set default ownerships and file permissions to the folder I am trying to write to using Linux ACL settings, but it seems R (or sparklyr?) does its own thing and ignores the actual permission settings.

Is there a known workaround for this issue? How can I support multiple users on top of regular file storage without having to spin up dedicated clusters for every user?

title: sparklyr::spark_submit(master='yarn-cluster',...) job always results in FAILED status
description:
## Issue

Launching a job with `sparklyr::spark_connect(mode='yarn-cluster',...)`  always results in a final status of "FAILED".
In particular, this occurs even when the batch R script has clearly run to the end. This problem may exist with other connection modes.

## Tentative solution 

This solution is based on my haphazard understanding of both the sparklyr and spark ApplicationMaster code.

Sparklyr calls [System.exit(0)](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/620b27b1caa6343543d1399f73dc8b58fc5dc654/java/spark-1.5.2/backend.scala#L429) after closing the gateway.  According to [this comment in Yarn's ApplicationMaster.scala](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/e857b7ad1c78c57d06436e387473d83e61293c7c/resource-managers/yarn/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/deploy/yarn/ApplicationMaster.scala#L254), it seems code should not call `System.exit(0)`, and instead let the ApplicationMaster figure it out once the gateway has closed.

title: `spark_submit(...)` not terminated after submission
description: [This line](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/eb3e795447887908d9e795512ad08eeeb32eede5/R/shell_connection.R#L442) is supposed to terminate batch connections before going any further. However, `batch` is the file name from `spark_submit()`. Not sure if this should be switched to `isBatch` instead, or I am missing something.

title: Cannot find RScript with spark_submit(master='yarn-cluster', ...)
description:
I'm trying to use `sparklyr::spark_submit(master='yarn-cluster'...)`. Unfortunately, I receive an "RScript not found" type error. R is not installed on nodes, however I distribute a conda environment to each node, and R is available there. I have confirmed the archive actually gets distributed. Things work fine using SparkR.

I have tried many workarounds, most of which involve around trying to:
1. Run a bash command prior to sparklyr calling RScript which adds the relevant directory to the PATH, or
2. Modifying the RScript command to reflect the absolute path for RScript. 

I haven't achieved 1 because it doesn't seem I can set `rscript.before` in such a way that it gets run during gateway initialization. [This](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/620b27b1caa6343543d1399f73dc8b58fc5dc654/java/spark-1.6.0/rscript.scala#L48) indicates how the `rscript.before` command is retrieved, while [this](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/1dd5c51575b6934b3841147b5a9de6fae4b08404/java/spark-1.5.2/backend.scala#L249) shows that during gateway initialization, options are intentionally left empty.

I can't seem to do 2 because the absolute paths used depend on properties I don't know until application launch(? right?), so I can't modify `spark.r.command` appropriately. 

I've looked at both sparklyr, sparkR and spark's connection code extensively, trying to figure out the difference as to why, for example, it can find R/RScript, but to no avail -- I can get the gist, but don't use Java/Scala myself, and am probably missing some nuance.

I appreciate the help, and am happy to provide additional specific information as requested -- sorry that there's so many moving pieces I don't want to dump a bunch of information, which I would first have to anonymize. Thank you!

title: Anyone interested in maintaining Apache Sedona R module?
description:
# Anyone interested in maintaining Apache Sedona R module

Dear all,

Sorry, this is not an actual issue report. But I don't know where I can find other members in the R community. We, the Apache Sedona community (https://github.com/apache/sedona), are in urgent need of a volunteer to help maintain Sedona R module.

Apache Sedona is a cluster computing system for processing large-scale geospatial data. It extends Spark and Flink with comprehensive geospatial processing capability. It provides Scala/Java/SQL/Python/R interfaces. Currently, its R module is built on Sparklyr and connects Apache Spark. Sedona has over 10M downloads overall and receives over 800K downloads every month.

Recently, the main contributor of Apache Sedona R module no longer has time maintaining this library. The current GitHub Action of Sedona R has been failing for a few weeks and does not enjoy the new functions introduced in Sedona core.

Members in our community are familiar with Scala/Java/Python but don't know much about R. However, I believe Sedona R is still a great addition to the R geospatial community at large.

Please feel free to let me know if you are interested. My contact is Jia Yu, email: jiayu@apache.org

Thanks,
Jia

PMC Chair of Apache Sedona

title: rlang deprecation warnings
description:
sparklyr uses {forge} mainly to cast object types, and {forge} uses deprecated functions in {rlang} supersed by functions in in package {vctrs}.

{forge} hasn't seen any updates in 4 years, and mentioned vctrs in 2018 https://github.com/rstudio/forge/issues/2

If {forge} isn't updated, the alternative would be to switch to {vctrs} in {sparklyr}. {forge} does add checking for NAs, length of arguments, and that sort of things.

---
warnings:
```
`as_integer()` is deprecated as of rlang 0.4.0
Please use `vctrs::vec_cast()` instead.
```

title: Read operations that depend on `spark_partition_register_df` fail
description:
Spark no longer permits views to include multiple name parts.

For example, the following will fail:
```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(method  = "databricks")
spark_read_table(sc, "default.test_data")
```

```
Error : org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException:
[TEMP_VIEW_NAME_TOO_MANY_NAME_PARTS] CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW or the corresponding Dataset APIs only accept single-part view names, but got: default.test_data.
```

This is due to the addition of [this exception](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/b85fe2bff300d095ef0492887a96f022f5b0d84b/sql/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/Dataset.scala#L3817-L3822). 

To have the prior example work users must either:

-  Set spark config `allowsTempViewCreationWithMultipleNameparts` as `TRUE`.
-  Set the database/catalog via `tbl_change_db`, e.g. `tbl_change_db(sc, "default")`

`spark_partition_register_df` likely needs to change such that when `createOrReplaceTempView` is called ([ref](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/38f8bcfd7cb0e6adee1643758b933162ee878c6b/R/dplyr_spark_data.R#L13-L19)) it will use a different randomized/sanitized name.


_Note: Example were run on Databricks but the code is same for core Spark._

title: Is there a way to get sparklyr to push down queries into jdbc database connection?
description:
I was wondering if there is a better way to ask spark to push down queries to the underlying database.

This will push the query down to the underlying database, and takes about 1 second.

```r
monthly_counts <- sparklyr::spark_read_jdbc(
    sc, 
    memory = FALSE, 
    name = "mytablename", 
    options = list(
      url = "jdbc:sybase:Tds:myhostname.something.com:5000",
      driver = "com.sybase.jdbc4.jdbc.SybDriver",
      user = "username",
      password = "password",
      fetchsize = "10000",
      query = "SELECT `month_numeric`, COUNT(*) AS `count_rows`
  FROM `mytablename`
  GROUP BY `month_numeric`",
      pushDownPredicate = TRUE
    ) 
  ) %>%
dplyr::collect()

```

But the following code doesn't seem to push the query down to the underlying database, since it takes about a minute for a table with about 10 million rows and I gave up after several hours for a table with about a billion rows.

```
  my_table <- sparklyr::spark_read_jdbc(
    sc, 
    memory = FALSE, 
    name = "mytablename", 
    options = list(
      url = "jdbc:sybase:Tds:myhostname.something.com:5000",
      driver = "com.sybase.jdbc4.jdbc.SybDriver",
      user = "username",
      password = "password",
      fetchsize = "10000",
      dbtable = "mytableschema.mytablename",  # NOTE, same result if I use something like `query = "SELECT * FROM mytablename"` 
      pushDownPredicate = TRUE 
    ) 
  ) 
  
# using this sparklyr function to avoid complicating the query by trying to retain order
#    this will help us make sure to produce the exact same SQL as above for an "apples to apples" comparison
  withr::with_options(
    new = list(sparklyr.dplyr_distinct.impl = "tbl_lazy"),
    code = {
      monthly_count_lazy <- my_table %>%
        dplyr::group_by(month_numeric) %>%
        dplyr::summarize(
          count_rows = dplyr::n()
        ) 
     })
       
     monthly_count_sql <- monthly_count_lazy %>%
       dbplyr::sql_render()
     print(monthly_count_sql)
    # prints out following SQL (showing it is identical to the query we manually passed in the other approach)
    # <SQL> SELECT `month_numeric`, COUNT(*) AS `count_rows`
    # FROM `mytablename`
    # GROUP BY `month_numeric`
    
     monthly_count <- monthly_count_lazy %>%
       dplyr::collect()
```

Is there another way to ask spark to push down the query to the underlying database?

I've looked and looked for options, but couldn't find anything.  I'd much rather just specify the table name up front, and use dplyr pipelines to define the rest of my query and then collect, like I do in the second example.  But if it's going to pull all the data into spark and redo the aggregation there, it's not going to be efficient.

This reference made it seem like it might be possible, but didn't give any real instructions on how to go about it:

https://microsites.databricks.com/sites/default/files/2022-07/Spark-Data-Source-V2-Performance-Improvement_Aggregate-Push-Down.pdf

And this reference helped me realize the first approach would work:

https://docs.databricks.com/external-data/jdbc.html#language-scala

But I haven't found any spark setting or sparklyr setting that would help clarify if I can make my regular pipeline push down the work to the underlying database.

title: Yarn cluster app lookup should prefer the config setting to the environment variable
description: [In yarn-cluster.R](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/eb3e795447887908d9e795512ad08eeeb32eede5/R/yarn_cluster.R#L13), the app is looked up by the environment variable over the config value `sparklyr.yarn.cluster.lookup.username`. These should be reversed, as `sparklyr.yarn.cluster.lookup.username` is narrower in scope than the environment variable `USER`.

title: dbplyr/tidyr::fill() does not work with Databricks ODBC driver
description:
This is similar to https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/651 and https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1026, but for Databricks the server expects:

`LAST_VALUE(expr, true)`

instead of

`LAST_VALUE(expr) IGNORE NULLS`

The `true` there means _"yes, ignore nulls"_: https://docs.databricks.com/sql/language-manual/functions/last_value.html

I was able to make it `fill()` work by running this prior to calling it:

```
`last_value_sql.Spark SQL` <- function(con, x) {
  dbplyr:::build_sql("LAST_VALUE(", ident(as.character(x)), ", true)", con = con)
}
```

Thanks to all involved with this great resource.

I am posting this issue here as oriented at https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1083.

I tried to use `group_by` and `spark_apply` on the Parquet file but the process is extremely slow. The input Parquet data is 128GB saved on HDFS. The grouping variable has $2^21$ unique values.  What I did is I apply logistic regression on each subset (each subset is the same size, 64kb) groupby the the grouping variable, collect the coefficients estimate from each logistic regression on the subset and return the average of the coefficients. Here is my code:

```r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)

spark_version <- "2.2.0"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-client", version = spark_version)
    start_time <- Sys.time()
    ## spark configuration
    config <- spark_config()   # Create a config to tune memory
    config$spark.executor.instances <- 199
    config$spark.network.timeout <- "800s"
    config$spark.sql.shuffle.partitions="2000"
    config$spark.executor.memory <- "20G"
    config[["sparklyr.shell.driver-memory"]] <- "10G"
    config$spark.executor.cores <- 2
    # create the Spark context

title: Export additional functions to make extensions easier to write
description:
I'm writing additional spark_read/write_* functions in an extension (apache.sedona). They rely on the generic Spark SQL read `spark.read.format("my new format).option(...).load("my path")` like so many of the read/write functions in Sparklyr.
Would it be possible to export some of the internal functions that are used by these readers?
I'm thinking:
* `spark_data_read_generic`: invokes the generic Spark SQL read
* `spark_data_write_generic`: invokes the generic Spark SQL write
* `spark_partition_register_df`: registers the sdf and returns a tbl
* `spark_read_compat_param`: creates a default name for the table

The alternative is either to use them non-exported (:::) but that will not pass on CRAN, or to copy the copy in our package, and that's not great either.

title: `spark_apply()` with `group_by` parameter and `arrow` package returns summary results by batch, not group
description:
# Summary

It seems that using the `arrow` package (v9.0.0.1) with `sparklyr::spark_apply()` (v1.7.5) and its `group_by` parameter may cause unexpected results due to batches being used by the worker(s). Namely, summary results are returned by batch rather than by group. Detaching `arrow` leads to summary results by group rather than by batch. My apologies if this is expected behavior or previously reported (I couldn't find it) or if this belongs under `arrow`'s issues.

_Unfortunately, my real problem demands results by group but I receive results by batch even **without** using `arrow.` I'll add that reprex if I figure it out._

# Observed

title: Multiple warnings : "ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT"
description:
## ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT

**Issue** 
Sparklyr script output is filled with the same warning message (over and over again) :

_ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead?_

I have had this problem for ~ 1 year (probably a bit more). 
I tried the solution : 
```r
options(sparklyr.dplyr_distinct.impl = "tbl_lazy")
```
but the warning messages are still there (see reproducible example). 
I have the same issue everywhere (local, databricks, etc.)
I don't know exactly what is causing the warning but it appears generally when I use dplyr::group_by() with dplyr::arrange().

---
**Reproducible example** 
```r
library("dplyr"); library("sparklyr") 
spark_version <- "3.1.3"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)
options(sparklyr.dplyr_distinct.impl = "tbl_lazy") 

# --- coping mtcars data into spark for the example
sdf_mtcars = sdf_copy_to(sc = sc, x = mtcars, name = "sdf_mtcars")

# --- example generating the warning message (twice)
# note : I had to use mutate() twice to make the warning appear
# the warning does not appear in this simple example with if only one of the two columns cum_mpg or max_mpg is created
example_mtcars = sdf_mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  arrange(mpg, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(cum_mpg = cumsum(mpg)) %>%
  mutate(max_mpg = cummax(mpg)) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  sdf_collect()
```
**Warning messages** : 
1: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
2: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 

---
**utils::sessionInfo()** 
- R version 4.2.1 (2022-06-23)
- other attached packages:
[1] dbplyr_2.2.1   sparklyr_1.7.8 dplyr_1.0.10  

(but the warning is the same with other older versions of those packages, R and spark)

Thank you.

title: Ordering issue with sparklyr::nest
description:
Hi all, 

We encountered an issue with nesting in sparklyr, specifically with order of nested values when SDF is being repartitioned.
Having only 1 partition solves this example, but for larger data sets looks like sparklyr::nest repartitions automatically, so there is no way (that we could find) to solve it.

```r
# sparklyr_1.7.1
spark_version <- "3.1.1"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

data <- dplyr::tibble(
  id = c("id001", "id001", "id001", "id001", "id001", "id001"), 
  to_nest_lvl1 = c("x", "x", "y", "y", "z", "z"),
  to_nest_lvl2 = c("a", "b", "a", "b", "a", "b"))

data
# # A tibble: 6 × 3
# id    to_nest_lvl1 to_nest_lvl2
# <chr> <chr>        <chr>       
# 1 id001 x            a           
# 2 id001 x            b           
# 3 id001 y            a           
# 4 id001 y            b           
# 5 id001 z            a           
# 6 id001 z            b    

# First nest lvl1, then lvl2
data %>%
  tidyr::nest(lvl1 = to_nest_lvl1) %>%
  tidyr::nest(lvl2 = to_nest_lvl2)
# # A tibble: 1 × 3
# id    lvl1             lvl2            
# <chr> <list>           <list>          
# 1 id001 <tibble [3 × 1]> <tibble [2 × 1]>

# Same on repartitioned sdf
data %>%
  sparklyr::sdf_copy_to(sc, ., random_string()) %>%
  sparklyr::sdf_repartition(2) %>%
  tidyr::nest(lvl1 = to_nest_lvl1) %>%
  tidyr::nest(lvl2 = to_nest_lvl2)
# # Source: spark<?> [?? x 3]
# id    lvl1       lvl2      
# <chr> <list>     <list>    
# 1 id001 <list [3]> <list [1]>
# 2 id001 <list [3]> <list [1]>
```

If you collect and View nested SDF, you can see that order of first nesting process was changed.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/51319014/163540556-28bdbc62-8db3-4da2-b282-e44b69cf48ee.png)

title: Analogue to createTable and recoverPartitions
description:
In the native Spark API (e.g. `SparkR`) the process of running daily jobs which build up the same table is pretty straightforward:

```
library(SparkR)
library(magrittr)
# ... ETL ...

S3PATH = ...
TBL = 'my_table.my_schema'

SDF %>% write %>% partitionBy('column1', 'column2') %>% 
  mode('overwrite') %>% parquet(S3PATH)

sql(sprintf('DROP TABLE IF EXISTS %s', TBL))
createTable(TBL, S3PATH)
recoverPartitions(TBL)
```

Unfortunately, I don't see a straightforward way to imitate this in the `sparklyr` API.

`spark_write_parquet` covers the first bit pretty effectively, but I don't see a way to register a table to an existing S3 bucket besides manually (and laboriously) constructing a query of the form

```
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS my_schema.my_table (
  {{manually specified schema}}
)
PARTITIONED BY (
  {{manually specified partitions}}
)
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION 'S3PATH'
```

And then, even more tediously,

```
ALTER TABLE my_schema.my_table
ADD IF NOT EXISTS PARTITION ( {{manually specified again}} )
```

Is there any plan to have something like `spark_register_table` and `spark_recover_partitions`?
