title: Working with datasets within the Foreach-loop with sparklyr
description:
Hey Guys,

with the [update of sparklyr](https://blog.rstudio.com/2020/05/06/sparklyr-1-2/) you can now run the foreach loop in parallel via spark.
An example is given on the page by:
```r
library(sparklyr)
library(foreach)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.4")

registerDoSpark(sc)

foreach(i = 1:3, .combine = 'c') %dopar% {
  sqrt(i)
}
```
In this case, however, only calculations are performed and no local datasets need to be accessed within the Foreach-loop. But in my case I have to work with records within the-Foreach loop.
If I now execute the Foreach-loop with spark the records are not detected and I get an error message. When I load the records with `copy_to` into the Spark environment, I cannot access them properly within the Foreach-loop. 

Is there a way to use the Foreach-loop for spark for my case, or do I have to use an alternative to the Foreach-loop?

You can see a part of my code below, but the parallelization was still executed locally with SNOW. The goal now is to translate the code so that it runs with Spark. 


```r
xtsDataTrainTransformedList <- 
      foreach(slice = 1:length(listSlices), .options.snow = opts,
              .packages = c("dplyr","data.table", "forecast"), .export = ls(envir = globalenv())) %dopar% {
                
                xtsDataTrain <- window(xtsData, 
                                       start = listSlices[[slice]]$startTrain, 
                                       end = listSlices[[slice]]$endTrain)
                
                TransformationDT <- data.table(BoxCox = FALSE,
                                               Stationarization = TRUE,
                                               Standardization = TRUE)
                
                xtsDataTrainTransformed <- applyTransformation(xtsData = xtsDataTrain,
                                                               TransformationDT = TransformationDT,
                                                               param = param)
                
                return(xtsDataTrainTransformed$xtsDataTransformed)
              }
```
Thank you already now for the Feedback!

title: support the equivalent of `dplyr::sample_frac(..., weight = ...)` in sparklyr
description:
As discussed in https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/issues/2592, because there is no Spark SQL equivalent of it yet, it cannot be implemented as part of some R-to-SQL translation layer in dplyr, but will instead need to be implemented as a completely separate helper method in sparklyr.

Regardless of what form it might take, this does feel like a feature that is sorely lacking. So, it should be part of sparklyr 1.4.

title: Only apply arrow format env var for spark < 3
description:
For compatibility with older versions of Arrow used by Spark, we set this environment variable when writing arrow data: https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/master/R/core_arrow.R#L3-L4

Spark 3.0 will include a bump of the Arrow version it uses (in Java) from 0.12.0 to 0.15.1 (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/26133). So with that Arrow version, we won't need this legacy format flag. (It shouldn't crash if we use the flag, but there was a reason for the format change in Arrow, and we should avoid legacy codepaths if we can.)

What this means is that we should move where that env var is set (temporarily or otherwise) to the appropriate place that know what Spark version it's communicating with. As it stands currently in core_arrow.R, the spark context isn't known.

FR: Sliding Window on Stream
description:
Hi,

I'm not sure if this is already supported but I was not able to find it, therefore this feature request. It would be nice to define sliding windows on a stream. This seems to be possible when using pyspark:

```
# Group the data by window and word and compute the count of each group
windowedCounts = words.groupBy(
    window(words.timestamp, "10 minutes", "5 minutes"),
    words.word
).count()
```

I'm not aware of an equivalent of the "window" function within sparklyr. In the pyspark example the desired measure is calculated every 5 seconds over a sliding window of 10 seconds.

title: SQL translation for lubridate functions are overwriting Hive functions
description:
Since release of [dbplyr 1.4.0](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/news/index.html#sql-translations), Hive functions like `hour`, `minute` and `second` aren't working properly. `dbplyr` is translating them to `EXTRACT`, which is not recognized by Spark, causing an `org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.parser.ParseException` error.

Example:
```
mutate(spark.tbl, date_hour = hour(date))

# SQL: SELECT EXTRACT(hour FROM `date`) AS `date_hour`
```
Temporary solution (more difficult to read):
```
mutate(spark.tbl, date_hour = sql("hour(`date`)"))

# SQL: SELECT hour(`date`) AS `date_hour`
```

title: Set timezone when sending POSIXt data to Spark
description:
https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-8566 was reported on `arrow`. In brief, in the latest release of `arrow`, we [fixed a bug in datetime data handling](https://github.com/apache/arrow/commit/507762fa51d17e61f08d36d3626ab8b8df716198): previously, a "GMT" timezone was hardcoded everywhere, while now we send the actual timezone. It appears that when this timezone is not set, at least in the version of Spark that the user was on, Spark crashes. 

I'm not sure where exactly the bug lies--it's possible that the Arrow Java library Spark is using doesn't have the same expectations as the C++ library that R is using--though I'll dig a bit more. Regardless, we can be defensive and protect against this failure in `sparklyr`. Since R interprets POSIXt data without a timezone set as being in the system's current timezone, doing something like this on columns of data before sending to Spark should fix the issue:

```r
if (inherits(x, "POSIXt") && is.null(attr(x, "tzone"))) {
  attr(x, "tzone") <- Sys.timezone()
}
```

Would you be interested in a PR?

title: Setting maxRecordsPerBatch when using Arrow and spark_apply does not work as expected
description:
Hello sparklyr team,

The issue is that when setting value of maxRecordsPerBatch to anything larger than **10,000** spark_apply uses 10,000 instead of the specified value in the configuration.

This problem is related to the closed issue #2243. The solution provided in the closed ticket doesn't seem to work. 

Below is a reproducible example

```r
# Setting enviroment variable: JAVA_HOME and SPARK_HOME
Sys.setenv(JAVA_HOME="/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk1.8.0_202.jdk/Contents/Home/")
Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = "~/spark/spark-2.4.3-bin-hadoop2.7/")

# Loading libraries
library(sparklyr)
library(arrow)

# disconnecting all spark connection
sparklyr::spark_disconnect_all()

# Use case 1: maxRecordsPerBatch < 10,000
conf <- spark_config()
conf$spark.r.libpaths = c("~/Documents/Rpackages,/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.6/Resources/library")
conf$spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch <- 5000 # less than 10,000

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = conf)
sdf_len(sc, 2 * 10^4) %>% spark_apply(nrow) #result IS as expected

sparklyr::spark_disconnect(sc)

# Use case 2: maxRecordsPerBatch > 10,000, passed as numeric
conf2 <- spark_config()
conf2$spark.r.libpaths = c("~/Documents/Rpackages,/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.6/Resources/library")
conf2$spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch <- 20000 # more than 10,000

sc2 <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = conf2)
sdf_len(sc2, 2 * 10^4) %>% spark_apply(nrow) #result NOT as expected: 10000 per batch
```

title: Error with ft_chisq_selector and ml_cross_validator
description:
I am trying to optimize the parameter num_top_features from ft_chisq_selector, using ml_cross_validator. I get this error: 
```
Error: `x` must not be NULL.
```

The pipeline and CV work if I omit the ft_chisq_selector parameters from the cross-validator.

This part works fine:
```r
# Prepare data
Titanic %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(Survived= ifelse(Survived== 'Yes', 1, 0)) %>%
  copy_to(sc, .) ->
  data

# Pipeline
pipeline <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_string_indexer(input_col = 'Class', output_col = 'Class_ind') %>%
  ft_string_indexer(input_col = 'Sex', output_col = 'Sex_ind') %>%
  ft_one_hot_encoder(input_col = 'Class_ind', output_col = 'Class_enc', drop_last = FALSE) %>%
  ft_one_hot_encoder(input_col = 'Sex_ind', output_col = 'Sex_enc', drop_last = FALSE) %>%
  ft_vector_assembler(input_cols = c('Class_enc', 'Sex_enc'), output_col = 'features') %>%
  ft_chisq_selector(features_col= 'features', output_col= 'features_selected', label_col= 'Survived', 
                    selector_type = 'numTopFeatures', num_top_features = 1) %>%
  ml_logistic_regression(features_col = "features_selected", label_col = "Survived", family= "binomial")

# Transform and fit (works)
ml_fit_and_transform(pipeline, data)
```

Defining the cross-validator produces the error:
```r
# Cross validator (produces error)
cv <- ml_cross_validator(
  sc,
  estimator = pipeline,
  estimator_param_maps = list(
    chisq_selector = list(
      num_top_features = c(1, 2)
    ),
    logistic_regression = list(
      elastic_net_param = c(0.5),
      reg_param = c(0.01)
    )
  ),
  evaluator = ml_binary_classification_evaluator(sc, label_col = "Survived"),
  num_folds = 10
)

cv_model <- ml_fit(cv, data)
```

Defining the cross validator without the chisq_selector parameters works fine.

title: Spark function returning SeqWrapper object is not converted to an array or list
description:
In the Spark NLP library is a method on the `LightPipeline` object called `annotateJava()`. According to the Spark NLP Scala docs this method returns `Map[String, List[String]]`. When I call this method inside the sparknlp package the resulting R object is a named list of `scala.collection.convert.Wrappers$SeqWrapper` objects. These `SeqWrapper` classes should become R arrays or lists in R.

Here is a reproducible example:
```r
remotes::install_github("r-spark/sparknlp", ref = "dev")
library(sparklyr)
library(sparknlp)

version <- Sys.getenv("SPARK_VERSION", unset = "2.4.3")

sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(master = "local", version = version, config = spark_config())

pipeline <- nlp_pretrained_pipeline(sc, "explain_document_ml", lang = "en")

testDoc <- "French author who helped pioneer the science-fiction genre. Verne wrate about space, air, and underwater travel before navigable aircrast and practical submarines were invented, and before any means of space travel had been devised."

result <- nlp_annotate(pipeline, testDoc)
result
```
you'll see that the `result` list contains something like this:
```

<jobj[44]>
  scala.collection.convert.Wrappers$SeqWrapper
```

description:
Spark has good support for nested structures using the `struct` and `array` types. Here I've nested `iris` in a way that would naturally map to a spark data.frame with one character column and one array column where each element in the array is a struct (i.e., row of the nested data.frame)
```
iris_nst <- iris %>%
  rename_all(function(x){gsub("\\.", "_", x)}) %>%
  tidyr::nest(Sepal_Length, Sepal_Width, Petal_Length, Petal_Width)
iris_nst
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   Species    data                 
#   <fct>      <list>               
# 1 setosa     <data.frame [50 × 4]>
# 2 versicolor <data.frame [50 × 4]>
# 3 virginica  <data.frame [50 × 4]>
```

However, `copy_to` only supports basic types
```
copy_to(sc, iris_nst)
 Error: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Invaid type list
	at sparklyr.SQLUtils$.getSQLDataType(sqlutils.scala:61)
	at sparklyr.SQLUtils$.createStructField(sqlutils.scala:66)
	at sparklyr.SQLUtils.createStructField(sqlutils.scala)
	at sun.reflect.GeneratedMethodAccessor31.invoke(Unknown Source)
	at sun.reflect.DelegatingMethodAccessorImpl.invoke(DelegatingMethodAccessorImpl.java:43)
	at java.lang.reflect.Method.invoke(Method.java:483)
	at sparklyr.Invoke.invoke(invoke.scala:137)
```

The clunky work-arounds that I've used are (1) map the nested columns to JSON before strings before calling `copy_to` and (2) writing the entire data.frame to JSON (locally or on HDFS) and reading it in using `spark_read_json`. Option (1) changes the data and makes the data hard to use in spark-land, option (2) is more functional, but requires an extra step.

Are there any plans to support list-types in `sparklyr.SQLUtils$.createStructField`?

title: spark_apply and data.table
description:
Hello,

I tried to use data.table in spark_apply since I have data management pipeline done with data.table and I wanted to apply it to a spark dataframe with spark_apply but it doesn't seem to work, am I doing something wrong ?

```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)
                    
y <- spark_apply(
  iris_tbl,
  function(e) {
    library(data.table)
    x <- collect(e)

    x <- setDT(x)
    
    x <- x[
      , log := log(Sepal_Length)
    ]
    
    x
  },
  group_by = "Species"
)
```

I know I can use dyplyr instead of data.table but I would like to know why it doesn't work ?

Thanks you !

title: `summary()` does not return coefficients for `ml_linear_regression` when `fit_intercept = FALSE`
description:
When suppressing the intercept in `ml_linear_regression()` using the `fit_intercept = F` parameter, the returned object does not display the coefficients in the expected way. The coefficients are there in the model object, but it seems like one of the summarization steps is not behaving correctly, probably due to the null intercept. 

Setup 
``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(sparklyr)

spark_version <- "2.4.3"

sc <- spark_connect(master = 'local',
                    version = spark_version)

# copy mtcars into spark
mtcars_tbl <- copy_to(sc, 
                      df = mtcars, 
                      overwrite = TRUE)
```

This works as expected:
```r
# fit LM with intercept 
fit_with_intercept <- mtcars_tbl %>%
  ml_linear_regression(mpg ~ wt + cyl, 
                       fit_intercept = TRUE) # param set to TRUE (default)

# Works as expected: 
fit_with_intercept %>% summary()
#> Deviance Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -4.2893 -1.5512 -0.4684  1.5743  6.1004 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)          wt         cyl 
#>   39.686261   -3.190972   -1.507795 
#> 
#> R-Squared: 0.8302
#> Root Mean Squared Error: 2.444
```

This does not work correctly. Should return `NULL` for the coefficients
```r
# fit LM without intercept 
fit_without_intercept <- mtcars_tbl %>%
  ml_linear_regression(mpg ~ wt + cyl,
                       fit_intercept = FALSE) # param set to FALSE 

# Does not return coefficients 
fit_without_intercept %>% summary()
#> Deviance Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -13.466  -6.181   1.476  10.597  22.996 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> NULL
#> 
#> R-Squared: 0.735
#> Root Mean Squared Error: 10.78

# Coefficients seem to be missing in fit object 
fit_without_intercept$coefficients
#> NULL
```
Coefficients are there, just not pulled into the summary part of the fit object. 
```r
# But coefficients do exist in the model object within the fit object
fit_without_intercept$model$coefficients
#> [1] 1.173788 2.187405

# The coefficients in the model object appear to be the correct coefs 
#   when compared to the regular, in-memory, lm-fit. 
lm(data = mtcars, 
   formula = mpg ~ -1 + wt + cyl) %>% 
  coef()
#>       wt      cyl 
#> 1.173788 2.187405
```

title: Group_by and mutate
description:
Hi, 
 I'm trying to make a cummulative product by groups and add in each step the result. When I do this with a R dataframe all goes OK, but when I have tried to do it with sparklyr this operations add the same result (the final comproduct) at all rows.

Example:
I create a simple dataframe
df_prueba <- data.frame(
    id = rep(c(1,2), each = 5),
    values = rep(1:5, 2))

**With a data.frame:**

df_prueba %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(acumulacion = cumprod(values))

 2     1      2           2
 3     1      3           6
 4     1      4          24
 5     1      5         120
 6     2      1           1

title: "Unexpected end of input" error when using spark_apply
description:
Hi,

I am running into a timing-related error when using `spark_apply`.  I am running on Windows with `master = "local"`.  When this situation occurs, the spark job fails out completely (i.e. it doesn't retry) and the entire job has to be re-executed.  

The main symptom I see is that the `spark.log` file contains:
```
Error: unexpected end of input
Execution halted
```

A broader context for the errors is a sequence such as the following:
```

20/03/18 18:53:19 INFO sparklyr: Worker (3179) launching command Rscript --vanilla C:\Users\****\AppData\Local\spark\spark-2.4.3-bin-hadoop2.7\tmp\local\spark-9ceaf65c-67a9-40ea-a953-08e1bfbe4078\userFiles-5f79455b-d40c-432b-93e9-7810d02130d6\sparkworker.R 3179 49310 FALSE;8880;localhost;FALSE;FALSE;FALSE

.

20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Session (8491) is waiting for sparklyr client to connect to port 49317
20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Worker (8491) is starting rscript
Error: unexpected end of input
Execution halted
20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Worker (8491) using source file C:\Users\****\AppData\Local\spark\spark-2.4.3-bin-hadoop2.7\tmp\local\spark-9ceaf65c-67a9-40ea-a953-08e1bfbe4078\userFiles-5f79455b-d40c-432b-93e9-7810d02130d6\sparkworker.R
20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Worker (8491) launching command Rscript --vanilla C:\Users\****\AppData\Local\spark\spark-2.4.3-bin-hadoop2.7\tmp\local\spark-9ceaf65c-67a9-40ea-a953-08e1bfbe4078\userFiles-5f79455b-d40c-432b-93e9-7810d02130d6\sparkworker.R 8491 49317 FALSE;8880;localhost;FALSE;FALSE;FALSE
20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Worker (8491) is starting R process
20/03/18 18:53:21 ERROR sparklyr: Worker (3179) failed to complete R process
(20/03/18 18:53:21 ERROR sparklyr: Worker (3179) failed to run rscript: ,java.lang.Exception: sparklyr worker rscript failure with status 1, check worker logs for details.)
20/03/18 18:53:21 INFO sparklyr: Worker (3179) completed wait using lock for RScript
20/03/18 18:53:21 ERROR Executor: Exception in task 72.0 in stage 2.0 (TID 573)
java.lang.Exception: sparklyr worker rscript failure with status 1, check worker logs for details.
	at sparklyr.Rscript.init(rscript.scala:83)
	at sparklyr.WorkerApply$$anon$2.run(workerapply.scala:123)

```
In this example, session 3179 starts up then a couple seconds later session 8491 starts up.  I believe the `Error: unexpected end of input` is coming from session 3179, and that session subsequently fails out.

After looking at the `sparklyr` code, I believe the root issue is that both sessions are trying to use the exact same file location for `sparkworker.R`.  In this example, session 3179 has written that file but while the `Rscript` process for 3179 is still reading `sparkworker.R`, session 8491 rewrites the file out from underneath 3179.

This is definitely a timing related issue, but I am able to reproduce it pretty consistently with the following code:
```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

df_result <- sdf_len(sc, 500, repartition = 500) %>%
  spark_apply(function(df) df * 10) %>%
  collect()
```

I tested a fix/workaround in `workerapply.scala` to include the `sessionId` in the `sparkerworker.R` file name so that each session has its own copy:
```scala
  def workerSourceFile(rscript: Rscript, sessionId: Int): String = {
    val rsources = new Sources()
    val source = rsources.sources

    val tempFile: File = new File(rscript.getScratchDir() + File.separator + "sparkworker_" + sessionId.toString + ".R")
    val outStream: FileWriter = new FileWriter(tempFile)
    outStream.write(source)
    outStream.flush()

    tempFile.getAbsolutePath()
  }
```
So far this seems to avoid/resolve the issue, though there may be better solutions (e.g. perhaps just write the file once instead of re-writing for every session?).

Thanks!

title: Sparklyr and Arrow Max Records
description:
Hey Sparklyr Team,

I noticed that when using spark_apply with arrow, there is a default maximum records per batch of 10000 if I forget to set "spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch" when connecting to spark. This is the line of code: [spark_apply line 191](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/master/R/spark_apply.R#L191).

A demonstration of bad results when using the default settings is here: https://github.com/rychien-official/sparklyr_maxrecords/blob/master/readme.md

I am wondering if there is a technical reason for hard coding maximum records per batch during spark connection? It would be nice to modify spark_apply to be able to pass through maximum records per batch as a parameter. I'd be happy to create a pull request and do so.

Thanks!

-Ryan

 .         sessionId, config = config, isStarting = TRUE)
 . }, error = function(e) {
 .     abort_shell(paste("Failed while connecting to sparklyr to port (", 
 .         gatewayPort, if (spark_master_is_yarn_cluster(master, 
 .             config)) {
 .             paste0(") and address (", gatewayAddress)
 .         }
 .         else {
 .             ""
 .         }, ") for sessionid (", sessionId, "): ", e$message, 
 .         sep = ""), spark_submit_path, shell_args, output_file, 
 .         error_file)
 . })
5. tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
6. tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
7. value[[3L]](cond)
8. abort_shell(paste("Failed while connecting to sparklyr to port (", 
 .     gatewayPort, if (spark_master_is_yarn_cluster(master, config)) {
 .         paste0(") and address (", gatewayAddress)
 .     } else {
 .         ""
 .     }, ") for sessionid (", sessionId, "): ", e$message, sep = ""), 
 .     spark_submit_path, shell_args, output_file, error_file)
9. withr::with_options(list(warning.length = 8000), {
 .     maxRows <- 100
 .     Sys.sleep(1)
 .     logLines <- if (!is.null(output_file) && file.exists(output_file)) {
 .         outputContent <- readLines(output_file)
 .         paste(tail(outputContent, n = maxRows), collapse = "\n")
 .     }
 .     else ""
 .     errorLines <- if (!is.null(error_file) && file.exists(error_file)) 
 .         paste(tail(readLines(error_file), n = maxRows), collapse = "\n")
 .     else ""
 .     stop(paste(message, "\n", if (!is.null(spark_submit_path)) 
 .         paste("    Path: ", spark_submit_path, "\n", sep = "")
 .     else "", if (!is.null(shell_args)) 
 .         paste("    Parameters: ", paste(shell_args, collapse = ", "), 
 .             "\n", sep = "")
 .     else "", if (!is.null(output_file)) 
 .         paste("    Log: ", output_file, "\n", sep = "")
 .     else "", "\n\n", if (!is.null(output_file)) 
 .         "---- Output Log ----\n"
 .     else "", logLines, "\n\n", if (!is.null(error_file)) 
 .         "---- Error Log ----\n"
 .     else "", errorLines, sep = ""))
 . })
10. force(code)
11. stop(paste(message, "\n", if (!is.null(spark_submit_path)) paste("    Path: ", 
  .     spark_submit_path, "\n", sep = "") else "", if (!is.null(shell_args)) paste("    Parameters: ", 
  .     paste(shell_args, collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "") else "", 
  .     if (!is.null(output_file)) paste("    Log: ", output_file, 
  .         "\n", sep = "") else "", "\n\n", if (!is.null(output_file)) "---- Output Log ----\n" else "", 
  .     logLines, "\n\n", if (!is.null(error_file)) "---- Error Log ----\n" else "", 
  .     errorLines, sep = ""))

title: Fix unit tests that attempt to create tables that already exist
description:
# Reporting an Issue with sparklyr
Currently many unit tests are failing with Databricks Connect, because each test assume a clean slate. One consequence is when test attempts to create a table that has already been created by another test, we encounter a failure message.

We can fix this by one of the following two approaches:
1. Randomizing the names of tables that are created by tests and used
2. Cleaning the state after each test (e.g., removing tables)

We think No 2 is more sustainable and is generally a better practice.

title: Use a unique filename for bundle files
description:
# Reporting an Issue with sparklyr
When multiple users share a cluster to run sparklyr jobs that invoke `spark_apply()` they sometime run into the following failure 
```
Failed to fetch spark://10.139.64.13:45141/files/packages.tar during dependency update
	at org.apache.spark.executor.Executor$$anonfun$updateDependencies$3.apply(Executor.scala:936)
	at org.apache.spark.executor.Executor$$anonfun$updateDependencies$3.apply(Executor.scala:927)
	at scala.collection.TraversableLike$WithFilter$$anonfun$foreach$1.apply(TraversableLike.scala:733)
	at scala.collection.mutable.HashMap$$anonfun$foreach$1.apply(HashMap.scala:130)
	at scala.collection.mutable.HashMap$$anonfun$foreach$1.apply(HashMap.scala:130)
	at scala.collection.mutable.HashTable$class.foreachEntry(HashTable.scala:236)
	at scala.collection.mutable.HashMap.foreachEntry(HashMap.scala:40)
	at scala.collection.mutable.HashMap.foreach(HashMap.scala:130)
	at scala.collection.TraversableLike$WithFilter.foreach(TraversableLike.scala:732)
	at org.apache.spark.executor.Executor.updateDependencies(Executor.scala:927)
	at org.apache.spark.executor.Executor$TaskRunner.run(Executor.scala:486)
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1149)
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:624)
	at java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:748)
Caused by: java.lang.RuntimeException: Stream '/files/packages.tar' was not found.
```
We believe this is due to using the [same file name](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/9bf75dcec51196aa3bffcf16dc5c66e01ed71e68/R/spark_apply_bundle.R#L9) `packages.tar` in all jobs.

# Solution
Simply change `spark_apply_bundle_file()` to prepend a GUID to `packages.tar`.

title: spark_apply and spark_write_avro are extremely slow
description:
Hello, I am having trouble getting spark_apply and spark_write_avro (or spark_write_*) to run quickly. Below is some example code and the configuration I am using. This is on a 4 node yarn cluster with 31 cores each (32 total, 1 reserved). This is a sandbox cluster and nobody else is using the cluster when I am running this code.

The first time I run a spark_apply in a session, it takes a very long time (several hundred seconds) on a fairly small file (50 columns, ~6000 rows). And it doesn't even matter what the spark_apply is doing (see the below code for an example).

The second time I run spark_apply in the same session, it takes considerably less, but it still takes a long time to print the results. Worse, when I go to write out the output to avro or csv, it also takes a long time to write (2 columns, ~6000 rows). My first thought is there is a configuration problem, but I don't see what configuration could change this.

Timing problems are the same when I run this interactively via R or through `nohup Rscript file.R &`. 

Is this behavior expected (cluster overhead) or is there something going on here that needs fixed?

```r
spark_version <- "2.4.0"
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
require(sparklyr)
require(sparkavro)
require(config)
require(caret)
require(dplyr)
})

config <- get(file="spark.yml")
Sys.setenv(YARN_CONF_DIR= "yarn_conf") # this just contains the name node and resource manager urls
con <- spark_connect(config=config)

myData <- myData %>%
  rename_all(toupper) %>% # goto uppercase
  select(all_of(fromVars)) %>% # subset to wanted columns
  rename_at(vars(all_of(fromVars)), ~toVars) %>% # map input names to output names
  compute()

sdf_dim(myData) # Output: [1] 6213   50

####################################
## Now for the part that takes forever
start <- proc.time()

# I could use real code below, but this doNothing takes about the same time :(
doNothing <- spark_apply(myData, function(x) {return(x)})

end <- proc.time()
print(end-start)

#  1.171   0.833 266.349  # ive seen this go up to 500

####################################

# real example code below
dataTransformation <- function(df, context)
{
  mapvalues <- plyr::mapvalues
  df$new_field=mapvalues(df$old_field, c('A','B',NaN,NA,' ','" "',''), c(1,0,0,0,0,0,0),F)

score <- function(df, model, outputNames)
{
```

title: [Question]: How do I filter a stream such that only the last 5 entries are kept
description:
Hi,

I have an input stream that sends quite a lot of data. Since I'm only interested in the last 100 entries I'd like to get rid of all the rest.

My approach is as follows:
`
input_stream <- stream_read_scoket(sc, options = list(host = "localhost", port = 9997L))
output_stream <- stream %>% stream_watermark() %>% stream_write_memory(name = "last_100_only")
`

But non of the following filters seems to work:

# top_n
`
input_stream <- stream_read_scoket(sc, options = list(host = "localhost", port = 9997L))
output_stream <- stream %>% stream_watermark() %>% top_n(100, timestamp) %>% stream_write_memory(name = "last_100_only")
`

# arrange and head
`
input_stream <- stream_read_scoket(sc, options = list(host = "localhost", port = 9997L))
output_stream <- stream %>% stream_watermark() %>% arrange(desc(timestamp)) %> head(100) %>% stream_write_memory(name = "last_100_only")
`

How do I filter an incoming stream, such that not all input is kept?

title: spark_apply error when using if() and logical evaluation
description:
Hi

I'm trying to debug some code I'm trying to run using spark_apply. When it runs, I get an error, and I think I've managed to isolate the behaviour that causes it. 

In short, the code contains an evaluation of the number of unique values in a data frame column. If there are fewer than 2 unique values, it should return an error. Otherwise, it should return a value. The evaluation happens OK, and the result of the evaluation can be returned fine. But if the result of the evaluation is used in an if() statement, there's an error, *even if the condition is not met*. This only seems to happen if the first 10 values in the column are the same - any kind of mixing of the first 10 values makes it work OK. Specifying a column type doesn't seem to help. Assigning the outcome of the evaluation to an object and then using that object in the if() statement doesn't seem to help. The error is reproducible in Spark 2.2.0 and Spark 2.4.3, and with R 3.5.1 and R 3.5.3.

It wouldn't be possible to shuffle data to ensure there weren't 10 of the same cases in a row in the real function, so I'm stuck now.

Any ideas about how to deal with this, or any idea of what is going on, would be really appreciated!

Reproducible example as follows:

```
library(sparklyr)
Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = "/usr/hdp/current/spark2-client")
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

## define functions
# function 1 counts n unique, evalutes whether < 2, returns result
countfunc_works <- function(x){
  n_unique <- length(unique(x[,1]))
  return(n_unique<2)
}

# function 2 counts n unique, returns n_unique-1  if < 2, else returns n unique
# note in full code, would have a stop() statement instead of return(n_unique-1)
countfunc_fails <- function(x){
  n_unique <- length(unique(x[,1]))
  if(n_unique<2){
    return(n_unique-1)
  }
  return(n_unique)
}

## define data
# data with 10 zeros and 1 one
x1 <- c(rep(0, 10), 1)
exdat1 <- data.frame("x"=x1)
exdat1_spark <- copy_to(sc, exdat1)

# data with 9 zeros, 1 one, and 1 zero
x2 <- c(rep(0, 9), 1, 0)
exdat2 <- data.frame("x"=x2)
exdat2_spark <-copy_to(sc, exdat2)


## run functions
# both work, condition evaluates as FALSE, returns value
spark_apply(exdat1_spark, countfunc_works)
spark_apply(exdat2_spark, countfunc_works)

# exdat1 fails, exdat2 works
spark_apply(exdat1_spark, countfunc_fails)
spark_apply(exdat2_spark, countfunc_fails)
```

description:
I found the following issue on databricks (6.2 ML) and local spark install. The example here is from local.


---

Executing R functions on groups via spark_apply does not function as expected. Consider this test function:

```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris)

test_fun <- function(dat, x, y){
  dat$x <- x
  dat$y <- y
  dat
}


```
Running inside an anonymous function results in an error:


```r
iris_tbl %>%
  spark_apply(function(d) test_fun(d, x = 1, y = 2), group_by = "Species")

```

But, running the bare function without any arguments does _not_ fail:

```r
iris_tbl %>%
  spark_apply(test_fun, group_by = "Species")
```

This returns a dataframe with one column from within the function appended with one of the other columns in the dataframe:

title: spark_connect() should handle openjdk 11 gracefully
description:
**Error:**
``` r
sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(master = "local[*]")
#> Error in validate_java_version_line(master, version): Java version detected but couldn't parse version from: openjdk version "11.0.2" 2019-01-15
```

<sup>Created on 2019-02-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

**Root Cause:**
The version string for openjdk 10 and above includes a release date.  Starting with openjdk 11.0.2, that release date is in 2019.  `validate_java_version_line()` fails to handle dates in 2019 (and presumably earlier release dats with a 9 in the month or the day) due to the following code

```
splatVersion <- splat[grepl("9|[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+", splat)]
```
if the intention of that regexp is to match jdk 9 versions strings, it should either have a caret (^) before the 9 or something after it to prevent matches against a ISO date string.

Given that java 9 is end of life, a better answer is simply to remove the `9|` from the regexp entirely

title: ml_clustering_evaluator() returns error if used with ml_cross_validator()
description:
`ml_clustering_evaluator()` works fine on single prediction tables, but fails when used as the evaluator within `ml_cross_validator()` or `ml_train_validation_split()`. Basing the reprex on the working example from [this RStudio blog post from last year](https://blog.rstudio.com/2018/05/14/sparklyr-0-8/) which used `ml_multiclass_classification_evaluator()`.

Verifying single table case:
```
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.4.0")
dplyr::copy_to(sc, iris, "iris_tbl")


pipeline <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_vector_assembler(
    input_cols = c("Sepal_Width", "Sepal_Length", "Petal_Width", "Petal_Length"),
    output_col = "features"
  ) %>%
  ml_kmeans(k = 3, uid = "kmeans")
```
The following works as expected:

```
ml_fit_and_transform(pipeline, dplyr::tbl(sc, "iris_tbl")) %>% 
  ml_clustering_evaluator()
```
This returns the average silhouette score for the single K-means model with k=3. 

However if we try to use `ml_cross_validator()` over the `k` parameter with a similar pipeline then it fails:
```
pipeline_cv <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_vector_assembler(
    input_cols = c("Sepal_Width", "Sepal_Length", "Petal_Width", "Petal_Length"),
    output_col = "features"
  ) %>%
  ml_kmeans(uid = "kmeans")

# Specify hyperparameter grid
grid <- list(
  kmeans = list(
    k = c(2, 3, 4)
  )
)

# Create the cross validator object
cv <- ml_cross_validator(
  sc, 
  estimator = pipeline_cv, 
  estimator_param_maps = grid,
  evaluator = ml_clustering_evaluator(sc),
  num_folds = 3, 
  parallelism = 1
)

# Train the models
cv_model <- ml_fit(cv, dplyr::tbl(sc, "iris_tbl"))
```

This returns the error `Error in spark_connection(jobj) :
  argument "jobj" is missing, with no default`. The same error occurs for `ml_train_validation_split()`.

```r
spark_version <- "2.3.0"
```

title: how to specify ratings in ml_als for implicit ratings
description:
in the implicit feedback paper https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4781121, ratings are decomposed into **preference** (a binary which is 0 if ratings = 0 and 1 otherwise) and **confidence** which is a transformation of the original rating value and can take various forms, e.g. 
$c_{ui} = 1 + \alpha(r_{ui})$ or 
$c_{ui} = 1 + \alpha log(1+(r_{ui}/\epsilon)$

My question is: what should x be in the ml_als call for implicit data?  Should it be our chosen **confidence**?  and what is the output of the prediction?  is it the original rating value or the confidence or some indication of the preference...?

title: How to create an managed Delta table?
description:
How do you create an managed Delta table in Sparklyr? Here's the Spark SQL equivalent of what I am trying to do:

```
CREATE TABLE events
USING delta
PARTITIONED BY (date)
SELECT action, from_unixtime(time, 'yyyy-MM-dd') as date
FROM json.`/databricks-datasets/structured-streaming/events/`;
```

This registers the table in the Hive metastore, and copies the data into Delta format `/user/hive/warehouse/events`.

The closest thing I can find is `spark_write_delta()`, but requires a `path` parameter, and by implication is creating a unmanaged table. Perhaps a solution would be to add a `delta` option to `spark_write_table()`?

I am using sparklyr 1.05.

title: How to create a unmanaged global table?
description:
I've also posted this to [Stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59102418/how-to-create-a-unmanaged-global-table-from-sparklyr) as I am not sure if it's a bug, or a gap in my knowledge.

---

How do you create an unmanaged global table in Sparklyr? Here's the Spark SQL equivalent of what I am trying to do:

```
CREATE TABLE people (id INT, name STRING)
USING CSV LOCATION '/FileStore/people/people.csv'
```

This registers the table in the Hive metastore, but leaves the data in-situ, and doesn't copy it to `/FileStore/tables/people`. These are Databricks locations, but I believe the same concepts apply to Spark more generally.

The closest thing I can find is `spark_read_csv()` followed by a `spark_write_table()` but this creates a *managed* global table in `/user/hive/warehouse/`, where the data is copied, and I am trying to create an *unmanaged* global table.

title: spark_write_table inconsistent behaviour with spark_write_<format>
description:
`spark_write_table` name is a bit misleading. It's not actually writing the table to disk in the sense that `spark_write_parquet` and other format-specific functions do. I believe its job is to register the table in the global context, so it can be used by other users/languages and between sessions.

With this in mind, it's not obvious to me how to register a dataframe in the global context, without first creating a duplicate in the local context.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect("local")
mtcars_tbl <- copy_to(sc, mtcars)
spark_write_table(mtcars_tbl, "mtcars") #error, table "mtcars" already exists locally
```

title: Retrieve logical plan using sparklyr
description:
We are trying to get the logical plan that Spark generates for a given query. According to the Spark docs [here](https://spark.apache.org/docs/1.6.3/api/java/org/apache/spark/sql/DataFrame.html#explain(boolean)) you should be able to retrieve this using the scala command:
```scala
df.explain(true)
```
or in sparklyr with the example code:

```r
spark_version <- "2.4.3"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)
iris_sdf <- copy_to(sc, iris)

iris_sdf %>% 
  spark_dataframe %>% 
  invoke("explain", T)
```
This command runs, but simply returns `NULL`. My guess is that sparklyr does not retrieve content that is printed to the console. Is there a way around this or another way to retrieve the logical plan using sparklyr? The physical plan is easy to get using `dplyr::explain([your_sdf])`, but does not return the logical plan that was used to create it.

```r
#' Compute union_all of tables.  Cut down from \code{replyr::replyr_union_all()} for debugging.
#'
#' @param sc remote data source tables are on (and where to copy-to and work), NULL for local tables.
#' @param tabA not-NULL table with at least 1 row on sc data source, and columns \code{c("car", "fact", "value")}.
#' @param tabB not-NULL table with at least 1 row on same data source as tabA and columns \code{c("car", "fact", "value")}.
#' @return table with all rows of tabA and tabB (union_all).
#'
#' @export
example_union_all <- function(sc, tabA, tabB) {
  cols <- intersect(colnames(tabA), colnames(tabB))
  expectedCols <- c("car", "fact", "value")
  if((length(cols)!=length(expectedCols)) ||
     (!all.equal(cols, expectedCols))) {
    stop(paste("example_union_all: column set must be exactly", 
               paste(expectedCols, collapse = ', ')))
  }
  mergeColName <- 'exampleunioncol'
  # build a 2-row table to control the union
  controlTable <- data.frame(exampleunioncol= c('a', 'b'),
                             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if(!is.null(sc)) {
    controlTable <- copy_to(sc, controlTable,
                            temporary=TRUE)
  }
  # decorate left and right tables for the merge
  tabA <- tabA %>%
    select(one_of(cols)) %>%
    mutate(exampleunioncol = as.character('a'))
  tabB <- tabB %>%
    select(one_of(cols)) %>%
    mutate(exampleunioncol = as.character('b'))
  # do the merges
  joined <- controlTable %>%
    left_join(tabA, by=mergeColName) %>%
    left_join(tabB, by=mergeColName, suffix = c('_a', '_b'))
  # coalesce the values
  joined <- joined %>%
    mutate(car = ifelse(exampleunioncol=='a', car_a, car_b))
  joined <- joined %>%
    mutate(fact = ifelse(exampleunioncol=='a', fact_a, fact_b))
  joined <- joined %>%
    mutate(value = ifelse(exampleunioncol=='a', value_a, value_b))
  joined %>%
    select(one_of(cols)) %>%
    dplyr::compute()
}
```

title: Conversion between R and Scala
description:
Dear sparklyr team,

according to some tries and errors on my side, I found out that 
- a ``scala Map`` seems to be well translateable to a ``R named list``
- however a ``R named list`` will be translated to an java Array which is recognized as ``scala Seq`` of respective Type, i.e. it looses its name information
- a ``R environment`` in fact gets translated to ``java Map``, which however unfortunately does not translate that easily to a scala Map

These three observations together suggest to me that:
1. ``scala Maps`` as well ``java Maps`` should be translated to ``R environments`` instead of ``R lists``
1. ``scala Maps`` might be very much preferable over ``java Maps`` as the translation of ``R environments``, just because all suggested examples of extending sparklyr use scala code and not java

what do you think?

title: Support For Long-Format Data
description:
Sparklyr is inconsistent in supporting long-format data, which is more convenient for extremely wide datasets. This is especially true for enterprise environments, where users may not be able to override the spark.sql.pivotMaxValues cap.

For instance, ml_als is intuitive - it accepts long-format data triples {"rating_col", "user_col", "item_col"} instead of requiring a sparse matrix representation. This is readily generalized to {"observation_id", "outcome_label", "variable_name", "variable value"} for other ml algorithms. 

However, ml_bisecting_kmeans and others require the matrix format, which means using sdf_pivot and commonly na.replace() in succession. The blend of reshape2 and dplyr syntax is awkward in a step that seems like it should really be hidden from the user. Supplying the fill option in the function would also be consistent with the way gather and spread are implemented.

The self-referencing ft_r_formula documentation doesn't make parsing out the exact differences in arguments to ml functions easy:

> features_col  -  Features column name, as a length-one character vector. The column should be single vector column of numeric values. Usually this column is output by ft_r_formula.
> label_col  -  Label column name. The column should be a numeric column. Usually this column is output by ft_r_formula.

title: `ft_vector_assembler()` converts some numeric types to `DoubleType`
description:
When creating a vector column with `sparklyr::ft_vector_assembler()`, data types are not preserved. For instance, creating a vector column out of `IntegerType` data results in a `DoubleType` vector column. If the vector column is then broken back into scalar columns, the resulting scalar columns will have `DoubleType`, rather than their original `IntegerType`.

### Example Code:

```r
library(sparklyr)

# connect to Spark
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local[*]")

# make a simple data.frame with IntegerType values
df <- data.frame(
  as.integer(c(1, 2, 3)),
  as.integer(c(4, 5, 6)),
  as.integer(c(7, 8, 9)),
  as.integer(c(10, 11, 12)))

# add nice column names
names(df) <- c("a", "b", "c", "d")

# copy R data.frame to Spark
df_sparklyr <- copy_to(sc, df, overwrite=TRUE)

# add new vector column created from scalar columns
vector <- df_sparklyr %>% ft_vector_assembler(c("d", "b"), "vector_col")

# print new Spark DataFrame to see that vector column is DoubleType
print(head(vector))

# split vector column back into constituent columns
split <- vector %>% sdf_separate_column("vector_col", c("d'", "b'"))

# recovered scalar columns have had their types altered
print(head(split))

# print out session info
devtools::session_info()
```

### TO-BE

```r
sdf <- sparklyr::sdf_sql(sc, "select 1")
```

```r
# The feature cols

  c("mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "drat", "wt", "qsec", "vs", "gear", "carb")

# Vector assembler
vector_assembler <- 
  ft_vector_assembler(
    sc,
    input_cols = feature_cols,
    output_col = "features")

# Estimator
estimator <- 
  ml_random_forest_classifier(
    sc, 
    label_col = "am") 

# Create the pipeline
pipeline <- ml_pipeline(vector_assembler, estimator)

# Fit the pipeline
pipeline_model <- pipeline %>%
  ml_fit(mtcars_sdf)

# Feature importance (doesn't work)
ml_tree_feature_importance(
  ml_stage(pipeline_model, 2)
)

# But they're there
ml_stage(pipeline_model, 2)$feature_importances

# Do it without the pipeline (works)

  mtcars_sdf,

)

ml_tree_feature_importance(model)
```

title: ml_decision_tree failing with response-features syntax
description:
First off, thanks to everyone for the great work on this package. 

We recently upgraded to v0.7.0 and are running into issues with some ML function calls that use response-features and that worked under v0.6.4. A simple reprex similar to what we're running:

``` r
library(sparklyr)
config <- spark_config()
```

title: ML_pipelines: managing table reading
description:
I am using Spark `ML_pipelines` to easily deploy operations that I have developed in `Sparklyr` in a production environment using `SCALA`. It is working pretty well, except for one part: it seems that when I read a table from `Hive` and then create a pipeline that applies operations to this table the pipeline will also save the table reading operation and thereby the name of the table. However I want the pipeline to be independent of this. 

Here is a reproducible example:

`Sparklyr` part:

    sc = spark2_context(memory = "4G")
    
    iris <- copy_to(sc, iris, overwrite=TRUE)
    
    spark_write_table(iris, "base.iris")
    spark_write_table(iris, "base.iris2")
    df1 <- tbl(sc, "base.iris")
    
    df2 <- df1 %>%
      mutate(foo = 5)
    
    pipeline <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
      ft_dplyr_transformer(df2) %>%
      ml_fit(df1)
    
    ml_save(pipeline,
            paste0(save_pipeline_path, "test_pipeline_reading_from_table"),
            overwrite = TRUE)
    
    df2 <- pipeline %>% ml_transform(df1)
    
    dbSendQuery(sc, "drop table base.iris")

`SCALA`part:

    import org.apache.spark.ml.PipelineModel
    import org.apache.spark.SparkContext
    import org.apache.spark.SparkConf
    
    val df1 = spark.sql("select * from base.iris2") 
    
    val pipeline = PipelineModel.load(pipeline_path + "/test_pipeline_reading_from_table")
    val df2 = pipeline.transform(df1)

I get this error:

    org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: Table or view not found: `base`.`iris`; line 2 pos 5;

      at org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.trees.TreeNode$$anonfun$foreachUp$1.apply(TreeNode.scala:126)
      at scala.collection.immutable.List.foreach(List.scala:381)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.trees.TreeNode.foreachUp(TreeNode.scala:126)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.CheckAnalysis$class.checkAnalysis(CheckAnalysis.scala:78)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.Analyzer.checkAnalysis(Analyzer.scala:91)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.execution.QueryExecution.assertAnalyzed(QueryExecution.scala:52)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset$.ofRows(Dataset.scala:67)
      at org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession.sql(SparkSession.scala:637)
      at org.apache.spark.ml.feature.SQLTransformer.transformSchema(SQLTransformer.scala:86)
      at org.apache.spark.ml.PipelineModel$$anonfun$transformSchema$5.apply(Pipeline.scala:310)
      at org.apache.spark.ml.PipelineModel$$anonfun$transformSchema$5.apply(Pipeline.scala:310)
      at scala.collection.IndexedSeqOptimized$class.foldl(IndexedSeqOptimized.scala:57)
      at scala.collection.IndexedSeqOptimized$class.foldLeft(IndexedSeqOptimized.scala:66)

I can see 2 solutions:

1. It seems that persisting `dataframe` would be a solution, but then I would need to find a way not to overload my memory, hence my question on [unpersisting][1] on SO

title: mutate_all() not working with list(~.) instead of funs(.)
description:
The `funs` call in `dplyr`'s `mutate_all()` has been soft deprecated as of dplyr 0.8.0.

Instead of writing:

```
library(dplyr)
mtcars %>% 
  mutate_all(funs(. * 1000))
```

You should write:

```
mtcars %>% 
  mutate_all(list(~. * 1000))
```

This works fine in R but does not work in `sparklyr`:
``` r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

config <- spark_config()
config$`sparklyr.shell.driver-memory` <- "2G"
config$`sparklyr.shell.executor-memory` <- "2G"

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = config, spark_version = "2.1.0")
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'openssl':
#>   method      from
#>   print.bytes Rcpp

mtcars_spark <- copy_to(sc, mtcars, "mtcars")

mtcars_spark %>% 
  mutate_all(list(~. * 1000))
#> Error in as.pairlist(list(...)): object 'mpg' not found
```

title: dynamic allocation error even though spark.shuffle.service.enabled = true
description:
Problem:

I want to connect to a spark standalone cluster using dynamic allocation. 

According to this [page](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/job-scheduling.html#configuration-and-setup), dynamic resource allocation is "disabled by default and available on all coarse-grained cluster managers, i.e. standalone mode, YARN mode, and Mesos coarse-grained mode." The page goes on, "In standalone mode, simply start your workers with spark.shuffle.service.enabled set to true." 

This does not appear to work with sparklyr. 

Setup:

Running spark 2.4.3 using a docker swarm cluster. It is a standalone cluster, at the moment using two worker containers and one master container. Using rstudio server Version 1.2.1335 in a docker swarm service based on rocker/tidyverse:latest. 

I can connect to the spark cluster using rstudio and sparklyr 2.4.3. This works using:
`spark_connect(master = "spark://master:7077"` 

But, I cannot connect to the spark standalone cluster from rstudio using sparklyr with: `config$spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled <- "true". `

Throws an error:
```
ERROR SparkContext: Error initializing SparkContext.
org.apache.spark.SparkException: Dynamic allocation of executors requires the external shuffle service. You may enable this through spark.shuffle.service.enabled.
```
Now, I did enable shuffle service in the spark docker containers, by adding to the spark-defaults.conf file:
`spark.shuffle.service.enabled           true`

And I suspect that worked, because when I look at the docker logs for the workers, I see:
`INFO ExternalShuffleService: Starting shuffle service on port 7337 (auth enabled = false)`

Has anyone gotten dynamic allocation to work using sparklyr and a standalone cluster? Not sure what I should do to narrow down the problem from here. Suggestions welcome. Thanks!

title: Improve streaming documentation
description:
Recently, sparklyR started to support streaming queries. This is great. However, a couple of details are still unclear to me (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55616300/sparklyr-streaming-join-with-state) namely:

## Windowed aggregation
```scala
    val windowedCounts = words
        .withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes")
        .groupBy(
            window($"timestamp", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"),
            $"word")
        .count()
```

In R

```r
    stream_watermark(df, column="timestamp", threshold="10 minutes")
```

replaces

```scala
df.withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes")
```

Where can I find `window($"timestamp", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"),`?

## Streaming joins
How is https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/structured-streaming-programming-guide.html#inner-joins-with-optional-watermarking ported to sparklyR?

```scala
    // Join with event-time constraints
    impressionsWithWatermark.join(
      clicksWithWatermark,
      expr("""
        clickAdId = impressionAdId AND
        clickTime >= impressionTime AND
        clickTime <= impressionTime + interval 1 hour
        """)
    )
```
### trigger
How can I set triggers as defined in: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/structured-streaming-programming-guide.html#triggers

`stream_trigger_interval` can specify fixed trigger intervals, but what about unspecified or run once or continuous?

Goal: The traditional GISer can hands on big raster data easier.

There are two types of data in geospatial processing: vector and raster.
For the vector type, [geospark](https://github.com/harryprince/geospark), which brings [sf](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf) to spark is working very well on it as a sparklyr plugin and the tradional GISer can migrate from local sf or postgis to big data in few hours.

And for the raster type, [RasterFrames](http://rasterframes.io) is doing a similar thing, which powered by [geotrellis](http://geotrellis.io/) and wish to bring [`stars`](https://github.com/r-spatial/stars) to spark too.

title: Unable to pass field name to bracketed case_when statement using `.`
description:
`case_when()` requires highly repetitive statements and `switch()` is not available within sparklyr mutate statements. In with base dplyr it's possible to pass a field name into a braced `case_when()` to construct a more concise case_when clause, but this functionality doesn't appear to be present in sparklyr.

```
spark_version <- "2.3.0"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

# local table
test_dt <- data.table(
  a = c(1, 2, 3),
  b = c(123.12, 234.23, NA),
  very_long_vegetable_field_name = c("apple", "banana", "carrot"),
  d = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  e = c("2018-01-01", "2018-01-01", "2018-01-01") 
)

# remote table
test_spark <- copy_to(sc, test_dt)

## standard case_when syntax succeeds
test_dt %>%
  mutate(f = case_when(very_long_vegetable_name == "apple" ~ "fruit",
                       very_long_vegetable_name == "carrot" ~ "root",
                       TRUE ~ "unknown")
         )

test_spark %>%
  mutate(f = case_when(very_long_vegetable_name == "apple" ~ "fruit",
                       very_long_vegetable_name == "carrot" ~ "root",
                       TRUE ~ "unknown")
         )

# evaluating local table with quoted field name succeeds

test_dt %>%
  mutate(f = very_long_vegetable_field_name %>%
           { case_when( . == "apple" ~ "fruit",
                        . == "carrot" ~ "root",
                        TRUE ~ "unknown")
           }
         )

# evaluating spark table fails with `Error: Can't extract an environment from NULL`
test_spark %>%
  mutate(f = very_long_vegetable_field_name %>%
           { case_when( . == "apple" ~ "fruit",
                        . == "carrot" ~ "root",
                        TRUE ~ "unknown")
             }
         )
```

```r
q <- 'select startdate, calls from call_db where BizSeg = \"SM\" and startdate = \"2018-10-14"\ limit 100'
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7535009/53343959-274d1d00-38d7-11e9-9c1c-f777dd30cc3e.png)


I have no idea how date got shifted by one day.

When I ran the exact same query with PySpark I got the correct results that match the Hive CLI.

Appreciate any help to decipher this.

title: Single thread after data manipulation + writing out RDD
description:
I posted a stackoverflow question here, but figured it might be suitable ask here as well:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54121555/sparklyr-single-thread-when-caching-writing-out-rdd-or-converting-to-h2o-frame

I've noticed very poor performance when reading in a parquet file + performing data manipulation operations, followed by caching, writing out to parquet/csv, or converting an h2o frame (using rsparkling).

This isn't an issue when simply reading in the file, then directly writing it back out or converting to an h2o frame.

Looking at my running processes, it appears spark runs these operations using a single core (only after the manipulation steps).

I noticed these messages in the spark log:

WARN WindowExec: No Partition Defined for Window operation! Moving all data to a single partition, this can cause serious performance degradation.

INFO ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray: Reached spill threshold of 4096 rows, switching to org.apache.spark.util.collection.unsafe.sort.UnsafeExternalSorter

Details on my Spark configuration:
sparklyr 0.9.3
spark 2.3.2

config$`sparklyr.shell.driver-memory` <- "200G"
config$`sparklyr.shell.executor-memory` <- "200G"
config$`spark.executor.memoryOverhead` <- "5G"
config$`spark.executor.cores` <- '50'
config$`spark.ext.h2o.nthreads` <- '50'
config$`spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` <- '50'
increased heartbeat since spark jobs were timing out, but still running
config$`spark.executor.heartbeatInterval` <- '1000000s'
config$`spark.network.timeout` <- '10000000s'
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local[50]", config = config)

Comparisons I ran:

- Load-in 40 GB parquet file: 3 minutes (always)

- Perform no operations, write back out to parquet takes 3 minutes (same when converting to h2o.frame using rsparkling)

- Perform any data manipulation operations, write to parquet/csv/h2o.frame all take ~40 minutes

What I've tried:

- sdf_repartition(partitions = 50)... it appears setting the repartition option in spark_read_parquet() isn't working on my machine...

- Messing around with other config options:

1. config$`spark.sql.windowExec.buffer.spill.threshold` <- '40000000'

2. config$`spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled` <- "false"

- Manually caching the table before running manipulation operations (but I don't think I should have to do this, since the spark_read_parquet by default loads the data into memory.)

title: No tidy() support for pipeline output
description:
The following examples are conceptually equivalent, yet only the first works.  This makes building exploratory models that rely on `ft_*()` operations difficult

``` r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- 
  spark_connect(master = "local")
mt <- 
  sdf_copy_to(sc, mtcars)
mt %>% 
  ml_linear_regression(am ~ cyl + mpg) %>% 
  tidy()
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   term        estimate std.error statistic p.value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)  -0.460     0.929     -0.495  0.624 
#> 2 cyl          -0.0117    0.0793    -0.147  0.884 
#> 3 mpg           0.0467    0.0235     1.99   0.0564
mt %>% 
  ft_r_formula(am ~ cyl + mpg) %>% 
  ml_linear_regression() %>% 
  tidy()
#> Error: No tidy method for objects of class ml_linear_regression_model
```

<sup>Created on 2018-11-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Given that 
`mt %>% ft_r_formula(am ~ cyl + mpg) %>% ml_linear_regression(fit_intercept = FALSE) %>% coef()`
and
`mt %>% ft_r_formula(am ~ cyl + mpg) %>% ml_linear_regression(fit_intercept = FALSE) %>% summary()`
work correctly, it is surprising that I cannot use tidy() against the pipeline output.

title: Improved Examples
description:
- [ ] Ensure all our public functions have examples associated to them.
- [ ] Make sure file read/write examples explain how to properly use file prefixes, when to use `file://`, `hdfs://` or `hdfs:///` which is required in some cases.

title: Improved Errors
description:
Current Spark error messages show the full call stack which is confusing to R users. Some potential improvements would be to:
- [ ] Add support in RStudio for collapsing external call stacks.
- [ ] Outside RStudio, hide the call stack and print an error like `Error: Can't find matched method. Run spark_error() for additional details`.
- [ ] Many of our errors come from binding the wrong parameter types, say, if I pass a date to an integer parameter, it will get piped to Scala code and error out. We should make `invoke()` return an explicit signature from Scala such that we can throw a `parameter 'x' expected to be integer`.
- [ ] For `spark_apply()` we should consider handling errors automatically. When `spark_apply()` fails, we could consider rerunning in error-mode where we would wrap the call into `tryCatch({closure() ; "{partition: 'abcsd23dsfsdc', rows: 100, seconds: 10, status: 'OK'}"}, error = function(e) { "{partition: 'abcsd23dsfsdc', rows: 100, seconds: 10, status: 'Failed', message: 'e$message'}" }`. Which we then use to print a summary of which partitions failed and why, optionally, we could also support collecting specific partitions with `spark_apply(, collect = "abcsd23dsfsdc")` which would allow users to easily debug locally.

title: SQL translation turns aggregation into window function on SPARK
description:
I'm using sparklyr on Databricks (though the issue is not databricks specific) and I see an issue in the SQL translation for aggregation functions. 

When using a simple aggregation function in a mutate clause, this is translated as a window function in SparkSQL. In a traditional database this is not a big deal, but on SPARK this causes all data to be pulled to a single node which causes poor performance/crashes. 

I'm on Databricks runtime 4.3 (spark version 2.3.1). This appears to be an issue in sparklyr's SQL translation that causes issues with SparkSQL.

I have previously loaded the "diamonds" dataset into a table; any example dataset would work.

```r
spark_version <- "2.3.1"
sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

tbl(sc, 'diamonds') %>%
  mutate(average_carat = mean(carat)) %>%
  show_query()
```

The output is:
SELECT `carat`, avg(`carat`) OVER () AS `average_carat`
FROM `diamonds`

The culprit is the OVER() which turns this into a window function with the whole dataframe as the window. Spark knows how to implement avg('carat') efficiently in a distributed manner, but avg('carat') OVER() pulls all the data onto a single worker node.

title: Support other namespaces in kubernetes
description:
# Trying to create a connection to kubernetes via a different namespace from "default"
Use-case: 

Kubernetes Cluster is shared and have different namespaces for each respective usage. In this space, spark namespace is the one we want to use. I followed the below code to create the connection and when default is used, it works fine. When another namespace is used first the parameter is not added to spark.shell.conf and second it doesn't work as per the default

```r
library(sparklyr)

config=spark_config_kubernetes(master="k8s://https://etc", 
                               version = "2.3.2", 
                               image = "sparkimage",
                               driver = random_string("sparklyr-"),
                               account = "sparklyr",
                               jars="local:///opt/sparklyr",
                               forward = TRUE, 
                               executors = 4,
                               config = list(
                                 spark.kubernetes.namespace = "default",
                                 sparklyr.gateway.address = "ip"
                               )
)
sc <- spark_connect(config = config )
# the above code works fine but whatever is inside config list is not passed as parameter to spark.shell.config. 

#Then i've tried the following: 

config$sparklyr.shell.conf=c("spark.kubernetes.namespace=spark",config$sparklyr.shell.conf)

#This adds the spark as a namespace to spark.shell.config however it fails with the below error: 

Error from server (NotFound): pods "sparklyr-62935dd025c7" not found

#Pods actually gets created in the namespace and it runs however the connection might search for the pod before it gets provisioned. There seems to be a delay in getting access to pod and due to the error the connection breaks and fails. This doesn't happen in default namespace. 
```

Hopefully this is clear enough and hopefully the community can help?

Thank you,
Eliano

title: Consider moving read/write options to ...
description:
This,

```r
config <- spark_config()
config$`sparklyr.shell.driver-class-path` <- 
  "~/Downloads/mysql-connector-java-5.1.41/mysql-connector-java-5.1.41-bin.jar"

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = config)

spark_read_jdbc(sc, "person_jdbc",  options = list(
  url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/sparklyr",
  user = "root", password = "<password>",
  dbtable = "person"))
```

could be cleaned up into:

```r
spark_read_jdbc(sc, "person_jdbc",
  url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/sparklyr", user = "root",
  password = "<password>", dbtable = "person")
```

by making use of `...` arguments, there might be other `read_*` and `write_*` functions worth considering.

title: Error during spark_connect
description:
When trying to connect to Spark using `spark_connect` with the latest development version of sparklyr we're getting the following error:

```
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn", config = config)
Error: `nm` must be `NULL` or a character vector the same length as `x`
Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace
> rlang::last_error()
<error>
message: `nm` must be `NULL` or a character vector the same length as `x`
class:   `rlang_error`
backtrace:
 ─sparklyr::spark_connect(master = "yarn", config = config)
 ─sparklyr:::register_mapping_tables()
 ─sparklyr:::read_extension_mappings(file_name = "param_mapping.json")
 ─purrr::map_chr(...)
 ─purrr::keep(., nzchar)
 ─purrr::map(., jsonlite::fromJSON)
 ─purrr::set_names(., pkgs)
 ─rlang:::set_names_impl(x, x, nm, ...)
```
Our connection code looks like this:
```R
config <- spark_config()
config$sparklyr.log.console <- FALSE
sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn", config = config)
```

reverting to the 0.9.2 version on CRAN fixes the issue.

title: Secure Sockets
description:
Draft to support high-performance socket connections in Livy ( https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1579) and also other job-spawning technologies.

**Overview:** Livy has been really popular in the `sparklyr` community, mostly out of necessity since it enables connectivity for tightly managed clusters or clusters that ran out of capacity to install additional boundary machines were RStudio could be installed, etc. While Livy has proved to be a good solution for connectivity, it's performance is less than ideal since it's primary purpose is to provide a remote REPL.

**Solution:** One solution would be to request system administrators to make a few additional ports available for `sparklyr` to upgrade the HTTP connection into a high-performance binary connection `sparklyr` already supports. However, some additional work is required to provide proper secure access and to the potentially internet visible ports.

**Work Items:**
- [ ] Support to generate private key in Scala or R, consider [KeyPairGenerator](http://www.novixys.com/blog/how-to-generate-rsa-keys-java/) or [PKI](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PKI/PKI.pdf).
- [ ] Support to exchange private/public keys through Livy. If Livy is compromised, one could attack directly the Livy connection anyways.
- [ ] Support to encrypt/decrypt data in Scala, consider [RSA Cypher](https://gist.github.com/urcadox/6173812).
- [ ] Support to encrypt/decrypt data in R, consider [PKI](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PKI/PKI.pdf).
- [ ] Support to start `sparklyr` backend in Livy, this is already supported when using `spark_apply()` with Livy but not currently initialized in the driver node.
- [ ] Support to upgrade HTTP Livy connection, when possible.

**Notes:**
This port upgrade would be supported in Amazon AWS since a security group can be defined; however, other platforms like Azure HDInsight [does not seem to support port configuration](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27779538/opening-a-port-on-hdinsight-cluster-on-azure).

title: Extracting characters based on regex pattern
description:
I'm creating a small package that should be able to extract some patterns from columns of characters and return it to the user.
Today, what I have implemented uses the functions `regexp_replace()` and `regexp_extract()` from `SparkR`. But, since `SparkR `is no longer available on cran anymore, I was looking for some implementation using sparklyr's own methods.

I saw https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/536#issuecomment-339778070 in which was proposed by @kevinykuo to use `explode()` (also from SparkR) with sparklyr's `ft_tokenizer`, but this also represents dependency on SparkR.

an example:
```
names <- data.table(name = c("Marty McFly","Emmet Brown","Biff Tannen"))
patterns <- c("McFly|Emmet|Biff")
names_tbl <- copy_to(sc,names)
returns <- names_tbl %>%
  dplyr::mutate(regex = regexp_replace(name,patterns,"")) %>%
  dplyr::select(regex) %>%
  dplyr::collect()

> returns
# A tibble: 3 x 1
    regex
    <chr>
1  Marty 
2   Brown
3  Tannen
```

Also have to figure out how to trim the strings.
Is there a way to extract patterns without using SparkR?

title: spark_apply() can not find Rscript
description:
I can run a [simple `spark_apply()` script](https://github.com/WinVector/ODSCWest2017/blob/master/SparklyRMachineLearning/Exercises/solutions/06-Spark-Extension.Rmd) on my local machine, and it works fine.  However if I run the same script on a Hortonworks cluster I get the following error:

```
## Error: org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure: Task 0 in stage 13.0 failed 4 times, most recent failure: Lost task 0.3 in stage 13.0 (TID 16, mksd1sldscbs005.c.iron-potion-771.internal, executor 2): java.io.IOException: Cannot run program "Rscript": error=2, No such file or directory
```

I believe there is an Rscript binary in `/usr/local/bin/Rscript`, but I don't see any in the `Spark` software install directory (I don't see `Rscript` in the `Spark` software install directory on my local machine either).  For control of `R` software version should not `spark_apply()` only use `R` binaries found in the `Spark` install (perhaps use `R` in batch mode if there is no `Rscript`)?

Link to stand-alone example script [here](https://github.com/WinVector/ODSCWest2017/blob/master/SparklyRMachineLearning/Exercises/solutions/06-Spark-Extension.Rmd).

I guess I am asking: is spark_apply() supposed to use the `R` that is part of the `Spark` install (and match versions), or is it supposed to use an `R` that is separately globally installed on the worker nodes?

title: Deploy R kernel into Jupyter
sparklyr and SparkR - the future?
description:
Just checked out @nwstephens's [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oItFZfzqqMY) at Spark Summit East where he answers some questions regarding sparklyr vs. SparkR towards the end. I've been thinking about this and am just a little bit concerned about how things might play out.

While I'm a fan of having different ways to solve a problem, sometimes it gets in the way of collaboration. As an example, most of the work I've done involves data manipulation/transformation, and it's been difficult for dplyr and data.table "speakers" to work together on the same task. What I'm worried about is that we'll have a "sparklyr camp" and a "SparkR camp" come next year, and we'll further factionalize the community and in turn discourage new data scientists from picking up R.

Would be interested to get some thoughts from the main contributors and results of discussions with the SparkR folks.

title: sparklyr proxy setting with livy
description:
Hi,

It seems there is a potential security risk when accessing spark through Livy.
The issue whenever the `proxy_user` parameter is not set or empty, the *knox user* is used to launch Spark Job (tested with Hortonworks HDP 2.6.4). If I'm not mistaken, this impersonation could potentially lead to unwanted actions (such as stopping authentication services).

All other ways seem to authenticate the user properly.
Is this a known issue and if not are there ways to mitigate the associated risk ?

---

```r
spark_version <- "2.2.0"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

# your reproducible example here
config <- livy_config(config = spark_config(), proxy_user='xxxx')
sc <- spark_connect(master = "<address>", method = "livy", config = config)
```

title: Support for timing out while processing a partition in `spark_apply()`

title: `ml_als()` saves unexposed RDDs in memory
description:
Running `ml_als()` with data frame input stores two in-memory RDDs: `userFactors` and `itemFactors`. However, these are not visible to `dplyr::src_tbls(sc)` and cannot be uncached with `tbl_uncache()`.

Using sparklyr 0.9.2.9000 with Spark version 2.3.0. 

```
foo <- data.frame(user = rep(0:9, 10),
                  item = sample(0:9, 100, replace = TRUE), 
                  rating = rnorm(100))
dplyr::copy_to(sc, foo, "foo_tbl", overwrite = TRUE)
fit <- dplyr::tbl(sc, "foo_tbl") %>% ml_als()
```

Checking saved RDDs:
```
spark_context(sc) %>% invoke("getRDDStorageInfo")
```

This shows us three RDD objects, named "userFactors", "itemFactors", and "In-memory table \`foo_tbl\`". We can access the user and item factor matrices through `fit$user_factors` and `fit$item_factors`, however these two tables do not show up when we run `dplyr::src_tbls(sc)` and cannot be removed from memory with `tbl_uncache()`:

```
dplyr::src_tbls(sc) #only shows "foo_tbl"
tbl_uncache(sc, "userFactors") #returns "Table or view not found" error
tbl_uncache(sc, "itemFactors") #returns "Table or view not found" error
```

Note: if we change the `ml_als()` argument "final_storage_level" from the default "MEMORY_AND_DISK" to "NONE", then after the ALS fitting finishes running the stored RDDs are "userOutBlocks", "userInBlocks", "itemOutBlocks", "itemInBlocks", and "ratingBlocks". These are usually temporary RDDs which get stored and updated through the ALS iterations, but they appear to be persistent after using these settings and have the same issues as "userFactors" and "itemFactors" in the previous example.

title: Sparklyr shouldn't provide stream_read_jdbc and  stream_write_jdbc
description:
As of today (Spark 2.3 / 2.4-RC) Spark doesn't support streaming reads and writes with JDBC source. While the latter one might be implemented in the future, the former one is probably less likely.

Therefore exposing aforementioned functions is highly misleading.

title: NA prints FALSE in logical col
description:
It seems that `NA` values in Spark DataFrames are handled correctly internally (neither `TRUE` nor `FALSE` and `is.na` returns `TRUE`) but printed incorrectly. Consider the examples below:

```r
iris2 <- copy_to(sc, iris, overwrite=TRUE)
iris2 <- iris2 %>% 
  mutate(logical_col = case_when(Species=="virginica" ~ NA,
                                 TRUE ~ Species=="setosa"))
iris2 %>% sdf_sample(fraction = 1/10)
# # Source: spark<?> [?? x 6]
# Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species    logical_col
#   *        <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>      <lgl>      
#   1          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 setosa     TRUE       
#   2          5.1         3.3          1.7         0.5 setosa     TRUE       
#   3          5.1         3.3          1.7         0.5 setosa     TRUE       
#   4          5.2         2.7          3.9         1.4 versicolor FALSE      
#   5          5.6         2.5          3.9         1.1 versicolor FALSE      
#   6          6.8         2.8          4.8         1.4 versicolor FALSE      
#   7          6.7         2.5          5.8         1.8 virginica  FALSE      <- uh oh!
#   8          6.4         2.7          5.3         1.9 virginica  FALSE      
#   9          6           2.2          5           1.5 virginica  FALSE      
#  10          6.3         2.7          4.9         1.8 virginica  FALSE      
#  # ... with more rows
```
Interestingly, the printed value is the same but it is known that `NA` and `FALSE` are different under the hood somewhere.
```r
iris2 %>% count(logical_col)
# # Source: spark<?> [?? x 2]
#   logical_col     n
#   * <lgl>       <dbl>
#   1 FALSE          50
#   2 TRUE           50
#   3 FALSE          50   <- huh?
```

title: Interaction with categorical includes all levels
description:
I am trying to run a `ml_generalized_linear_regression` with a categorical variable interacted with another variable. I expect that the interaction terms in my regression will include all levels of the categorical variable except one (the same one removed from the constant term). The constant terms of the categorical are correct and remove one level in the input features (level 'c' below). However, all levels are included in the interaction term (e.g. `b_c:a` should NOT have a coefficient estimated below).

```
test_df <- data.frame(
  a=rep(1:5,100) + rnorm(sd = .01,n = 500),
  b=rep(c('a','b','c','d','a'),100),
  c=rnorm(500)+1:500
)

test_df <- copy_to(sc, test_df, "test_df", overwrite = T)

ml_generalized_linear_regression(test_df, formula = c ~ b + a + b:a)
```
