title: Compression Codec Not Found on spark_read_csv, and null pointer on spark_read_jdbc
description:
The goal is to copy a text file into a Spark Dataframe, then copy that Spark Dataframe to a JDBC database table, and then read that JDBC table back into a second Spark Dataframe.  For this test we use SQLite.  In SparklyR we first define the driver class path in the config.  When we try to copy the text file into Spark using spark_read_csv we get a Compression codec com.hadoop.compression.lzo.LzoCodec not found error.  If we do not define the driver class path in the config then we are able to copy the text file into Spark.

The SQLite database for this test already has one table.  We try to read that table via JDBC into a Spark Dataframe using spark_read_jdbc and get a Null Pointer exception.

We show that we are able to read that JDBC table using RJDBC::dbGetQuery, to eliminate any database or JDBC driver issues, and to focus on sparklyr issues.

```r
#R database access via JDBC
library(RJDBC)

#R access to Spark via DPlyr
library(sparklyr)

# Datatabase Access Verbs
library(dplyr)

config <- spark_config()
config$`sparklyr.shell.driver-class-path` <- 
  "/home/hadoop/sqlite-jdbc-3.23.1.jar"

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local",
                    config = config)

# 2.3.1
spark_version(sc)

# Copy data to Spark with driver-class-path loaded
# Generates Error: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: 
#   Compression codec com.hadoop.compression.lzo.LzoCodec not found.
# This does not happen when we do not load the driver-class-path in the sc
trips_ref = spark_read_csv(sc, "test_spark", "file:///home/hadoop/test1.csv")

# Null Pointer Exception\
# Error: java.lang.NullPointerException
# at org.apache.spark.sql.execution.datasources.jdbc.JDBCRDD$.resolveTable(JDBCRDD.scala:70)
spark_read_jdbc(sc, "flight_jdbc",  options = list(
  url = "jdbc:mysql:file:///home/hadoop/my-sqlite.db",
  driver = "org.sqlite.JDBC",
  dbtable = "flight_info"))

# This shows there's no SQLite issue
#SQLite JDBC Driver
jdbcDriver <- JDBC(driverClass="org.sqlite.JDBC",
                   classPath="/home/hadoop/sqlite-jdbc-3.23.1.jar")

# Connecting to SQLite instance
jdbcConnection <- dbConnect(jdbcDriver, "jdbc:sqlite:file:///home/hadoop/my-sqlite.db")

flight_data = dbGetQuery(jdbcConnection,"select * from flight_info")

```

title: spark_read_table tries to remove Source table
description:
When overwrite = TRUE spark_read_table tries to remove Source table:

_if (overwrite) spark_remove_table_if_exists(sc, name)_

name - is a parameter in spark_read_table and it is a source table not a destination dataframe and thus should not be overwritten. A solution could be either to introduce 2 parameters - source and destination as it was in deprecated spark_load_table (name, path parameters), or to remove overwrite parameter and spark_remove_table_if_exists from spark_read_table.

title: Feature Request: Support spark shell parameters like spark.driver... via normal config
description:
Sparklyr has the very awesome position of starting an internal spark subprocess - which is different to all other spark interfaces out there today. This makes it possible to control all spark-configuration in detail.

When using spark client mode (as is almost always the case with sparklyr) all the ``spark.driver..`` config values like `spark.driver.extraJavaOptions` are unfortunately not set appropriately.
You have to circumvent them by using the respective shell parameter versions, like

```R
library(sparklyr)
conf = spark_config()
conf$`sparklyr.shell.driver-java-options`="-Dtest=42"  # <-- 
sc = spark_connect(master="local", version = "2.1.0", config = conf)
invoke_static(sc, "java.lang.System", "getProperty", "test")
# [1] 42
```

it would be awesome to be able to set the standard config parameters instead, like it is already possible at the command line for spark-submit and spark-shell via `--conf`.  So that at the marked line above it would say instead 
```R
...
conf$spark.driver.extraJavaOptions="-Dtest=42"  # <--
...
```

This should be in principle possible and could be realized 
- by either translating the config parameters to their respective shell flags 
- or by merging them respectively with the spark default properties file to a new properties file

title: coefficients from logistic regression have arbitrary sign?
description:
I have found that _sometimes_ the sign of coefficients from `ml_logistic_regression` are opposite what I would expect, although predictions from the model come out sensibly, which makes me think there is some kind of remapping under the hood. Here is a minimal example illustrating what I would consider a problem:
```r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)
# sc is a spark context.
# make dummy data
train_data <- iris %>%
  mutate(is_setosa=as.numeric((Species=='setosa'))) %>%
  mutate(is_not_setosa=1-is_setosa) %>%
  setNames(gsub('\\.','_',names(.)))
# fit logistic models in R
r_mod_fwd <- glm(formula=is_setosa ~ Sepal_Length,data=train_data,family=binomial(link='logit'))
r_mod_rev <- glm(formula=is_not_setosa ~ Sepal_Length,data=train_data,family=binomial(link='logit'))
# copy data to spark
spark_data <- copy_to(sc,train_data,'like_iris',overwrite=TRUE)
# fit logistic models in spark
s_mod_fwd <- spark_data %>% ml_logistic_regression(formula = is_setosa ~ Sepal_Length)
s_mod_rev <- spark_data %>% ml_logistic_regression(formula = is_not_setosa ~ Sepal_Length)
# get the coefficients:
# in R they are opposites
coefficients(r_mod_fwd)
coefficients(r_mod_rev)
# in spark, not so much:
coefficients(s_mod_fwd)
coefficients(s_mod_rev)
# why?
```
When I run this, I get the output: (sorry for the cut and paste job; `reprex` was being fussy about my spark context)
```
> coefficients(r_mod_fwd)
 (Intercept) Sepal_Length
      27.829       -5.176
> coefficients(r_mod_rev)
 (Intercept) Sepal_Length
     -27.829        5.176
> # in spark, not so much:
> coefficients(s_mod_fwd)
 (Intercept) Sepal_Length
      27.829       -5.176
> coefficients(s_mod_rev)
 (Intercept) Sepal_Length
      27.829       -5.176
```
Logistic regression in `R` does the right thing, flipping the sign of coefficients when I fit the 'opposite' model. However, the fit via `ml_logistic_regression` seems to choose the reference class the same way in both fits, and remaps them later.

I checked, and prediction seems fine here, respecting whatever remapping is going on, so we have
```r
# prediction is fine, of course
sdf_predict(s_mod_fwd,spark_data) %>% collect(n=3) %>% dplyr::select(Sepal_Length,label,rawPrediction,predicted_label) %>% knitr::kable()
sdf_predict(s_mod_rev,spark_data) %>% collect(n=3) %>% dplyr::select(Sepal_Length,label,rawPrediction,predicted_label) %>% knitr::kable()
```
These give, respectively, 

| Sepal_Length| label|rawPrediction |predicted_label |
|------------:|-----:|:-------------|:---------------|
|          5.1|     1|-1.432, 1.432 |1.0             |
|          4.9|     1|-2.468, 2.468 |1.0             |
|          4.7|     1|-3.503, 3.503 |1.0             |

And 

| Sepal_Length| label|rawPrediction |predicted_label |
|------------:|-----:|:-------------|:---------------|
|          5.1|     1|-1.432, 1.432 |0.0             |
|          4.9|     1|-2.468, 2.468 |0.0             |
|          4.7|     1|-3.503, 3.503 |0.0             |

title: support for Java `char` type
description:
How does one pass Java `char` values from R? 

Example:
```
> invoke_new(con, "java.lang.Character", "f") 
Error: java.lang.Exception: No matched constructor found for class java.lang.Character
```

Not sure how best to support this. Could have a `java_char()` function that wraps a single-character string in R, marking it for conversion to `char`.

Come to think of it, there should probably also be a `java_short()`, `java_long()`, and `java_float()`.

title: inconsistent users between spark connection and livy session
description:
Run the following code snippet:


```r
master <- "https://xxxx:8442/gateway/default/livy2/v1"

cnfg1 <- livy_config(username = "user1"
                    ,proxy_user = "user1"
                    ,password = "password1"
                    ,num_executors = 20
                    ,executor_cores = 3
                    ,executor_memory = "2G"
                    ,driver_memory = "1G"
                    )

sc1 <- spark_connect(master = master
                    ,method = "livy"
                    ,config = cnfg1
                    )

spark_disconnect_all()

cnfg2 <- livy_config(username = "user2"
                    ,proxy_user = "user2"
                    ,password = "password2"
                    ,num_executors = 20
                    ,executor_cores = 3
                    ,executor_memory = "2G"
                    ,driver_memory = "1G"
                    )
                    
sc2 <- spark_connect(master = master
                    ,method = "livy"
                    ,config = cnfg2
                    )
```
We expect the sc2 is a connection created by user2.  And actually sc2$config$livy.proxyUser is indeed user2.  But when we list livy sessions by the Livy Rest API "GET /sessions", the session's proxyUser is user1 instead of user2, which seems to be wrong.

I believe this is because of the httr's connection pool.  Adding the following in the function livy_destroy_session seems to be working, but I'm not sure if there is any side effect.

```
httr::handle_reset(paste(sc$master, "sessions", "/"))
```

I'm using the master branch. 

Any suggestion would be appreciated. Thanks.

title: requirement failed: The columns of A don't match the number of elements of x
description:
Hello,

Following up on some `gitter` chat with @kevinykuo 

Here is the issue. When I train my Naive Bayes model:

```
mymodel <- mydata%>% select(myday,headline, type) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(headline)) %>% 
  mutate(class = if_else(type == 'good', 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(headline, class) %>% 
  na.omit() %>% 
  ft_regex_tokenizer(input.col='headline',
                     output.col = 'mytoken', 
                     pattern = "\\s+", 
                     gaps =TRUE,
                     min_token_length = 3) %>% 
  ft_count_vectorizer(input_col = 'mytoken', output_col = 'final') %>% 
  ml_naive_bayes( label_col = "class", 
                  features_col = "final", 
                  prediction_col = "pcol",
                  probability_col = "prcol", 
                  raw_prediction_col = "rpcol",
                  model_type = "multinomial", 
                  smoothing = 1, 
                  thresholds = c(1, 1))
```
which works.
```

> mymodel
NaiveBayesModel (Transformer)
<naive_bayes_123456789> 
 (Parameters -- Column Names)
  features_col: final
  label_col: class
  prediction_col: pcol
  probability_col: prcol
  raw_prediction_col: rpcol
```

Then I test with the same dataset

```
df_process <- mydata%>% select(myday,headline, type) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(headline)) %>% 
  mutate(class = if_else(type == 'good', 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(headline, class) %>% 
  na.omit() %>% 
  ft_regex_tokenizer(input.col='headline',
                     output.col = 'mytoken', 
                     pattern = "\\s+", 
                     gaps =TRUE,
                     min_token_length = 3) %>% 
  ft_count_vectorizer(input_col = 'mytoken', output_col = 'final')

ml_transform(x = mymodel, df_process)
```

works perfectly et the prediction column `pcol` is there and makes sense.

Now I load another dataset, that contains different textual data that can be formatted in the same way. The difference is that the headlines look-like-this-so-I-use-regex-to-parse-them (and sometimes I can have something like sparklyr-is-good sparklyr-is-there (two matches), so I need to explode the matching list)

```
other_df <- df_new  %>% filter(!is.na(u)) %>%

                                              output.col = 'myoutput',

                                              gaps =FALSE,
                                              min_token_length = 3) %>% 
  mutate(myword = explode(myoutput)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(myword)) %>% 
  ft_regex_tokenizer(input.col='myword',
                     output.col = 'mytoken', 
                     pattern = "-", 
                     gaps =TRUE,
                     min_token_length = 3) %>% 
  ft_count_vectorizer(input_col = 'mytoken', output_col = 'final') %>% 
  mutate(class = 1) %>% 
  select(final, u, mytoken, class) %>% 
  na.omit()
```

title: Livy Unable to Access Hive Databases Created in HUE
description:
We have been experimenting with Livy as a Spark connection will not work for a current use case. However, when making a Spark connection via Livy, we are unable to view any Hive Databases or Tables that were generated in HUE (Hadoop User Experience). I believed that this was because Livy was not connecting to the correct "hive-site". We have taken the following steps to no avail:

1.) We have copied the hive-site.xml file from /etc/hadoop/conf into /etc/spark/conf.

2.) We have tried to set HIVE_CONF_DIR in the livy-env.sh file.

3.) We have tried setting the livy.repl.enable.hive.context parameter to "true" in the livy.conf file.

We have made a little progress the past two days. Looking at the `hive_context_config(sc),` within RStudio after making a `sc <- spark_connect(method = "livy"),` it was noticed that the "spark.sql.warehouse.dir" parameter was not set to the proper warehouse. This has been resolved, but we are still not able to see any Hive Databases or Tables that were created in HUE through a Livy connection (in other use cases using Spark there are no issues).

We are able to create Databases through a Livy connection and see them in HUE under the correct warehouse, but after closing that connection and opening a new one, we are no longer able to see those databases. 
For instance, Livy-connection-1 creates a database "trial", then we disconnect Livy-connection-1 in RStudio. Start Livy-connection-2, after we run the command `DBI::dbGetQuery(sc, "show databases"),` we are only able to see a "default" database, the "trial" database is no longer accessible through Livy-connection-2.

Any information about this issue is greatly appreciated. We believe there to be a disconnect between a Livy connection and Spark connection when accessing Hive storage.

Thank you, 
Cody

title: Results of ft_one_hot_encoder() are short by one state when input contains zeroes
description:

```r
library(tibble)

d <- data_frame(

)

d_tbl %>%
```

Each vector in `y` has length 2, but it should have length 3, since there are three states.

description:
Version 2.3.0 has been removed from the Apache server at https://www-us.apache.org/dist/spark/
It has been replaced by version 2.3.1 (not supplemented).  The code and jsons in sparklyr have not been updated.

My temporary solution was to replace all 2.3.0 instances in code and jsons with 2.3.1, and prevent the "latest" json being fetched from `spark_versions_url()`

```
    statementReponse <- livy_get_statement(sc, statementReponse$id)

    Sys.sleep(sleepTime)

    waitTimeout <- waitTimeout - 1
    sleepTime <- sleepTime * 2
  }
```

title: maybe cast to double instead of decimal(2,1)
description:
dear sparklyr team,

I am wondering, whether this was always the case or came with recent sparklyr version 0.8.4:
in combination with dplyr, an R ``numeric`` value (i.e. a double value) is explicitly casted as ``decimal(2,1)`` and not ``double``.

EDIT: You can see this for instance when casting the sparklyr dataframe to a spark dataframe. It holds for plain constant values
```R
sdf <- copy_to(sc, data_frame(i = 1), "df", overwrite = TRUE)
mutate(sdf, i2 = 4) %>% spark_dataframe
#<jobj[200]>
#  org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
#  [i: double, i2: decimal(2,1)]
```
as well as array construction for instance
```R
mutate(sdf, a = array(2,3)) %>% spark_dataframe
#<jobj[206]>
#  org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
#  [i: double, a: array<decimal(2,1)>]
```
Notably, when an R data_frame is converted to spark dataframe, a numeric column gets encoded by ``Double`` type (as seen in both examples with the column `i`). EDITEND

Is this intended?
wouldn't it be better to use Double instead, as it is more standard?

title: WITH clause not supported in Spark SQL
description:
Spark SQL supports the WITH clause for common table expressions. Sparklyr assumes that it can execute any SQL handed to it from e.g. `tbl(sc, sql(some_sql))` as a subquery, but WITH clauses do not seem to be supported as subqueries.

For example, a trivial example:
```sql
WITH demo AS ( SELECT 1 AS n ) SELECT n FROM demo
```

succeeds when run from a Databricks SQL cell.

Called from R, it fails:
```
> tbl(sc, sql("WITH demo AS ( SELECT 1 AS n ) SELECT n FROM demo"))

Error : org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.parser.ParseException: 
mismatched input 'FROM' expecting <EOF>(line 2, pos 0)

== SQL ==
SELECT *
FROM (WITH demo AS ( SELECT 1 AS n ) SELECT n FROM demo) `zzz17`
^^^
WHERE (0 = 1)
```

The wrapper around the query seems to be applied by `db_query_fields.spark_connection` since abba9a24f.

title: Improve Serialization
description:
There are two areas worth considering here:

1. Improve `collect()`serialization. This is already implemented as columnar-based collect; however, I believe only for numeric and logical data types.

2. Implement `copy_to()` through columnar `invoke()`.

Assuming (2) is on a par with current implementations of `copy_to()`, we can stop here; otherwise, we would have to explore additional serialization improvements.

Related issues:
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/202 and https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/187: Should be fixed with this work item since `Date` would serialize properly into Spark.
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/151, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/163, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/506, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/528 https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/680, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1143: Issues with `""` and `NA` should be addressed by a common serialization mechanism. Notice also that some `NA` in `flights` are being copied as `NaN`.
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/304 not clear what the issue in `robotics.csv` was nor we have a repro, but this change should help fix that.
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/307 titanic data under `copy_to`, improving fidelity here would solve this issue as well.
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/515 Revisit special types: `NaN`, `NA`, `NULL` and `""`.
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1020 `\n` in `copy_to`
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1013 Serialize correctly `DATE`, `DATETIME`, and `TIMESTAMP` while coming from JDBC. Probably no need to do anything JDBC specific, but worth testing
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1030 handle vector columns in `copy_to()`
- https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1034 column based copy_to could be reused to speed up `spark_apply()`
- [Collect NA in logical columns](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47539670/convert-a-string-to-logical-in-r-with-sparklyr/47559040).

title: Error in spark_apply when some groups return an empty data.frame

I'm using `sparklyr` in a project where I process some user data. I have a function that takes a dataset for each user, and returns another dataset. In some cases, the output dataset can be empty. In these cases, `spark_apply` returns an error.

Let's simulate a simple example. 

# Results using `dplyr`
We define a function that returns the complete rows of a `data.frame`, where some columns can be excluded. We then apply this function on each group in the data.
```r
library(dplyr)
process_data <- function(DF, exclude) {
    DF <- subset(DF, select = colnames(DF)[!colnames(DF) %in% exclude])
    DF[complete.cases(DF),]

    grp = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 5),
    x1 = 1:15,
    x2 = c(1:9, rep(NA, 6)),
```

title: Can idle sparklyr sessions be cleaned up?
description:
referencing https://stackoverflow.com/q/49033520/1785752.

Since hadoop clusters tend to be shared resources, forgetful analysts who do not `spark_disconnect(sc)` when finished working cause problems. This tends not to by an issue for pySpark because jupyter enables the [culling of kernels](http://www.spark.tc/limit-notebook-resource-consumption-by-culling-kernels/). However RStudio Server is friendlier and, though it does suspend sessions, will reinstate them when a user comes back. This is generally very useful *except* that session suspend does not terminate a spark process.

Is it possible to add a timeout argument (if R or the spark session have been idle for x amount of time)? Can a callback be used to trigger Spark sessions to disconnect when RStudio suspends a session?

title: spark_apply set .libPaths
description:
I know that a lot of work has gone into making packages available to R workers living in spark executors. However one option that does not seem to be supported is simply setting `.libPaths` to something.

Naturally users _could_ do
```
tbl %>%
  spark_apply(function(x, context){.libPaths("something"), ...})
```
but it would be nice to enable a system level configuration (think RStudio Server running on a cluster edge node). Would it be possible to support something similar to `spark.r.command` (e.g., `spark.r.libpaths`) which, if set, will cause `.libPaths(config$spark.r.libpaths)` to be executed before `f` in the workers.

title: `spark_apply()` could significantly improve performance for data transfer into Scala
description: See https://stackoverflow.com/questions/46396736/sparklyrs-spark-apply-function-seems-to-run-on-single-executor-and-fails-on-mod/46410425#46410425 My repro, Amazon EMR cluster `1 x master: m3.xlarge`, `1 x core: m3.xlarge`: ``` testdf <- data.frame(string_id=rep(letters[1:5], times=1000000), # 5000 row table string_categories=rep(c("", "1", "2 3", "4 5 6", "7"), times=1000000)) testtbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, testdf, overwrite=TRUE, repartition=100L, memory=TRUE) # Write function to return dataframe with strings split out myFunction <- function(inputdf){ inputdf$string_categories <- as.character(inputdf$string_categories) inputdf$string_categories=with(inputdf, ifelse(string_categories=="", "blank", string_categories)) stringCategoriesList <- strsplit(inputdf$string_categories, ' ') outDF <- data.frame(string_id=rep(inputdf$string_id, times=unlist(lapply(stringCategoriesList, length))), string_categories=unlist(stringCategoriesList)) return(outDF) } # Use spark_apply to run function in Spark outtbl <- testtbl %>% spark_apply(myFunction, names=c('string_id', 'string_categories')) sdf_nrow(outtbl) [1] 8e+06 ``` followed by ``` outtbl <- testtbl %>% spark_apply(function(e) nrow(e), names=c(count = "double"), memory = FALSE) x <- outtbl %>% collect() sum(x) [1] 5000000 ``` Notice fetching data into R taked about `~3min`, fetching and retrieving all the data about `~30min`

title: Cannot pass data as a Scala List object
description:
There doesn't appear to be any documentation around this so I assume this is an issue. According to [this link](https://campus.datacamp.com/courses/introduction-to-spark-in-r-using-sparklyr/going-native-use-the-native-interface-to-manipulate-spark-dataframes?ex=10), passing an R `list` to an `invoke` function will pass a Spark `ArrayType`. How exactly do I pass a Spark `ListType`? I am trying to call [this function](https://github.com/SteveBall/SML/blob/master/src/main/scala/com/ons/sml/businessMethods/methods/Lag.scala) from R but when giving it a list, it obviously doesn't work because the data types don't match up. So how exactly do we pass lists? I feel like there should be an `ensure_scala_list` function. The code that I am running can be found below.

```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

  "v" = c(11, 12, 13, 21, 22)
) %>%

  spark_dataframe()

# Invoke the lagFunc method
invoke_static(
  sc,
  class = "com.ons.sml.businessMethods.methods.Lag",

) %>% invoke(

  df = lag_data, 
  partitionCol = list("id"), 
  orderCol = list("t"), 
  targetCol = "v",

)
```

title: Consider reporting structured connection failure information
description:
Customer provided feedback that `spark_connect()` should support retrieving structured connection failure information.

Their particular use case involves using `spark_connect()` from a shiny application through a Shiny app where users can select their cluster configuration (memory, executors, etc).

However, it is not uncommon for this connection to fail if cluster is under load or lacks the requested resources. Therefore, we could consider implementing:

```r
config <- spark_config()
config$sparklyr.connect.structured <- TRUE
config$spark.executor.memory <- "10000g"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = config)
```

which instead of failing, `sc` would return:

```
list(
   connected = FALSE,
   failure = "Failed to allocate executor with 10000g of memory"
)
```

The `failure` message would be provided by the underlined cluster manager but `sparklyr` would make it easily available for users of `sparklyr`.

title: It would be helpful if Sparklyr were a bit more DBI compliant
description:
It would be helpful if `Sparklyr` were a bit more `DBI` compliant.  In particular it would be very handy (when writing generic code expected to work over different data sources) if:

  * `Sparklyr`'s implementation of `dbWriteTable()` allowed the overwrite argument.
  * `Sparklyr`'s implementation of `dbWriteTable()` allowed at least `row.names = FALSE` (it would be find to error-out on an attempt to set this to `TRUE`).
  * `Sparklyr` connections could be close via `DBI::dbDisconnect()`.


``` r

library("sparklyr")
library("DBI")
sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(version="2.1.0", 
                              master = "local")

DBI::dbWriteTable(sc, 
                  "d",
                  data.frame(x=1),
                  overwrite = TRUE)
#> Error in .local(conn, name, value, ...): unused argument (overwrite = TRUE)

DBI::dbWriteTable(sc, 
                  "d",
                  data.frame(x=1),
                  row.names = FALSE)
#> Error in .local(conn, name, value, ...): unused argument (row.names = FALSE)

DBI::dbWriteTable(sc, 
                  "d",
                  data.frame(x=1),
                  temporary = TRUE,
                  append = FALSE)

DBI::dbRemoveTable(sc, "d")

DBI::dbDisconnect(sc)
#> Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable) : unable to find an inherited method for function 'dbDisconnect' for signature '"spark_connection"'

sparklyr::spark_disconnect(sc)
```

title: Unclear error 8880 connected to an error in the dependencies file
description:
This isn't really an issue, there was a bug in my code but it is interesting behaviour I wanted to share.

I am writing a package which extends `sparklyr`. My `dependencies` file is as follows:

```
spark_dependencies <- function(spark_version, scala_version, ...) {
  sparklyr::spark_dependency(
    jars = c(
     system.file(
       "java/sparkts-0.4.0-SNAPSHOT-jar-with-dependencies.jar",
       package = "sparkts"
     )
    ),
    packages = c(
    )
  )
}

#' @import sparklyr
.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  sparklyr::register_extension(pkgname)
}
```

However my package originally had a different name and I had forgot to change the line `package = "sparkts"`. On my Mac this didn't cause any error at all. On my Windows machine however, I did get errors.

I was able to connect to Spark with

```
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
```

But when I ran `devtools::test()`, which includes the `spark_connect()` function, R would not connect to Spark and gave the following error

```
Error: Test failed: 'the standard error calculations are as expected'
Failed while connecting to sparklyr to port (8880) for sessionid (4612): Gateway in port (8880) did not respond.
   Path: C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\spark\spark-2.1.0-bin-hadoop2.7\bin\spark-submit2.cmd
   Parameters: --class, sparklyr.Shell, --jars, "", "C:\Users\me\Documents\R\win-library\3.4\sparklyr\java\sparklyr-2.1-2.11.jar", 8880, 4612
   Log: C:\Users\me~1\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpURoBhf\file98843ce4b1e_spark.log
```

Changing the package name in the dependencies file fixed this, but I find it odd that R could connect to Spark when typing the command in the console and not when used in a test. And this behaviour only occurred on Windows. Mac didn't have any issue with it. Is it possible to give a clearer error message about this?

library(sparklyr)

```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

x = cbind(rep(1,5), 1:5)
y = rnorm(5)

df = as.data.frame(cbind(x,y))

copy_to(sc, df)

ml_generalized_linear_regression(x= tbl(sc, "df"), formula = y ~. , family = "gaussian", link = "log")


glm(formula = y ~. , family = gaussian(link = "log"), data = df, start = rep(1,3))

```

title: Issues with spark_apply() in datasets containing NA
description:
This is related to the issue #774. Even though that issue has been closed, it would seem that even in version 0.6.0 the issue still exists in some form. Here is an example: 

```
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = 'local')

na_tbl_local <- structure(list(A = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), 
                               B = c(NA, 1L, NA, 1L, 1L, NA), 
                               C = c(NA, NA, 1L, NA, NA, NA), 
                               D = c(1L, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA), 
                               E = c(NA, NA, NA, 1L, NA, NA), 
                               F = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, 1L)), 
                          .Names = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), 
                          row.names = c(NA,-6L), 
                          class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)
na_tbl <- copy_to(sc, na_tbl_local, name="na_tbl")

spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(data) {
  I(data)
})

spark_apply(na_tbl, function(data) {
  I(data)
})
```

The first `spark_apply()` performs adequately, whereas the second one throws an error. I've first tried running this example on a remote EC2 cluster with spark 2.2.0 and sparklyr 0.6.0, and I appended the error in a comment to #774, so I won't repeat it here. Today I've installed the development version from github (0.7.0-9014), and tried running the same code locally. The error is then: 

```
Error in file(con, "r") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
In file(con, "r") :

```

Application is submitted, resource manager creates application master with spark gateway on one of nodes in cluster, but my client from rstudio is not trying to contact spark gateway residing on application manager, it always contacts localhost and so I get timeout from application.
This behavior can be changed using sparklyr.gateway.address, if I put there any node of cluster and application master starts on same node, connection is successful.

title: Map term indices to terms ft_count_vectorizer
description:
---

I am unable to efficiently map term indices created by ft_count_vectorizer to words.  Reproducible example below.

```r
spark_version <- "2.1.0"

library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

# connection
sc <- spark_connect(master = 'local')

# fake data
fake_data <- data.frame(a = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                        b = c("the groggy", "frog was", "a very groggy", "frog"))
fake_tbl <- copy_to(sc, df = fake_data, overwrite = TRUE)

# count vectorizer
fake_vectorizer <- fake_tbl %>%
  ft_tokenizer(input_col = 'b', output_col = 'tokens') %>%
  ft_count_vectorizer(input_col = 'tokens', output_col = 'features')

# model
fake_model <- fake_vectorizer %>%
  ml_lda(features_col = 'features', k = 2)

fake_model$topicsMatrix

# Which indices correspond to which words?
```

title: Support dplyr select helpers for ml_* and ft_* functions
description:
It would be useful to support `dplyr`s select helper functions to select columns for the `features` argument to `ml_*` functions, and for the `input.col` argument to `ft_*` functions.

I want to write something like this:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect("local")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)
iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_linear_regression("Species", starts_with("Petal"))
```

The current workaround is to use something like this, which is not as nice.

```r
library(stringr)
iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_linear_regression("Species", str_subset(colnames(.), "^Petal"))
```

title: Consider functionality to simplify EDA/generation of summary statistics
description:
> As a Data Scientist, I want a suite of functions for performing common exploratory data analysis tasks so that I won't have to develop them from scratch.

Understanding that every project/dataset is different, there are common things that people almost always look at, e.g. missing values, ranges of numeric variables, "levels" of string columns and their distributions. We can take inspiration from https://github.com/ropenscilabs/skimr and https://github.com/dcomtois/summarytools and perhaps implement methods from the former. We'll also have to think about whether these tools belong in `sparklyr`.

Currently, users can invoke [`describe()`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/b78e3849b20d0d09b7146efd7ce8f203ef67b890/sql/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/Dataset.scala#L2187-L2246) on the DataFrame (and this might not be obvious to new Spark users), but that only gives very basic stats for numeric columns. They can also write some `dplyr` pipelines, which might not be trivial (in the sense that you'll have to think about tidyeval if you want to automate.)

title: access to scala singletons
description:
My understanding is that Scala singletons are referenced by a `MODULE$` static field in Java. I can't find any way to access fields via the Spark connection. So I guess support for fields would do the job. But maybe there's a smarter way.

For now I'll just use reflection methods to access the field, but it would be nice to have that built in, along with some conveniences for interfacing with Scala constructs. I could contribute this if you're interested.

title: current design of sdf_mutate makes extensions awkward
description:
Currently `sdf_mutate` constructs a call such that
```r
df %>%
  sdf_mutate(out=some_function(in1, in2))
```
actually calls `some_function(in1, out, in2)` internally with unnamed arguments in the first two positions (`in2` in this case would keep its name if it had one). This works OK for `ft_*` functions that take a single column input. However it makes it difficult to design functions intended to be used from `sdf_mutate` that have multiple inputs and may refer to multiple columns of the input data frame.

For example, take the following `ft_starts_with` function that can call `startsWith(Column other)` or `startsWith(String literal)` from the [Spark Column API](https://spark.apache.org/docs/2.1.0/api/java/org/apache/spark/sql/Column.html#startsWith(org.apache.spark.sql.Column))
```r
ft_starts_with_v1 <- function(.data, col, output_col, pattern, ...) {
  pattern <- deparse(substitute(pattern))
  ft_starts_with_(.data, col=col, pattern=pattern, output_col=output_col, ...)
}


ft_starts_with_v2 <- function(.data, col, pattern, ..., output_col) {
  
  ft_starts_with_(.data, col=col, pattern=pattern, output_col=output_col, ...)
}

ft_starts_with_ <- function(.data, col, pattern, ..., output_col) {
  
  # get java refs
  sc <- spark_connection(.data)
  sdf <- spark_dataframe(.data)
  
  # function specific error checking
  if (!is.character(col) || !(col %in% colnames(.data)))
    stop("'col' must be a column of the input dataframe")
  col <- invoke(sdf, "col", col)
  
  if (!is.character(pattern))
    stop("'pattern' must either be a character string or else the name of a column")
  if (pattern %in% colnames(.data))
    pattern <- invoke(sdf, "col", pattern)
  
  # call udf - here I'm using the Spark Column API, it might also be a custom scala method
  spk_output_col <- invoke(col, "startsWith", pattern)
  df <- invoke(sdf, "withColumn", output_col, spk_output_col)
  sdf_register(df)
}
```

The current implementation leads to some unexpected results
```r
df <- copy_to(sc, data.frame(a=c("abc", "def", "ghi"), b=c("ab", "ab", "gh")))

df %>% sdf_mutate(sw=ft_starts_with_v1(a, pattern=b)) # works
df %>% sdf_mutate(sw=ft_starts_with_v1(a, pattern="ab")) # works
df %>% sdf_mutate(sw=ft_starts_with_v1(a, b)) # works, but only because "pattern" is the 3rd argument in the v1 function
df %>% sdf_mutate(sw=ft_starts_with_v1(pattern=b, col=a)) # fails because the "pattern=" name is clobbered and b is passed in as the 1st arg positionally, which maps it to "output_col" since "col" is supplied as a named argument
```

This pattern also makes the help that the RStudio IDE provides more difficult to interpret for users who may reasonably wonder what to do with the `output_col` input.

I suggest modifying `sdf_mutate` such that the output column is passed in as a named argument instead of by position. Also let all arguments (not just the 1st) be checked to see whether they should be evaluated locally or defer evaluation until later. I believe this already works for existing `ft_*` functions thanks to the coding consistency in using `output_col` in the function signature.

With this design change (see forthcoming PR) functions can be written more intuitively like `ft_starts_with_v2`. In that case all 4 of the above examples work.

title: Consider implementing dim(), nrow(), ncol() for Spark data frames
description:
There was a suggestion to support basic data frame operations in https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/315.

This would allow this code to work:

```{r}
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris)

dim(iris_tbl)
nrow(iris_tbl)
ncol(iris_tbl)

# others?
```

While this could be really helpful, it could also create the wrong expectations that an `sdf` supports all the functionality of a `df` including the `[]` and `[[]]` operators.  At the very least, we might want to override `[]`, `[[]]` and others to throw errors that make it clear this is unsupported and point users to `dplyrs` equivalents instead.

@jjallaire @kevinushey Not planning to work on this in the short term, but would be good to have your thoughts on this.

title: Can not set "livy.session.start.timeout"
description:
I am experiencing a long waiting time on server side and need to set a longer timeout. If I set the "livy.session.start.timeout" in the config and try to connect, an error is thrown:

Here is the connection codes:

```r
s_config <- spark_config()
s_config["spark_version"] <- "2.1.1"
s_config["livy.session.start.timeout"] <- 120
config <- livy_config(s_config, "***username***", "***pwd***")
sc <- spark_connect(master = "***url***", method="livy", config=config)
```
Here is the error:
```r
Error in livy_validate_http_response("Failed to create livy session",  : 
  Failed to create livy session (Client error: (400) Bad Request): "Unrecognized field \"session.start.timeout\" (class com.cloudera.livy.server.interactive.CreateInteractiveRequest), not marked as ignorable (15 known properties: \"executorCores\", \"conf\", \"driverMemory\", \"name\", \"driverCores\", \"pyFiles\", \"archives\", \"queue\", \"kind\", \"executorMemory\", \"files\", \"jars\", \"proxyUser\", \"numExecutors\", \"heartbeatTimeoutInSecond\" [truncated]])\n at [Source: HttpInputOverHTTP@6a20dd3f; line: 1, column: 79] (through reference chain: com.cloudera.livy.server.interactive.CreateInteractiveRequest[\"session.start.timeout\"])"
```

It seems this config is also sent to livy in the session config and it doesn't exist in livy's config. Livy failed to create the InteractiveRequest. Code is here:
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/8bf5d24ddebd0c5281e0758fd094f34b95f20ddc/R/livy_connection.R#L193

For further verification, I also set the CreateInteractiveRequest to ignore unknown configs and solves the problem. However, I thought this is a issue from this package and should be fixed.

title: yarn-client spark_disconnect(sc) not working in sparklyr > 0.6.2
description:
In sparklyr v0.6.3 & v0.6.4 in `yarn-client` mode, `spark_disconnect(sc)` does not shutdown the actual Spark job.
The Spark job is still listed as "RUNNING" in the resourcemanager. Even when killing this yarn application, the Spark driver Java process keeps running on the node where the sparklyr session has been created.

In sparklyr v0.6.2, the whole Spark job gracefully shuts down when `spark_disconnect` is used.

This whole issue can be reproduced using a very basic example:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-client")
spark_disconnect(sc)
```

title: Simplify return value from sdf_schema()
description:
At the moment, `sdf_schema()` returns a list of lists. It would be easier to work with if the return value was a tibble with two columns: `name` and `type`.

For example, this is verbose, hard to read, and hard to program with.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect("local")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)

sdf_schema(iris_tbl)
## $Sepal_Length
## $Sepal_Length$name
## [1] "Sepal_Length"
## 
## $Sepal_Length$type
## [1] "DoubleType"
## 
## 
## $Sepal_Width
## $Sepal_Width$name
## [1] "Sepal_Width"
## 
## $Sepal_Width$type
## [1] "DoubleType"
## 
## 
## $Petal_Length
## $Petal_Length$name
## [1] "Petal_Length"
## 
## $Petal_Length$type
## [1] "DoubleType"
## 
## 
## $Petal_Width
## $Petal_Width$name
## [1] "Petal_Width"
## 
## $Petal_Width$type
## [1] "DoubleType"
## 
## 
## $Species
## $Species$name
## [1] "Species"
## 
## $Species$type
## [1] "StringType"
```

This is much nicer, but it is a pain having to do this transformation myself.

```r
sdf_schema(iris_tbl) %>% 
  lapply(function(x) do.call(data_frame, x)) %>% 
  bind_rows()
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##           name       type
##          <chr>      <chr>
## 1 Sepal_Length DoubleType
## 2  Sepal_Width DoubleType
## 3 Petal_Length DoubleType
## 4  Petal_Width DoubleType
## 5      Species StringType
```

title: DST error on datetimes when reading from Cassandra into Sparklyr
description:
When reading a date from Cassandra into spark using `sparklyr_0.7.0-9035` (current version of master), DST (I assume) pushes the date back by one day.  This can prove costly if things end up being partitioned wrongly because of it.

This is not a problem on the current CRAN version of `sparklyr`

```
> installed.packages()["sparklyr",]["Version"]
     Version 
"0.7.0-9035" 
```

### Reproducible example

Set up keyspace and table in Cassandra
```
CREATE KEYSPACE "dst_bug"
WITH replication = {'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor' : 1} ;

CREATE TABLE dst_bug.tbl (
    dttm date,
    PRIMARY KEY (dttm)
) ;
```

```
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)
library(crassy)  # remotes::install_github("AkhilNairAmey/crassy")  # some helper bindings

config <- spark_config()
config$sparklyr.defaultPackages = "com.datastax.spark:spark-cassandra-connector_2.11:2.0.5"
config$spark.cassandra.connection.host = 'localhost'

sc <- spark_connect(
  master     = 'local', 
  version = "2.0.2",
  config = config
)

# Make some data
handle = copy_to(sc, tibble(dttm = as.Date("2017-05-13")), "spk_tbl")

# Insert into keyspace.tbl
crassy::spark_write_cassandra_table(handle, "dst_bug", "tbl")

# Read back data
crassy::spark_load_cassandra_table(sc, "dst_bug", "tbl", "read_spk_tbl")
```

Resulting in
```
> crassy::spark_load_cassandra_table(sc, "dst_bug", "tbl", "read_spk_tbl")
# Source:   table<read_spk_tbl> [?? x 1]
# Database: spark_connection
        dttm
      <date>
1 2017-05-12
```
where the date has shifted from `2017-05-13` to `2017-05-12`.

Consider officially supporting `features` and `response` arguments in ml_ routines
description:
With the new API we've soft-deprecated `features` and `response` in favor of the formula interface, which supports interactions [among other things](https://spark.apache.org/docs/2.2.0/ml-features.html#rformula). These arguments are still respected for backwards compatibility. I'm thinking about bringing these back as officially supported, mainly for the use case where users manipulate a long features vector. Also, these parameters (either as `response, features`, `y, x`, or variations thereof) are common in other ML APIs.

@edgararuiz thoughts?

title: Segfault on reinitialising connection
description:
Reopening #840 in a new issue as suggested:

@javierluraschi Finally think I've tracked this down...

Here's a Dockerfile reproducing the environment from `rocker/tidyverse`

```
FROM rocker/tidyverse:latest

RUN apt update && apt install r-cran-rjava -y

RUN install2.r sparklyr

RUN R -e 'sparklyr::spark_install("2.0.2")'

RUN printf "library(sparklyr)\n\nsc = spark_connect('local')\nspark_disconnect(sc)\nspark_connect('local')\n" > script.r
```

That last little bit of script sent into `script.r` is

```
library(sparklyr)

sc = spark_connect('local')
spark_disconnect(sc)
spark_connect('local')
```

Running `docker run --rm -it coredump Rscript script.r` yields

```
* Using Spark: 2.0.2
* Using Spark: 2.0.2

 *** caught segfault ***
address 0x55a590f25003, cause 'memory not mapped'
*** Error in `/usr/local/lib/R/bin/exec/R': malloc(): memory corruption: 0x000055a590e7d920 ***
```

What I've found is that putting a sleep in for 10 seconds between the disconnect and the reconnect solves this.  

___
My use case for doing this (connecting, disconnecting, reconnecting) is making certain all the memory is completely wiped and make reavailable when running sequential 2 hour long independent queries.  This shouldn't be a problem to me now as I know how to avoid the segfault, but thought you might wanna know what was going on!

Akhil

title: Support predicate pushdown when reading from generic source (spark_read_source)
description:
In [`sparkbq`](https://github.com/miraisolutions/sparkbq) we implemented a Google BigQuery data source that theoretically supports **predicate pushdown** by implementing `org.apache.spark.sql.sources.PrunedFilteredScan` (see corresponding Scala project [spark-bigquery](https://github.com/miraisolutions/spark-bigquery)). We are using `sparklyr`'s `spark_read_source` to integrate the data source.

The current API for `spark_read_source` (as of `sparklyr` 0.6.4) does not support predicate pushdown in that it couples reading from the data source with repartitioning and registration as a temporary table on the Spark side. See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/198da77016f309c110d08004b68efb27c8c9acc8/R/data_interface.R#L635-L636

As an example, if I do (pseudo-code)
``` r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

sc <- spark_connect(...)

result <-
  spark_read_source(
    sc,
    name = name,
    source = "com.miraisolutions.spark.bigquery",
    ...
  ) %>%
  filter(column == "some value")
```
then the data source specified in the call to `spark_read_source` will eventually be fully read without the possibility for the filter predicate to be pushed down to the data source (Google BigQuery in my case). Reason is the call to `spark_partition_register_df` inside `spark_read_source` that calls `registerTempTable` on the resulting Spark DataFrame. If `spark_partition_register_df` would be decoupled from `spark_read_source` then (generic) data sources could implement predicate pushdown and that would/should be transparent through the `dplyr` interface.  Registration of a Spark DataFrame and repartitioning are already available through `sdf_register` and `sdf_repartition`.

The example above would then look rather like
``` r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

sc <- spark_connect(...)

result <-
  spark_read_source(
    sc,
    source = "com.miraisolutions.spark.bigquery",
    ...
  ) %>%
  filter(column == "some value") %>%
  sdf_register(name = name)
```
In this case, the predicate may be pushed down to the data source which may avoid transferring a lot of data.

title: Function reference page does not contain all functions
description:
Hello,

The sparklyr function reference at https://spark.rstudio.com/reference/index.html does list all the functions available in the package. In particular, the function `sdf_quantile()` is not listed. Other functions may be affected.

This page seems to list the doc for all functions but the HTML files are not directly rendered in the browser making it less than ideal to see the doc without cloning the repo locally: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/tree/master/docs/reference

Is there a URL providing a complete and up-to-date function reference?

```
> packageVersion("sparklyr")
[1] ‘0.7.0.9031’

# The function indeed exists in this version of the package
> sparklyr ::sdf_quantile
function (x, column, probabilities = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), 
    relative.error = 1e-05) 
{
    sdf <- spark_dataframe(x)
    nm <- names(probabilities) %||% paste(signif(probabilities * 
        100, 3), "%", sep = "")
    column <- ensure_scalar_character(column)
    probabilities <- as.list(as.numeric(probabilities))
    relative.error <- ensure_scalar_double(relative.error)
    stat <- invoke(sdf, "stat")
    quantiles <- invoke(stat, "approxQuantile", column, probabilities, 
        relative.error)
    names(quantiles) <- nm
    quantiles
}
<environment: namespace:sparklyr>
```

Thanks!

title: Dates retrieved as doubles in spark_apply()
description:
```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

df <- data.frame(
    DATE = c("2001-02-15", "2003-03-05", "2001-02-15"),
    DATETIME = c("2001-02-15T00:00:00.000Z", "2003-03-05T00:00:00.000Z", "2001-02-15T00:00:00.000Z"))

df_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, df, overwrite = T)

df_tbl %>% spark_apply(function(e) {
    as.data.frame(lapply(e, anytime::anydate))
})
```

title: spark_write_source not appropriate for generic Spark data sources
description:
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/491194f64e92bc5985961e99f65a04fa9d5dffb6/R/data_interface.R#L429

For a generic data source `spark_write_source` (`
spark_data_write_generic`) should call `.format(source)` where `source` is the name of a class extending `org.apache.spark.sql.sources.CreatableRelationProvider` similar to `spark_read_source` where `source`  is the name of a class extending `org.apache.spark.sql.sources.RelationProvider`.

With the current implementation, the source class name is used as method name and leads to a `java.lang.IllegalArgumentException` being thrown.

title: Documentation question: is there any way to control how many rows spark_apply() cuts data into?
description:
Documentation question: is there any way to control how many rows spark_apply() cuts data into?

On my small machine it seems to work in about one quarter million row blocks (which is fine), but on a production server cluster it seems to send all of the rows to a single worker (which I do not want to happen).

Is there a control that says what the maximum number of rows per-chunk are?  Or is this something we can achieve through the `group_by` argument somehow?

title: Cluster mode doesn't wait for ACCEPTED application to be resourced by YARN
description:
Testing cluster mode on our internal Hortonworks cluster shows launch sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.  Failures appear to be due to timeout waiting for the application to start.  However, the application is in ACCEPTED state and a state-aware client could handle launch more robustly.  Propose a new logic to make launch more likely to succeed and give user control over timeouts at each stage.

Current behavior:
Sparklyr receives RM output which shows new SPARK application in ACCEPTED state.
Sparklyr polls RM until sparklyr.yarn.cluster.start.timeout
Sparklyr reports failure to launch after timeout.

Desired behavior:
Sparklyr receives RM output which shows new SPARK application in ACCEPTED state.  
Sparklyr stores the application id for the ACCEPTED application
Sparklyr client enters a polling loop (with a sleep shorter than the sparklyr shell connection timeout), and monitors the application status for change to RUNNING, FAILED, FINSHED or KILLED states.
On running state, sparklyr client attempts connection to remote.
On any other state, sparklyr client reports failure to launch.

There is potential to just increase the sparklyr.yarn.cluster.start.timeout, but a YARN-state awareness would have better results for the end user.  Failure to detect the application in a period of time may indicate a failure to submit, but detecting an application in ACCEPTED state indicates a succesful submit. There may also be a failure to start the remote spark application, but that cannot be resolved until the application enters the RUNNING state.  The same is true for failure to connect.

I propose separating timeouts for cluster mode, with a submit timeout, resource timeout, and a connect timeout.  This gives the user with knowledge of how they expect their cluster to behave control over how sparklyr waits for each stage.

title: columns lost when converting from json to parquet
description:
Hello @javierluraschi @kevinykuo ,

I hope all is good!

I am facing a serious issue here and I am not sure this is a bug or not. I have a bunch of large json files, and _some of them_ contain one more column than the others. Because of their size, I convert them to parquet using


```
for(i in 51:length(file_names)){
  df <- spark_read_json(sc, paste("/mypath/",file_names[i], sep = ""),
                        repartition = 0,
                        name = "df",
                        memory = FALSE,
                        overwrite = TRUE)
  spark_write_parquet(df,paste("/mypath/","parquet_",file_names[i], sep = ""), mode = "overwrite" )
  dplyr::db_drop_table(sc, "df")
}

```

Then, in my spark code I can easily do

`df_new <- spark_read_parquet(sc, "/mypath/parquet_**", overwrite = TRUE, name = "df_new", memory = FALSE)
`

to load everything at once.

Unfortunately, I now  realize that when I do so, `df_new` does not include the extra column that is present in some of the `json` files. Is that a bug?

Thanks!

title: Return list of character vectors from ft_tokenizer(), ft_regex_tokenizer()
description:
At the moment, `ft_tokenizer()` returns a list of lists of character vectors.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect("local")

text_data <- data_frame(
  x = c("This is a sentence", "So is this")
)
text_data_tbl <- copy_to(sc, text_data)

tokenized <- text_data_tbl %>%
  ft_tokenizer("x", "word") %>%
  collect()
tokenized$word
## [[1]]
## [[1]][[1]]
## [1] "this"
## 
## [[1]][[2]]
## [1] "is"
## etc.
```
It would be simpler to work with a list of character vectors.

In particular, in order to do sentiment analysis on Spark using `tidytext`, the data should be in the form of one word per row. So I want to call `ft_tokenizer()` followed by `unnest()`.

This requires the simpler return value from `ft_tokenizer()`, and implementations of `tidyr` methods for `tbl_spark`s, as discussed in https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/252.

`ft_regex_tokenizer()` has the same form for the return values.

title: ml_gradient_boosted_trees() is slow
description:
Unclear if it's a `sparklyr` problem or a Spark MLlib problem, but I think it's worth a quick investigation here.

`ml_gradient_boosted_trees()` seems to be pretty slow, even for moderately sized datasets.

For example, predicting the price in the `diamonds` dataset takes ~ 20 seconds:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)
library(stringr)

data(diamonds, package = "ggplot2")
diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(
    cut = str_replace(cut, " ", "_")
  )
sc <- spark_connect("local")

diamonds_tbl <- copy_to(sc, diamonds, overwrite = TRUE)

feature_cols <- diamonds_tbl %>% 
  colnames() %>% 
  setdiff("price")
system.time(
  model <- diamonds_tbl %>% 
    ml_gradient_boosted_trees("price", feature_cols)
)
```

compared to about 4 seconds for the equivalent using `mboost::mboost()`.

```r
library(mboost)

system.time(
  model2 <- mboost(
    price ~ carat + cut + color + clarity + depth + table + x + y + z, 
    diamonds
  )
)
```

I realize that the routines are not exactly comparable, but it seems a big enough difference to warrant some exploration.

title: consider how reference labels should be chosen / selected for ml routines
description:
There's a couple over-arching things we'd like to make easily configurable:
1. Given a categorical variable `x` with some labels `yes`, `no`, etc., we should provide some mechanism for mapping labels to dummy variable names; e.g. the column such that `x == "yes"` is called `RespondedYes`, or something to that effect. This is primarily to allow for nicer model / summary output.
2. We should provide some mechanism for allowing users to configure what level should be considered the reference label, for categorical variables. Normally, for R, this is done just by encoding the variable as a `factor`, with the first level implicitly acting as the reference label.

For 1., I think we could allow the user to supply a list of mappings for these generated names, e.g.

```
metadata = list(
  x = list(
    reference = "no",
    mapping = list(
      yes = "RespondedYes"
    )
  )
)
data_tbl %>% ml_linear_regression(y ~ x, metadata = metadata)
```

And we could provide helpers for constructing that metadata -- although it's a bit verbose, it should provide what we need.

title: An error probably caused by dplyr::rename_vars
description:
Try the following sciprt:
```
iris1=copy_to(sc,iris,'iris')
iris2=rename(iris1,SL=Sepal_Length,SW=Sepal_Width) %>%
  mutate(Petal_Width=Petal_Width+1)
show_query(iris2)
```
Error message:
```
Error in names(select)[match(old_vars, vars)] <- new_vars : 
  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments
```
You can also reproduce the error by:
```
dbplyr::op_grps(iris2$ops)
```

The problem is probably caused by dplyr::rename_vars:
```
function (vars, ..., strict = TRUE) 
{
    exprs <- exprs(...)
    if (any(names2(exprs) == "")) {
        abort("All arguments must be named")
    }
    old_vars <- map2(exprs, names(exprs), switch_rename)
    new_vars <- names(exprs)
    unknown_vars <- setdiff(old_vars, vars)
    if (strict && length(unknown_vars) > 0) {
        bad_args(unknown_vars, "contains unknown variables")
    }
    select <- set_names(vars, vars)
    names(select)[match(old_vars, vars)] <- new_vars
    select
}
<environment: namespace:dplyr>
```
`match(old_vars, vars)` may generate a vector containing NAs, which cannot be used for index in subsassignment.

I think the author meant this instead:
```
modified_rename_vars=function (vars, ..., strict = TRUE) {
  exprs <- exprs(...)
  if (any(names2(exprs) == "")) {
    abort("All arguments must be named")
  }
  old_vars <- map2(exprs, names(exprs), switch_rename)
  new_vars <- names(exprs)
  unknown_vars <- setdiff(old_vars, vars)
  if (strict && length(unknown_vars) > 0) {
    bad_args(unknown_vars, "contains unknown variables")
  }
  select <- set_names(vars, vars)
  sel_ov=match(old_vars, vars)
  names(select)[sel_ov[!is.na(sel_ov)]] <- names(old_vars)[old_vars %in% select]
  select
}
```

If we can confirm that this is the root cause, then we can inform the dplyr authors.

title: Support for yarn-cluster mode
description:
Currently, sparklyr submits a custom `sparklyr.jar` file through spark-submit with a given ports file. Then the jar initializes a socket and saves the socket details in the ports file. This file is used by sparklyr to rea this socket definition and connect to the running application within the jar in the driver machine. This works as expected for `yarn-client`; however, for `yarn-cluster` the file is located on a different machine that the r process running `sparklyr` won't be able to locate since it's not local anymore.

Marking this as feature request for discussion and planning work for next release.

title: Improve docs for mode arg of spark_write_*()
description:
The sparklyr docs for spark_write_*() include a mode arg but lack a reference to where one can determine the set of possible values for that arg.  I think the correct reference is http://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-programming-guide.html#save-modes.  

I had intended to make a PR, but I noticed multiple occurrences of `#' @param mode` for each function in conjunction with `#' @inheritParams spark_write_csv`.  So, I wasn't certain whether the same ref could serve all funcs (and if so whether the individual `#' @param mode` lines should be dropped in favor of a single inherited param.  

Some guidance would be appreciated.  [Relevant R file](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/master/R/data_interface.R).

title: Improve serialization from JDBC Sources
description:
Per @javierluraschi's comments in #941 I have opened this new issue. 

The problem is that date and date time fields from MySQL (and possibly other JDBC sources) are read into Spark (via `spark_read_jdbc`) as character instead of preserving the datetime structure.

In #941 you requested a sample schema and I have modified your example to include the three MySQL date/datetime types. This updated schema below is very similar to the schema's we're using for our database. In the real schema we use datetime for both the `created` and `updated` fields but for this testing example I have made one a timestamp field to cover all of the use cases. 

```
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEES(
   ID INT PRIMARY KEY       NOT NULL,
   NAME           TEXT      NOT NULL,
   AGE            INT       NOT NULL,
   ADDRESS        CHAR(50),
   SALARY         REAL,
   DOB            DATE      NOT NULL,
   CREATED        DATETIME  NOT NULL,
   UPDATED        TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
```
Thanks for taking a look!

``` r
d <- data.frame(x=1:3)

# expected behavior
d %>% 
  mutate(y=v)
#>   x y

dS <- copy_to(sc, d)
```

title: na.omit() not working efficiently.
description:
# Reporting an Issue with sparklyr na.omit()

---
Unfortunately I can not provide an workable example but here is my issue.
I have a dataset with 50 features, only 1 feature has a lot of missing values for this particular example and I want to use na.omit to remove ones with missingness. 

```r
spark_version <- "2.1.0"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)
data <- spark_read_csv(sc,'final', "hdfs://...")
           features <- paste0("V", 1:50)
            # only one with missing values is feature 1
            mod.dat <- data %>% select(features[1:10]) %>% na.omit()
```
* Dropped 7173698 rows with 'na.omit' (7985217 => 811519)
It created a nice mod.dat for my models. Running time is about 17 seconds. 

```r
            mod.dat <- data %>% select(features[1:30]) %>% na.omit()
```
* Dropped 7173698 rows with 'na.omit' (7985217 => 811519)
Then it will wait forever, NO OUTPUT, NO ERROR! It seemed to be waiting a calculation to be completed. 

So I had to use an alternative coding as follow:
```r
           mod.dat <- data %>% select(features[1]) %>% na.omit() 
           dftmp <- data %>% select(features[-1])
           mod.dat <- right_join(dftmp, mod.dat, by = "parcelid")
```
* Dropped 7173698 rows with 'na.omit' (7985217 => 811519)
Nice and easy! Running time is 15 seconds.
Just wondering how na.omit is behaving in the example. Apparently it has detection 7173698 rows with na or null values. Why does it take so long to process the additional features which donot  have nas?

title: Documentation request/query: what is guaranteed about row order in sparklyr?
description:
I have a documentation request: is it know or documented what is guaranteed about row order in sparklyr?  Correctly using a lot of code (such as even using `sdf_read_column()`) depends on the answer.

For R-local data (native data.frame, tibbles, and presumably data.table) row order is guaranteed preserved between operations (such as dplyr::mutate()).  For traditional database data sources (such as PostgreSQL) row order is not guaranteed and if the user wants such they must arrange by an explicit keyset.  

What is the answer for sparklyr and Spark?  And is their a referable document saying if row order is preserved or not?  Does it depend on the data source (maybe yes for Parquet files and Hive tables, and maybe no for others?).  Is order preserved on collect()?  I think it is critical to have a referable document that states what the guarantees are (else it is hard to tell if a lot of code is correct).

title: support for tryCatch() in spark_apply
description:
Hi,
For some purposes when I use `spark_apply` function, I would like to ignore errors and skip them in order to keep the code running for all groups of data. However, it seems that the `spark_apply` does not support `tryCatch()`  well...

First, I create some data and copy it to sc.
```r
> library(sparklyr)
> library(dplyr)
> library(data.table)
> spark_version <- "2.1.1"
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

> dat <- data.table(V1=rep(1:3,5), V2=rep(letters[1:3],5))[order(V1)]
> dat.sdf <- copy_to(sc, dat, overwrite = T)

10:  2  b
11:  3  c
12:  3  c
13:  3  c
14:  3  c
```

After that, when I use `tryCatch` in `spark_apply`,  it goes wrong...
```r
> spark_apply(dat.sdf, group_by = 'V2', f = function(g){
+   tryCatch({if(mean(g$V1)==2) stop("used for producing error") else 'OK!'}, 
+            error = function(e) 'Just skip the error!')
```

In fact, what I want is just like what `data.table` goes,
```r
> dat[, {
+   tryCatch({if(mean(V1)==2) stop("used for producing error") else 'OK!'}, 
+            error = function(e) 'Just skip the error!')

   V2                      V1
```

title: Investigate ghost sessions while launching `spark_connect`
description:
It is possible that `spark_connect` might leave an Spark application running; this usually involve error conditions while launching `spark_connect`, but users have reported reconnect failures since a Spark instance is already running in a bad state.

Most likely, there might be cases where the `sparklyr` backend does not terminate itself in some error conditions. There shouldn't be any code paths that leave the `sparklyr` backend alive after the r session ends.

We have a small Linux cluster running Cloudera CDH 5.10.0. When I try to do the spark_connect() from an R session started on a command line on the Hadoop cluster's name (master) node, I get the same msg as in an earlier CLOSED issue.  That is, my error msg is:

title: sparklyr::tally appears to count even when there is a column named n present
description:
sparklyr::tally appears to count even when there is a column named n present.

I think from the behavior on the local data frame and the `help(tally)` documentation it is supposed to sum the `n` column in this situation.

> tally() is a convenient wrapper for summarise that will either call n() or sum(n) depending on whether you're tallying for the first time, or re-tallying.

This is a _very_ low priority for me as I don't use `tally`.  Also this may be a [`dbplyr` issue](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3075).

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("dplyr"))
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.7.2.9000'
library("sparklyr")
packageVersion("sparklyr")
#> [1] '0.6.2'

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
#> * Using Spark: 2.1.0

dLocal <- data.frame(n = 1:3)
print(dLocal)
#>   n
#> 1 1

dRemote <- dplyr::copy_to(sc, dLocal)
print(dRemote)
#> # Source:   table<dLocal> [?? x 1]

spark_disconnect(sc)
```

title: Allow passing additional httr config parameters in livy_config
description:
Currently there is no way to control the behavior of the underlying `GET` and `POST` calls performed by `httr` when interacting with Livy. Only the headers are configurable:

```r
req <- GET(url,
             livy_get_httr_headers(config, list(
               "Content-Type" = "application/json"
             ))
...
req <- POST(paste(master, "sessions", sep = "/"),
              livy_get_httr_headers(config, list(
                "Content-Type" = "application/json"
              )),
              body = toJSON(
                data
              )
```

But no others parameters such as what certificate to use, which is a problem when interacting with self-signed certificates, which is the case for many private maintained clusters and dev enviroments.

Could `livy_get_httr_headers` be renamed to `livy_get_httr_config` and use this method to set the headers, configurations, options and such for httr?

We could use a prefix on `livy_config`, such as `livy.httr` to set up the different values on the `config` object

title: Add support for distributing/installing packages with `spark_apply`
description:
The following code works fine in a local installation:

```{r}
library(sparklyr)
library(stringr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)

iris_tbl %>% select("Species") %>% spark_apply(function(row) stringr::str_count(row, "a"))
```

```
# Source:   table<sparklyr_tmp_f89733580a95> [?? x 1]
# Database: spark_connection
   Species
     <int>
 1       1
 2       1
 3       1
 4       1
 5       1
 6       1
 7       1
 8       1
 9       1
10       1
# ... with 140 more rows
```

This also works fine under `master = "yarn-client"`, etc. as long as the cluster has the correct package versions installed; however, if the cluster lacks this package, execution will fail.

A possible workaround for some clusters/packages would be to check installation directly under the closure:

```{r}
iris_tbl %>% select("Species") %>% spark_apply(function(row) {
  if (!"stringr" %in% rownames(installed.packages())) install.packages("stringr")

  stringr::str_count(row, "a")
})
```

This is obviously not ideal and therefore, a better mechanism for distributing packages is necessary.

title: extracting column names from a spark data frame
description:
In base r, it is easy to extract the names of columns (variables) from a data frame

```
> testdf <- data.frame(a1 = rnorm(1e5), a2 = rnorm(1e5), a3 = rnorm(1e5), a4 = rnorm(1e5), a5 = rnorm(1e5), a6 = rnorm(1e5))  
> names(testdf)  
[1] "a1" "a2" "a3" "a4" "a5" "a6"
```

but while using sparklyr, things become more complicated. After copying the data frame to spark,

```
> testdf_tbl <- copy_to(sc, testdf, overwrite = TRUE)  
> names(testdf_tbl)  
[1] "src" "ops"
```

the variable names actually reside deep inside 'ops'

```
> testdf_tbl$ops$vars  
[1] "a1" "a2" "a3" "a4" "a5" "a6"
```

and if this were all, there would be no problems (and no need to ask this question). But, every time an operation happens on testdf_tbl, the names of the columns/variables change their position, as shown below..

```
> testdf_tbl <- testdf_tbl %>% select(-a1)  
> testdf_tbl$ops$vars  
NULL  
> testdf_tbl$ops$x$vars  
[1] "a1" "a2" "a3" "a4" "a5" "a6"  
```

performing another operation adds another $x to the path.. and so on.

```
> testdf_tbl <- testdf_tbl %>% select(-a2)  
> testdf_tbl$ops$x$vars  
NULL  
> testdf_tbl$ops$x$x$vars  
[1] "a1" "a2" "a3" "a4" "a5" "a6"  
```

To make matters worse, the list of variables does not reflect the select operations we have made,  a1, a2 are still listed as column names.

```
> head(testdf_tbl)
Source:   query [?? x 4]
Database: spark connection master=local[24] app=sparklyr local=TRUE

            a3           a4          a5         a6
         <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>
1 -1.146368875  1.691698406  0.43231629  1.3349111
2  0.664928710 -1.332242020  0.05380729  1.0139253
3  1.158095695 -0.097098980 -0.61885204  0.1504693
4  0.001595841 -0.003765908  0.27935192 -0.3039085
5 -0.133446040  0.269329076  1.57210274  1.7762602
6  0.006468698 -1.300439537  0.74057307  0.1320428
```

so clearly, the select operations have had an effect is terms of how the spark dataframe is used.

SURELY, there is/should be a simple, straightforward way to extract the current names of variables/columns in sparklyr, a la `names()` in base r.

title: include scala data files into compiled .jar
description:
Dear sparklyr-team

**Situation:** currently there seem to be no "sparklyr" way to include custom data files (on top of custom scala files) into the compiled .jar extension. I've looked into the code `spark_compile` and it seems to leave no room for adding other files than ***.scala under the "java" directory.

**Motivation:** My usecase is quite generic. I have a R functionality which relies on some data and to improve performance (especially memory), I want to port to the Scala side. In R it so lovely simple to package data together with your code. It would be glad to have this similarly easy when using Scala (through sparklyr).

**Work Around:** As one can link custom .jars to sparklyr, one current solution is to build an independent java .jar which contains all links to data. But this is cumbersome...

appreciating any listeners and thoughts,
best,
Stephan

title: Joins are not registering all columns in table
description:
Joins are not registering the second "by" column which prevents more than one join at a time, or joins inside of loops.

```r
spark_version <- "2.1.0"
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = spark_version)

x <- data.frame(a = c(NA,"b","b,","c"), b = 1:4) %>% copy_to(sc,.,'x')
y <- data.frame(c = c("a","b","b,",NA), d = 5:8) %>% copy_to(sc,.,'y')
z <- data.frame(e = c("a","b",NA,"c"), f = 9:12) %>% copy_to(sc,.,'z')

joined <- x %>% full_join(y, by = c("a" = "c"))

full_join(joined,z, by = c("c" = "e"))
```
Error: `by` can't contain join column `c` which is missing from LHS

```r
tbl_vars(joined)
```
[1] "a" "b" "d"
```r
tbl_vars( joined %>% collect() )
```
[1] "a" "b" "c" "d"

title: Set environment variables for `spark_apply()`
description:
Since Rscript requires to set environment variables like `RHOME` if Rscript is moved after installation. SparkR is able to set them as `--conf` options ([see also](https://www.continuum.io/blog/developer-blog/conda-spark)). If we have this function, we can use Parcel based installation of R.

I'm creating [R Parcel for CDH](https://github.com/chezou/cloudera-parcel) to run `spark_apply()` easily because CDH doesn't have R on worker nodes by default. 

I also tried to run following code, but `Rscript execution error: No such file or directory` error was returned. I guess [`ProcessBuilder` does not handle environment variables](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/cf0088d04f41f3fee361d9324e383dc1cad7d966/java/spark-1.6.0/rscript.scala#L35-L42) with this way.

```
library(sparklyr)

config <- spark_config()
config[["spark.r.command"]] <- paste(
  "R_HOME=/opt/cloudera/parcels/CONDAR/lib/conda-R/lib/R",
  "RHOME=/opt/cloudera/parcels/CONDAR/lib/conda-R",
  "R_SHARE_DIR=/opt/cloudera/parcels/CONDAR/lib/conda-R/lib/R/share",
  "R_INCLUDE_DIR=/opt/cloudera/parcels/CONDAR/lib/conda-R/lib/R/include",
  "/opt/cloudera/parcels/CONDAR/lib/conda-R/bin/Rscript",
  sep=" ")

sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-client", config = config)

sdf_len(sc, 5, repartition = 1) %>%
  spark_apply(function(e) I(e))
```

title: Classification prediction output
description:
Classification prediction output should be more user friendly.

Currently the output of `sdf_predict()` for classification models is very hard to work with. It should be possible for us to return something nicer, e.g. for multiclass we can have a `predict` column with predicted labels and a column for each label for probabilities.

Affected issues: 
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/907 - order of probabilities in output vector is confusing
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/928 - difficult to get predicted labels
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/762 - inconsistent prediction output column names
https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/605 - `ft_index_to_string()` doesn't behave as expected

title: Accuracy metric failing for Spark 1.6.0
description:
The `accuracy` metric in `ml_classification_eval` fails for Spark 1.6.0 but works for Spark 2.0.0. The accuracy metric does appear to be supported in Spark 1.6.0 see [here](https://spark.apache.org/docs/1.6.0/mllib-evaluation-metrics.html). Note that other metrics appear unaffected, like `f1`, which works for both versions of Spark. Example below.

```
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "1.6.0") # works for 2.0.0
titanic <- data.frame(Titanic, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
titanic_tbl <- copy_to(sc, titanic, overwrite = TRUE)
ml_fit <- ml_logistic_regression(titanic_tbl, Survived ~ .)
ml_pred <- sdf_predict(ml_fit, titanic_tbl)
ml_pred <- mutate(ml_pred, actual = ifelse(Survived == "No", 1L, 0L))
ml_classification_eval(ml_pred, "actual", "prediction", "accuracy") # works for "f1"
```
